Pillar Nine: Language Shapes What's Possible

← Pillar Eight: The Past Doesn't Go Away · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Ten: The Sacred is Here →

Pillar: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible · Across every book

Or, Why Grammatical Rebellion Can Set You Free

Words are never just neutral tools for describing the world. Marguerite Young used language as the very brick and mortar we use to build reality, and changing how we talk is a vital political act.

We dug deep into sedimentary time, exploring how the past is never truly behind us but rather accumulated right beneath our feet like layers of rock. Now we arrive at a crucial question: how do we talk about what we discover? What language do we use when we dig into the sediment? And does the language we have been given even allow us to tell the truth?

We tend to think of language as a neutral delivery truck. We imagine that facts and thoughts exist perfectly formed inside our heads, and we simply use words as a vehicle to ship those ideas over to someone else. We assume that standard grammar is just a set of harmless rules designed to keep our speech orderly and clear. We use language without thinking about it, as if the words are transparent and we can look right through them to the reality beneath.

But Marguerite Young steps in to show us that language is never neutral. It is not a transparent window. It is the active medium in which our reality is built, argued over, and either honored or betrayed. The grammar we use is not innocent. The words we choose are not arbitrary. The sentence structures we inherit carry an entire philosophy of what the world is and what is possible. Change the language, and you change what people can think.

The Trap of the Noun

To explain this pillar, the text connects Young's writing with the experimental insights of author Gertrude Stein. Stein spent her entire career proving that standard English grammar comes pre-packaged with massive assumptions about how the universe works.

Think about how standard sentences are set up: the primary building block of English grammar is the noun. Nouns represent solid, unchanging things or people. A noun sits there. It has identity. It has definition. A woman is a noun. A building is a noun. A nation is a noun. Verbs, on the other hand, are treated as secondary. They are just the actions that happen to or between those solid nouns. The woman does something. The building stands. The nation acts. In this grammatical structure, the verbs are servants of the nouns. The actions are less important than the things.

This structural setup quietly trains our brains to believe that the world is made of fixed, permanent objects that hold perfectly still. It makes us think that there are things that have stable identity, the noun, and then there are the temporary actions that happen to those things, the verb. This is a profound metaphysical claim. It is a claim about what exists and what is real. And it is built right into our grammar.

Authoritarian systems absolutely love this noun-heavy mindset. They rely heavily on a rigid grammar of control, using flat, simplified labels to categorize human beings. In the grammar of dominant political theories, you are required to be a unified, predictable agent: a single, solid noun. You are a woman or a man. You are a worker or a boss. You are a citizen or a criminal. You are loyal or disloyal. If your identity is complex, shifting, or does not fit into their pre-made bins, standard political language simply erases you from the conversation. The language cannot hold you. You become unspeakable.

Young combats this linguistic trap by turning her writing into a magnificent grammatical rebellion. She refuses to work in the grammar of nouns and passive verbs. Instead, she builds a grammar of process and becoming.

She writes in verbs. Her prose treats the self and the world as an ongoing process of becoming rather than a collection of static things. People are not fixed identities. They are processes. They are movements. They are verbs. Instead of describing what someone is, Young describes what they are doing, what they are becoming, what they are in the middle of. The sentence does not settle. It keeps moving.

She embraces the loop. The sentences in her book are famously long, circular, and packed with layers, resisting the pressure to settle into easy, simplified answers. A sentence in her novel might go on for a page, looping back on itself, adding new material, revising what it just said, refusing to arrive at a final meaning. The form enacts the philosophy. The endless sentence is a refusal to be finished, to be reduced, to be simplified into a single meaning.

She gives voice to the erased. By breaking traditional sentence structures, she constructs a fresh grammar capable of holding the full, messy truth of our inner multitudes. She finds a way to write about complexity that standard grammar could not contain. She finds a way to make the unspeakable speakable.

Stein did similar work in her poetry and essays. She wrote phrases like a rose is a rose is a rose, not as a celebration of fixed identity but as an investigation into how meaning changes each time we speak it. The rose is not a noun with a fixed definition. Each time you say rose, you are creating a new meaning. The repetition is not stale. It is generative. It is fresh.

The Danger of Speaking from Nowhere

Propaganda thrives when leaders pretend to speak from nowhere. When an authoritarian figure claims to speak with absolute, objective, universal authority, they are using that pretense as a tool of total domination. They are claiming that what they are saying is not a perspective. It is not a partial point of view. It is truth itself. It is objective reality. It has no location. It is not spoken by anyone. It is simply true.

Young's philosophy demands that we pull our language back down to earth. She insists that all speech is located. All speech comes from a body. All speech comes from a specific moment and a specific place. True accountability happens when we explicitly name our location, acknowledge that our perspectives are partial, and build our speech from the honest ground where we are actually standing.

When a writer or a leader says I am speaking from here, from this place, from this position, with these limitations, they are disarming the propaganda machine. They are saying: I do not claim to speak for everyone. I am not objective. I am not detached. What I am saying is rooted in where I stand. And you get to decide whether what I am saying resonates with where you stand.

Young's own stories do not pretend to be detached or universal. They are deeply rooted in the specific. The narrator of her novel is a specific woman, living in a specific place, shaped by specific relationships. The reader always knows where the speaker is standing. The reader always understands that this is one perspective, one location, one partial view. This honesty about location is what allows the complexity to breathe. Because the reader is not being asked to accept one universal truth. They are being invited into a specific location and asked to witness what is visible from there.

When we keep our language flexible, grounded, and honest about its own location, we destroy the machine's ability to manipulate our thoughts. A person who has learned to ask where is this speaker standing is a person who cannot be hypnotized by propaganda. They can never again accept a claim to speak from nowhere, to speak with absolute authority, to speak for everyone.

The Body That Speaks: Adrienne Rich

To understand what located speech actually costs and what it makes possible, consider Adrienne Rich, who spent the first decade of her career writing in a language that was not quite hers and the rest of it figuring out why.

Rich began publishing poetry in the early 1950s. Her first book won the Yale Younger Poets prize. The poems were technically accomplished, carefully measured, formally correct. W.H. Auden selected the manuscript and praised its craft. By every standard the literary establishment recognized, she had arrived.

But Rich knew something was wrong with those early poems. She could feel it. The language was elegant and controlled, and it was also, she later wrote, a performance of detachment she did not actually feel. She was writing in the voice of no one in particular, from nowhere specific, in the tradition of a literary culture that had been built largely by men who treated the universal as their natural inheritance. She had learned to speak from nowhere because nowhere was what the tradition rewarded. A woman who spoke from her specific body, her specific life, her specific location as a woman in a particular marriage in a particular era in a particular country, was not writing literature. She was writing confession, or complaint, or something lesser.

It took her years to understand that the nowhere voice was not neutral. It was a costume. And wearing it had cost her something she needed back.

When she started writing the poems that would become Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law in the late 1950s, she began, haltingly, to speak from somewhere. From the specific experience of being a woman in a culture that had plans for her that she had not made herself. The poems were messier than her early work. Less polished. More uncomfortable. The literary establishment was not entirely pleased. The universal had been interrupted by the particular, and the particular, when it is a woman's body and a woman's fury, tends to make people nervous.

She kept going. By the time she wrote Diving into the Wreck in 1973 and Of Woman Born in 1976, she had rebuilt her practice from the ground up. She was writing from her body, from her history, from her specific location as a woman and eventually as a lesbian, from the sediment of everything that had shaped her. The language she made from that location was not smaller than the nowhere language she had started with. It was larger. It was more honest. It had more grip.

Her essay "Notes Toward a Politics of Location," written in 1984, named what she had been doing all along. She argued that all knowledge is embodied, that all speech comes from somewhere, that the claim to speak from nowhere is not neutrality but a specific kind of power move, available mainly to those whose location the culture has decided to treat as the default human position. When a white Western man speaks from "the universal," he is not transcending his location. He is hiding it. He is using the privilege of his position to make his particular view appear to have no view at all.

Rich's insistence on located speech was not a retreat into the personal. It was an expansion of what counts as political. The body is political. The household is political. The specific history of a specific woman in a specific place is political. To speak from there, honestly and without apology, is to refuse the nowhere voice that power depends on. It is to say: I am not speaking for everyone. I am speaking from here. And from here, I can see things the nowhere voice cannot see and will not name.

A person who has learned to ask where is this speaker standing cannot be captured by propaganda that claims to speak from nowhere. A political system that insists on located speech, that names its interests and its position and its partial view, is a system that can be held accountable. It cannot hide behind the claim of universal truth. It is always a someone, standing somewhere, making choices that could have been made differently. That accountability is exactly what power tries to avoid, and exactly what Rich spent her life making impossible to avoid.

The Practice

Notice when you use totalizing, flat words to describe yourself or the people around you. Labels like I am a failure, or they are just lazy. These are nouns, fixed identities, simplified categories. Catch those rigid nouns and try replacing them with active, located verbs instead.

Instead of a fixed label, describe the specific, messy process of what is happening right now in your unique corner of the world. Instead of I am a failure, try I have not yet figured this out, or I am learning how to do this, or this particular thing did not work and I am adjusting. Instead of they are lazy, try they are tired, or they are struggling with something I do not fully understand, or their values around work are different from mine.

Pay attention to the way these grammatical shifts change what becomes possible to think. When you speak in verbs instead of nouns, suddenly people become complex again. They become alive. They become changeable. They become human instead of fixed categories.

Also notice when language is being used to hide location. When a politician or a news anchor speaks as if they are stating objective facts from nowhere, pause. Remember Rich's politics of location. Ask: where is this person standing? What is their interest? What location are they speaking from? What are they not naming about their own position?

And pay attention to where you are standing when you speak. Try beginning sentences with a location: from where I sit, in my experience, from what I have seen, in this particular place. This honesty about location does not weaken your argument. It strengthens it. It makes it possible to listen to you, because you are not claiming to speak for everyone. You are claiming to speak truthfully from where you are.

Chapter 6: Why Facts Aren't Enough

← Chapter 5: The Machine That Knows You · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 7: The Machine That Speaks for You →

"What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion?"

Here is a scene that has played out at a thousand kitchen tables and Thanksgiving dinners across the last decade. Someone you love says something that is verifiably, documentably false. You know it is false. You have the sources. You pull out your phone, you read the correction aloud, you show them the data, and you watch something harden in their face that was not there before. They don't change their mind. They dig in. The argument ends worse than it started, and the false belief is now more entrenched than it was before you opened your mouth.

This is not a failure of your delivery. It is a documented phenomenon. And it tells you something fundamental about how control systems actually work.

In 2012, researchers at Dartmouth, Georgia State, and Duke published a study on the "death panel" claim, the assertion made by Sarah Palin in 2009 that the Affordable Care Act would create government boards empowered to decide whether elderly people were worthy of medical care. PolitiFact named it Lie of the Year. It was examined and debunked by independent health care experts, fact-checkers, physicians, and members of both political parties. There was nothing in the legislation resembling a death panel. The researchers wanted to know whether more aggressive fact-checking could correct the belief.

They divided participants into two groups. One read a news article reporting Palin's claim. The other read the same article with an additional paragraph stating that nonpartisan health care experts had concluded she was wrong. Then they measured belief in death panels.

Among high-knowledge respondents with very positive feelings toward Palin, corrective information about death panels made misperceptions worse and opposition to the ACA stronger. The researchers called this the backfire effect: the finding that corrective information, delivered to people with strong prior beliefs, tended to shift how they interpreted the evidence rather than what they believed. Subsequent research has complicated the picture. Later studies, including follow-up work by Nyhan and Reifler themselves, largely failed to replicate the effect at scale, but the underlying dynamic the original study identified remains well-documented: motivated reasoning is real, and facts alone do not reliably dislodge identity-linked beliefs.

The more politically informed the person, the more effectively they used their knowledge to dismiss the correction and protect the belief. Intelligence, in this context, is not a defense against misinformation. It is a more sophisticated weapon for defending against the truth.

This is why every high-control system works the same way: it does not win people through argument. It wins them through identity. The death panel was not, at its core, a factual claim about legislation. It was an emotional claim about the relationship between the federal government and ordinary people's lives, about whether institutions could be trusted, about who had the power to decide when a person's life was worth sustaining. Those are not questions a fact-checker can answer. They are questions that go to the bone.

When you arrive at the table with your phone and your sources, you are answering a factual question that was never actually being asked. The person across from you is not, at their core, confused about policy details. They are afraid. They are angry. They feel invisible to institutions that have failed them. The demagogue, the cult leader, and the abuser all understand this. They do not offer information. They offer recognition. They say: your fear is real, your anger is justified, I see you, and here is the enemy responsible for your pain.

You cannot counter that with a paragraph from a nonpartisan expert. The expert is part of the system the person has already decided not to trust. Your correction does not land as information. It lands as an attack from the wrong side.

One political scientist noted that the death panel myth played a role in Democrats losing control of the public debate because they failed to address the underlying fears of big government that the myth was expressing. The facts were correct. The response was wrong. Correcting the claim without addressing the fear that animated it left the fear in place, now further confirmed by the fact that the other side cared more about defending the legislation than understanding the anxiety.

This does not mean abandoning truth. It means understanding what truth is actually competing against. A factual correction competes against a story that is meeting an emotional need. The correction wins only if it can meet that need better than the story does. That requires a different kind of engagement entirely.

Stop arguing about what is true. Start asking how they came to believe it. Ask what the belief gives them. Ask what they would need to see, specifically, to reconsider. Not to trap them. To understand what is actually at stake for them in holding the belief. Most of the time, underneath the specific false claim, there is a legitimate grievance, a real experience of being lied to by institutions, of watching promises fail, of feeling that the people making decisions about their lives do not know or care that they exist.

That grievance deserves acknowledgment before it deserves correction. Acknowledgment is not agreement. It is not surrender. It is the prerequisite for any conversation that has a chance of going somewhere.

The person you are trying to reach did not arrive at their position through logic. They arrived through experience, through belonging, through the particular story that made sense of their particular pain. You will not argue them out of it. But you might, if you are patient and honest and willing to be changed yourself, tell them a truer story.

This is harder than it sounds, and it is worth being honest about that. Telling a truer story requires you to be genuinely open to having your own story complicated in the process. The person across the table is not simply a vessel of misinformation waiting to be corrected. They are a person who has had experiences that led them to the position they hold. Some of those experiences are probably legitimate. Some of the institutions whose authority you are implicitly defending when you arrive with your sources have probably, at some point, failed that person or someone they love.

The pharmaceutical company that told a community its water was safe when it was not. The doctor who dismissed a patient's symptoms for years before a serious diagnosis arrived too late. The government agency that promised a benefit and delivered a bureaucratic maze. These are not conspiracy theories. They are documented failures, and they are part of the emotional landscape of the person you are trying to reach. If you want to tell a truer story, you have to include those failures in it. You have to be willing to say: yes, institutions have lied, yes, the system has failed people like you, yes, the anger is earned. And then: the specific claim being made right now is still not accurate, and here is why it matters.

That kind of conversation is not a debate. It is closer to what therapists call motivational interviewing: a process of genuine curiosity about how someone arrived at their current position, combined with honest reflection on where the position leads. It is slow. It rarely produces a dramatic conversion in a single exchange. What it produces, over time, is a relationship in which the other person does not experience you as an enemy of their intelligence, and in which honest disagreement is possible because trust has been established.

Most of us will not manage this perfectly. We will lose patience. We will reach for the phone and the sources when the frustration peaks. That is human. The goal is not perfection. The goal is to become incrementally more effective at the kind of engagement that actually opens something, rather than the kind that closes it.

One last thing on this. There will be people you cannot reach. There are positions so deeply integrated into a person's identity, so thoroughly supported by their community, so central to how they explain their own life to themselves, that no conversation you have with them will dislodge the belief in any timeframe you can observe. That is not a reason to give up on everyone. It is a reason to be honest with yourself about where your energy is best spent, and to prioritize the people who are still in the process of forming their positions over those who have already sealed them. The edge is where the work happens. The interior is for the long game, and the long game requires patience that most of us have to consciously practice.

The action: The next time you feel the urge to correct someone with facts, pause and ask one question first: what would it cost this person to be wrong? Not intellectually. Personally. What belonging, what identity, what explanation for their own suffering would they lose if the belief turned out to be false? Sit with that question before you speak. The answer will tell you whether you are about to have a conversation or a collision.

Longing 8: The Past Doesn't Go Away

← Longing 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 9: Language Shapes What's Possible →

Pillar: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away · Across every book

or On the two lies about time, and the layered truth that holds you steady against both.

There are two ways to lie about time, and power uses whichever one is nearer to hand. The first lie is the golden past. There was an age when things were whole and pure and good, and it was taken from you, and it can be restored if you follow. The second lie is the clean break. The past is rot, the slate can be wiped, and a new and purified people can begin at year zero with nothing behind them. Nostalgia and revolution look like opposites. They are the same falsehood about time, one facing backward and one facing forward, both promising that the layered, complicated, unromantic past can be either recovered or erased.

Young does not believe in either. Her novel is saturated with the past, but the past in it never recedes and never returns clean. It presses upward through everything, through the mother’s memories and the narrator’s search and the inherited griefs nobody chose. Time in her work is not a road you travel away from or back along. It is sediment. It accumulates. You stand on all of it at once.

The eighth pillar is this sedimentary time. The past is real and it is present, but as accumulation, not as a paradise to recover and not as a slate to clear. You carry all of it, the good and the shameful and the plain, layered in you, without gilding it and without pretending you can start fresh. And that steadies you against both lies. The man selling the golden age cannot move you, because you know the past was never golden. The man selling year zero cannot move you either, because you know the past does not wipe. It only buries, and it buries shallow.

You are made of what came before, all of it, unedited. That is not a cage, and it is not a sin to be cleansed. It is simply the ground you happen to be standing on, and the only honest thing to do with ground is to know what is under your feet.

Pillar Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

← Pillar Four: Witnessing is the Core Ethical Act · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Six: Unfinished is Honest →

Pillar: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Across every book

Or, Why Building Without a Blueprint is True Integrity

When there is no permanent foundation, why do we bother making anything at all? Marguerite Young shares a radical secret: the making itself is the whole point.

This far along, it is reasonable to pause here and ask a tough question: if there is no solid bedrock, no final destination, and no unshakeable foundation that holds, then what on earth is the point of building anything at all? Why write a book, start a relationship, launch a community project, or fight for a better world if everything is provisional?

Young's answer is Pillar Five, and it is the most quietly liberating thing her entire system contains: You build anyway.

The Beauty of the Loop

Young's principle is "recursive construction". The word recursive means a process that loops back into itself. It means using what you just experienced to inform what you do next, returning to your starting point over and over again, not to repeat your mistakes, but to find something brand new that you missed the first time around.

In Young's world, you do not build something once and then stand back to admire it forever. Instead, you create something, and the very act of making it reveals a truth you did not know when you started. So, you build again, incorporating what you just learned. Then that creation teaches you something else, and you loop back to adjust once more.

Under this pillar, life is not a static object: it is a process. The self is a verb, not a noun. The ultimate secret of this philosophy is that the value of your life does not live in the finished product, which is always going to be temporary and imperfect anyway. The making is the entire point.

This position argues that keeping your creations open, provisional, and under constant revision is not a failure. It is the only form of true integrity the world allows.

Why Tyrants Fear an Unfinished Structure

This brings us right back to our ultimate goal: jamming the authoritarian playbook.

Fascism and authoritarian systems big and small are obsessed with the fantasy of a permanent arrival. Dictators love to promise a flawless, permanent, final blueprint for a perfect society. They want to build structures that are frozen, where the rules can never change, the power can never be questioned, and the social hierarchy is locked in place forever.

When we embrace recursive construction, we shatter that entire trap.

We reject the frozen blueprint: By treating our communities, our rules, and our organizations as provisional projects, we ensure they can never be permanently frozen into tools of tyranny.

We build flexibility into the design: When an institution explicitly acknowledges that it is unfinished, it leaves the door wide open for ongoing revision and growth.

We normalize starting over: Authoritarian systems treat mistakes as crimes or signs of weakness. Young's pillar reminds us that looping back to correct our course is the natural, honest state of human progress.

A community that is always willing to look at its own setup, return to the beginning, and rebuild based on fresh insight is a community that a tyrant can never truly capture.

The Art of Permanent Revision: The Bauhaus

To understand what building provisionally actually looks like, it helps to look at a place where an entire school and philosophy was built on the principle that design is not about arriving at a perfect answer, but about staying in the process of asking better questions.

The Bauhaus was founded in 1919 in Weimar, Germany, as a school of art, architecture, and design. But it was not a school that had a fixed curriculum waiting to be taught. Instead, it was built on a radical principle: the process of making teaches you what you need to know. You learn by building. You revise based on what the materials tell you. You loop back and try again.

Walter Gropius, the founder, insisted that there was no such thing as a finished design waiting to be discovered. Instead, designers had to stay in an ongoing conversation between idea and material, between intention and reality. You make something, and the world tells you what needs to change. Then you build again.

The teachers at the Bauhaus, people like Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, László Moholy-Nagy, and Josef Albers, were not delivering a fixed body of knowledge. They were modeling a way of thinking: stay curious, stay open, keep making, keep learning from what you make. Klee taught that you learn to draw by drawing, not by memorizing rules. Kandinsky taught that color and form teach you about themselves only when you work with them directly. The entire school was organized around the principle that understanding comes through doing, and doing reveals what you need to understand next.

This approach to design was revolutionary. It rejected the idea that there was a perfect style, a correct answer, an arrival point where you could stop learning. Instead, it insisted that the work was the thing: the constant looping back, the revision, the willingness to fail and try again. Every student who came through the Bauhaus learned not a fixed set of aesthetic rules but a way of being in relation to making: stay awake, stay responsive, let the work teach you.

The Bauhaus produced an enormous amount of work: buildings, furniture, textiles, typography, posters, paintings. And all of it carried the mark of this philosophy: nothing was fixed. Everything was provisional. Everything invited revision and reinvention. The forms looked modern and forward-looking not because they had arrived at the future, but because they refused to settle into the past. They stayed in motion.

Then fascism came to Germany. And one of the first things the Nazi regime did was close the Bauhaus down.

This was not accidental. The Nazis understood something crucial: a school that teaches you to stay in process, to question, to revise, to refuse fixed answers, is a school that produces people who cannot be controlled by a fixed ideology. A person who has learned to think by making, to revise by looking at what actually works, to refuse false certainty, is a person who will never accept a dictator's fixed blueprint for the perfect society.

The Bauhaus had to be destroyed because recursive construction is the antithesis of totalitarianism. A regime that demands frozen rules, permanent hierarchy, and the absolute refusal to revise cannot tolerate a school built on the principle that everything is provisional and under constant revision.

The closing of the Bauhaus is one of history's clearest lessons: when you see a regime attack the places where people are learning to make things provisionally, to ask their own questions, to revise and build again, you are witnessing an attack on freedom itself. Because the capacity to keep building, to keep learning from what you make, to refuse to accept someone else's fixed blueprint, is what keeps you free.

The Practice

Identify one area of your life where you are paralyzed by the need to get it perfectly "right" or "finished" on the very first try. It could be a creative project, a difficult conversation, or a new habit. It could be a relationship or a community you are trying to build. It could be a vision you have for how you want to live.

Take the pressure off by telling yourself: This is provisional. Build a messy, imperfect first version of it today, knowing that you are going to loop back later to learn from it and adjust. Give yourself permission to live as a verb, not a noun.

Notice also when external systems try to pressure you into accepting their fixed blueprints as final. Notice when you are told "that is just how things are" or "it has always been this way" or "there is no alternative." Remind yourself: someone built this. It is a construction. It can be questioned, revised, rebuilt. You are not required to accept someone else's blueprint as your only option.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Across every book

What have you been calling natural that was actually built by someone?

The hunger is for the given order, the arrangement you did not build and need not question. Power loves the appeal to how things have always been. This pillar says it was all made, and what was made was made by hands like yours. That returns the dizziness of responsibility, but also the possibility of building it otherwise.

Notice

Notice one rule or arrangement in your life, at work, in your family, in your culture, that you have quietly treated as just how things are. Sit with the discomfort of asking who actually decided it.

Practice

Pick one thing you have called natural and trace its actual history. Who built it, when, and for what reason. You do not need a full research project, a rough sketch is enough to see that it was a decision, not a fact of nature.

Reflection

What would it take to build this arrangement differently?

Who benefits from this arrangement staying invisible, as though nobody made it?

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

← Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here →

Pillar: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible · Across every book

What slogan have you repeated lately without checking what it was doing to your thinking?

The hunger is for the word that settles everything, the slogan that ends the thought. Propaganda renames things and repeats a phrase until a false world closes over the real one. This pillar knows that language builds the world, and it stays accountable to what it is building. The open sentence is where you are still allowed to think.

Notice

Catch a slogan or phrase, personal or political, that you have repeated recently without examining it. It might be about yourself, a group of people, or a situation.

Practice

Rewrite that phrase in slower, plainer language. Let it get longer and more qualified. Resist the urge to land on a new, tidier version. Let the sentence stay open.

Reflection

What did the slogan let you avoid feeling or thinking about?

What changed when you gave the same idea room to be complicated?
creative-05-08-pillar-7-the-margins-reve:
Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away →

Pillar: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · Across every book

Who did you file as background today, and what did that cost them in your mind?

The hunger is to be at the center, to matter, and underneath that, to look down on whoever is not. Power builds a center and a margin and trades you a place in the center for your contempt toward the edge. This pillar grants full being to the marginal, so the machine of center and enemy loses its grip.

Notice

Name one person you passed today who felt like background, a cashier, someone on the street, a coworker whose name you do not know. Notice how quickly you filed them as minor.

Practice

Write a short paragraph imagining that person's actual day, with the same seriousness you would give a main character in a story. Give them a history, a worry, a person who loves them.

Reflection

Where do you place yourself, center or edge, in most of your daily thinking?

Whose contempt does that placement quietly require of you?
creative-02-03-chapter-3-reality-distort:
Chapter 3: Reality Distortions

← Chapter 2: The Logic of the Zealot · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 4: The Closed Loop →

"The illusion was the only reality, and our self-deception was the only rose."

The most effective form of control doesn't put you in a cage. It makes you build one yourself, because it has convinced you that the walls are not there.

Before a system can dictate your behavior, it has to dismantle your confidence in your own perception. This is not a metaphor. It is a documented, repeatable process. It works on individuals, on families, on congregations of thousands, and on entire nations. The mechanism is the same at every scale: deny what the person saw, replace it with an authorized version, and repeat until the person's own memory becomes the enemy.

We call this gaslighting, a word that has been softened by overuse. The clinical reality is harder. When your perception of events is systematically contradicted by an authority you have been taught to trust, your brain does not simply decide who is right. It experiences the contradiction as a threat to survival. We are social animals. To be told that what we saw did not happen, by someone with institutional power over us, registers in the nervous system as isolation. Isolation, historically, means death. The brain will rewrite its own memories to avoid that outcome. It will choose the authorized version not because it is true but because agreeing is the only way to stay inside the room.

This is not stupidity. This is the mind doing exactly what it evolved to do. And it is exactly what abusers, cults, and institutions count on.

The Pennsylvania grand jury report released in August 2018 is one of the most thorough public records of institutional gaslighting in American history. Over two years, investigators examined more than half a million internal Catholic Church documents across six dioceses and interviewed dozens of witnesses. The report documented credible abuse allegations against more than 300 priests, with identifiable victims exceeding 1,000 over a period of 70 years. What the report made visible was not just the abuse. It was the architecture built to make victims doubt themselves.

Church officials consistently used euphemisms like "boundary issues" to describe assaults. The grand jury concluded that diocesan leadership had constructed what it called "a playbook for concealing the truth." Tactics included reassigning accused priests to new parishes without explanation, leaning on local law enforcement to drop investigations, and framing the abuse in language so mild that victims who came forward were left without words to describe what had been done to them. One victim, quoted in reporting on the grand jury, asked the question that the entire system was designed to produce: "Who would have believed me? A priest, in 1948?"

That question is the system working as intended. The victim is not asking whether it happened. The victim already knows it happened. The victim is asking whether his own testimony has the right to exist in the same room as institutional authority. The answer the Church spent seventy years delivering was: it does not.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Josh Shapiro named the pattern directly: abuse, deny, cover up. The cover-up was not incidental to the institution. It was, as the grand jury found, sophisticated, coordinated across dioceses, and extended to the Vatican. The files were kept in what the Church called its "secret archives," with the bishop holding the only key.

This is what institutional gaslighting looks like when the documents survive. Most of the time they don't. Most of the time the person sitting across from an authority figure with no paper trail has only their own memory, which the system has already spent months or years teaching them not to trust.

The political version requires no secret archive. It happens in full public view. Donald Trump's claim that the crowd at his 2017 inauguration was the largest in history, contradicted immediately by aerial photographs, by Metro ridership data, and by the testimony of anyone present, was not a mistake. It was a test. The question being posed was not factual. It was hierarchical: whose account of reality gets to stand? When administration officials appeared on television the following day to describe the photographs as showing "alternative facts," the gaslighting was complete. The goal was never to convince anyone that the crowd was large. The goal was to demonstrate that the authorized version did not require evidence to displace the one you saw with your own eyes.

Populations that learn to accept this trade, their perception for the leader's version, become manageable in ways that populations anchored in shared reality do not.

The action: Keep a record the system cannot edit. When something happens that contradicts the authorized version, write it down immediately: what you saw, what was said, the date, any witnesses. Not for a confrontation. Not as evidence in an argument you are planning to have. Write it down for yourself, so that when the authorized version comes for your memory, you have a document in your own handwriting that says: this is what I saw. Your perception is not a democracy. It does not require a majority vote to be valid.
creative-03-03-pillar-three-grief-doesnt:
Pillar Three: Grief Doesn't End

← Pillar Two: Reality is Constructed · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Four: Witnessing is the Core Ethical Act →

Pillar: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End · Across every book

Or, Why Refusing to "Get Over It" Disrupts the System

We are constantly told that healing means moving on. Marguerite Young says grief is our permanent weather, and carrying it honestly is a profound act of political resistance.

We live in a society that treats grief like a temporary illness. We are told there is a neat little roadmap with stages: you deny it, you get angry, you bargain, you feel depressed, and finally, you arrive at "acceptance". The goal is always to get through it so your life can resume its forward motion. We tend to view grief as a passing storm, and if someone is still mourning years later, mainstream culture often worries that they are stuck, broken, or failing to heal.

But Marguerite Young says this story we tell about grief is a false comfort. In her system, grief isn't a temporary season: it is the climate.

The Climate of Loss

Young argues that grief is the permanent atmospheric condition of our world. Why? Because we live in a reality where everything we love is always already changing, the people we need are absent, and nothing holds still.

Young doesn't see this accumulation as a sickness. She sees it as the only honest response to an irreplaceable loss. To fully "get over" something means deciding it was replaceable, which Young finds dishonest. Grief doesn't diminish you: it gives you depth and education that you cannot acquire any other way.

Disrupting the Forced Performance of Recovery

So, how does carrying our sorrow permanently push back against authoritarian control?

Authoritarian systems pull off a massive "long con" by demanding a clean, shiny narrative of national triumph, quick recovery, and constant progress. Dictatorships love to hide the structural violence their power is built upon: the historical theft of land, centuries of exploitation, and the systematic exclusion of human beings. To keep the illusion going, the system forces a performance of recovery. It asks its most damaged people to demonstrate resilience, move on, and act like everything has been resolved.

When we practice honest grief, we directly jam that propaganda machine.

We refuse to look away: By staying in the room with our losses, we refuse to replace our genuine pain with a shallow performance of recovery.

We keep history present: Honest grief tells us that the past isn't safely behind us, but right beneath our feet, forcing us to reckon with the historical layers that still press down on the present landscape.

We demand public honesty: A politics built on this pillar avoids the fantasy of an ideological arrival, opting instead to build structures for ongoing, collective acknowledgment of what has been broken.

By refusing to wrap up our sorrow in a tidy political bow, we remain anchored in what is real, rendering us immune to the false promises of leaders who try to sweep historical harms under the rug.

The Weight of Refusal: The Madres de Plaza de Mayo

There are moments in history when the act of continuing to grieve becomes the most dangerous form of resistance a person can offer.

During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, approximately 30,000 people disappeared. They were not executed publicly, where their deaths could be witnessed and mourned. They were taken from their families, their fates unknown. The regime's strategy was deliberate: create uncertainty, deny everything, make the disappeared unspeakable. Then, demand that the families move on.

The mothers of these disappeared people refused.

Every week, the Madres de Plaza de Mayo gathered in the plaza in front of the presidential palace in Buenos Aires. They wore white headscarves embroidered with the names of their disappeared children. They did not perform acceptance or recovery. They held photographs. They called out names. They stood in public, in their grief, refusing the regime's demand that they forget, move on, and let the violence become invisible.

The regime hated this. They tried to scatter the mothers with violence. They tried to discredit them as hysterical and stuck. They tried to offer them compensation, as if money could replace a child or fill the space where a human being used to be. The official message was clear: healing means moving on. Get over it. Stop making trouble.

But the mothers understood something that Young teaches: grief that refuses to resolve is not a personal failure. It is a form of testimony. It is a way of saying: this loss is permanent. This person mattered. This violence was real. We will not pretend it didn't happen so you can feel comfortable. We will not replace our sorrow with a false narrative of recovery. We will stand here, week after week, in our unhealed grief, and we will make it impossible for the world to forget.

Their refusal to move on, to perform recovery, to treat their children as replaceable by time or compensation, became the most powerful form of resistance to the dictatorship. Because they would not allow the violence to become history, it remained news. It remained real. Their permanent grief forced everyone around them to reckon with what had been taken.

After the dictatorship fell, many of the disappeared were never found. The grief did not resolve into closure. The mothers continued to gather. Decades later, they are still there. This is not a failure of healing. This is integrity. This is the refusal to lie about what has been lost.

Young would recognize them immediately. They understand that grief is not a problem to be solved but a permanent condition of honoring what was irreplaceable. Their refusal to get over it is what kept the disappeared from becoming truly gone. It kept the violence from disappearing into official forgetting.

The Deeper Work

Honest grief does not mean wallowing or being stuck in despair. It means acknowledging that what was lost cannot be replaced, and that carrying that knowledge changes you forever. A society built on this pillar does not pretend to quick fixes. It does not ask its most damaged people to perform resilience for the comfort of those in power. It builds institutions for ongoing acknowledgment. It holds space for permanent sorrow alongside the work of continuing to live.

This is the grief Young writes into her work. The characters in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling do not recover from their losses. They carry them. They integrate them. They learn to live in a world that will never be whole again. And from that integration, something real becomes possible: not false hope, but actual clarity about what matters and what does not.

The Practice

Give yourself permission to stop trying to "fix" your old sadness. If a wave of grief for a person, a past version of yourself, or a collective loss hits you, do not treat it like a step backward. Let it be the weather. Remind yourself that carrying that sorrow honestly is not a weakness: it is a form of collective integrity.

Notice when you are pressured to perform recovery: by your workplace, your family, your social circle, or the larger culture. Notice the subtle message that moving on is what mature, healthy people do. Pause, and ask yourself: is this my grief asking to be put away, or is someone else asking me to put it away for their comfort?

If it is the latter, you can refuse. You can hold your sorrow openly. You can be the person who remembers, who speaks the name, who refuses to let what was lost become invisible. That is not pathology. That is love. That is resistance.
creative-02-04-chapter-4-the-closed-loop:
Chapter 4: The Closed Loop

← Chapter 3: Reality Distortions · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 5: The Machine That Knows You →

"Anything which was worth happening at all was worth happening twice: that nothing which happened once was real."

The present moment is the only place where you can act. It is also the first thing a control system takes from you.

Before a demagogue can own your future, before an abuser can extract your compliance, before a cult can have your savings and your passport, it must make the present unlivable. It does this by filling the air with phantom timelines: a catastrophe that is always arriving but never quite here, a golden future that is always just within reach, a debt from the past that is never fully paid. While you are navigating these invented timelines, you are not looking at what is actually happening in the room.

This is the closed loop. Past and future weaponized together, crushing the present between them, until you surrender your agency now in exchange for a safety that never comes.

Jim Jones founded Peoples Temple in Indianapolis in 1955. In 1961, he announced a vision: nuclear war was imminent. He told his congregation that the world would be engulfed by nuclear war on July 15, 1967, leading to a new socialist Eden on Earth, and that the Temple must move to Northern California for safety. Members uprooted their lives. They relocated. July 15, 1967 arrived and passed without incident.

Jones did not apologize. He did not acknowledge the failure. He reset the clock. The threat of nuclear apocalypse was supplanted by a new danger: a right-wing takeover of the United States. When that threat lost its urgency, a new one replaced it. By the time the congregation had followed Jones to a jungle compound in Guyana, the single radio in the compound was monitored at all times, and Jones would report events over the loudspeaker that followers had no way of verifying, ranging from warnings of an imminent nuclear holocaust to stories of the Ku Klux Klan marching through the streets of American cities.

The content of the crisis changed constantly. The function of the crisis never changed at all. A population in permanent emergency cannot assess what is being done to it. It can only respond. Jones understood this. He told members the fascist American government wanted to gas African Americans like the Germans gassed the Jews, and that the Temple was their only protection. He required loyalty tests involving sleep deprivation and physical pain. Pressure intensified for members to give the church all their possessions. If members wanted to leave, they had no money and no place to go. By the time Congressman Leo Ryan arrived in November 1978 to investigate conditions at Jonestown, Jones had confiscated passports. The doors had closed so gradually that most members had never seen them shut.

What happened in the months before November 18 is the part the history books rarely spend enough time on, because it is the part that most directly explains how 900 people arrived at the moment they did. Jones introduced what he called White Nights: emergency drills convened without warning, in the middle of the night, when the siren would sound and exhausted residents would rush to the pavilion surrounded by armed guards. Jones would tell them the settlement was under attack, by the CIA, by the Guyanese army, by mercenaries. He would tell them that the only honorable way out was revolutionary suicide. Residents were given cups of liquid and told it was poison. They were ordered to drink it to prove their loyalty.

Then Jones would reveal it was a test. The liquid was harmless. He would soothe them. He would praise their courage. He would send them back to bed.

These rehearsals occurred once a month when members first came to Jonestown. As Jones's paranoia grew, the White Nights increased to one every two weeks and would sometimes last for several days. Each one followed the same structure: the manufactured crisis, the demand for total surrender, the revelation that it was only a test, the praise, the return to ordinary life. Each one made the next one slightly more familiar. Each one narrowed the distance between the rehearsal and the act.

These rehearsals normalized the idea that death by poison could be a collective, even noble act, while conditioning followers to respond to crisis declarations with obedience rather than flight. By the time the real event arrived, it was not experienced as something new. It was experienced as another iteration of something that had already happened many times. The unthinkable had been made thinkable through repetition, through the slow compression of the distance between a test and a reality, until the distinction itself had been eroded.

On November 18, 1978, more than 900 people died.

The lesson here is not that Jones was uniquely evil or his followers uniquely credulous. The lesson is structural. The White Nights were not a feature of an extreme and isolated organization. They were an accelerated version of a process that runs, at lower temperatures, in every high-control system. The political movement that declares each election a final battle trains its members, over years, to accept emergency measures that would have been unthinkable at the beginning. The community that frames every doctrinal question as a test of loyalty trains its members to experience doubt as a form of betrayal. The relationship that uses crisis to extract compliance trains its participant to accept, incrementally, conditions they would never have agreed to at the start.

The mechanism in each case is the same as Jones's White Nights: repetition, escalation, and the normalization of surrender as a proof of devotion. What looks, from the outside, like a sudden and inexplicable capitulation is almost never sudden. It is the last step in a long series of smaller steps, each one reasonable in the context of the one before it, each one invisible in isolation.

The political version of this mechanic does not require a jungle compound. It runs on television and through a phone in your pocket. The formula is identical: the next election is the final battle, the enemy is at the gates, the normal rules of democratic process no longer apply because the situation is too urgent for process. When the predicted catastrophe fails to arrive, the clock resets. A new emergency fills the space. The specific content is interchangeable. The permanent state of emergency is the product being sold.

What the crisis engine is actually selling is the suspension of your judgment. A person who believes they are living through an unprecedented emergency will accept conditions they would never accept in ordinary time. They will give money, time, rights, and relationships to a leader who promises protection. They will not ask hard questions because hard questions feel like a luxury the crisis cannot afford.

The crisis cannot afford your questions because your questions are the only thing that can end it.

The way out is not to disprove the specific threat. The threats are designed to be replaced, not disproven. The way out is to notice the pattern: every solution requires your immediate surrender, the deadline always moves, the promised safety never arrives, and the person who benefits from the emergency is always the person announcing it.

The action: Keep a prediction registry. When a leader, an institution, or a media source announces an imminent catastrophe, write it down: the specific claim, the specific date or timeframe, and what you were asked to sacrifice in response. When the date passes, return to the entry. A system that has been wrong about the end of the world fifty times is not offering you protection. It is selling you a permanent emergency to justify permanent control. Your calm is not naivety. It is the most dangerous thing you can bring into the room.
