Chapter 2: The Logic of the Zealot

← Chapter 1: The Nostalgia Trap · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 3: Reality Distortions →

"What was the organization of illusion, of memory? Who knew even his own divided heart?"

There is a profound relief in being handed a world with no gray areas.

When life feels unstable, that relief can feel like rescue. Someone stands up and speaks with total, unblinking certainty. They have an answer for everything: who is destroying your country, who is corrupting your children, what God requires, what the enemy deserves. The questions that have been grinding you down for years dissolve in an instant. You don't have to figure anything out anymore. You just have to follow.

This is not a weakness of character. It is a feature of biology. When you are under chronic stress, your brain's capacity for nuanced reasoning goes offline. Complexity registers as a threat. The mind craves binary choices, absolute authority, a map with no ambiguity on it. Manipulators understand this with clinical precision. They don't offer a policy. They offer certainty. And certainty, delivered at the right moment to an exhausted person, functions exactly like a drug.

The system that captures you doesn't announce itself as a cage. It announces itself as clarity.

The International Churches of Christ, founded in Boston in the 1970s under the leadership of Kip McKean, presents one of the most thoroughly documented cases of how certainty becomes a control architecture. The ICOC did not recruit through coercion. It recruited people through belonging. New members were welcomed with extraordinary warmth, told they had finally found the one true expression of Christian community, and assigned a personal "discipler," a senior member who would guide every dimension of their spiritual and personal life. The system was called discipling. In practice, it meant that members were required to confess every doubt to their discipler and were not allowed to think negative thoughts about the group. Anything that made you doubt had to be avoided, which often meant cutting off friendships with people outside the group.

Doubt was not treated as a natural part of faith. It was treated as sin. The binary was total: you were either committed or you were worldly, either inside or outside, either saved or lost. Members were taught that commitment to the church superseded all other relationships. Universities banned ICOC recruiters from their campuses. The mainstream Churches of Christ publicly disavowed the organization.

The most striking piece of evidence came from researcher Flavil Yeakley, who administered Myers-Briggs personality tests to ICOC members, asking them to evaluate their past, present, and future selves. The findings showed personality types converging over time toward a single profile. The group was not just shaping behavior. It was reshaping individual minds into a uniform shape, producing people who thought the same way, responded the same way, and experienced doubt the same way: as personal failure rather than as legitimate questioning.

This is what absolute certainty produces at scale. Not conviction. Uniformity.

The political version of this mechanic is less subtle and more dangerous precisely because it operates in the open. Viktor Orbán's Hungary has spent fifteen years building what he calls "illiberal democracy," a system in which opposition media has been systematically purchased or bankrupted, university curricula have been rewritten, and civic organizations funded by foreign sources have been legally constrained or expelled. The framework is always binary: true Hungarians versus foreign agents, Christian civilization versus its enemies, the nation versus the globalists. There is no legitimate gray area in this framework. To question the premise is to declare yourself on the wrong side of it. The certainty is not incidental to the system. It is the system.

What both the ICOC and Orbán's framework share is the same immune response to doubt. When a former ICOC member left and spoke publicly about the group's practices, the organization's response was not engagement. It was the label: worldly, weak, seduced. When a Hungarian journalist publishes a critical investigation, the government's response is not rebuttal. It is the label: Soros agent, foreign operative, enemy of the people. The label does the work that argument cannot do. It doesn't need to be accurate. It needs to be fast.

Your own doubt is not a malfunction. It is your mind doing exactly what a free mind does: testing the walls of the room it's in.

The action: The next time a leader, a community, or a movement tells you that your doubt is a spiritual problem, a loyalty problem, or a character problem, write down the specific question you were not allowed to ask. Keep it. Return to it. A system that cannot survive your question is not offering you truth. It is offering you a cage with very clean walls.
creative-04-11-longing-11-the-crossing-p:
Longing 11: The Crossing Point

← Longing 10: The Sacred Is Here · The Creative Radical Collection · The Longing Under Each Pillar: A Workbook →

Pillar: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point · Across every book

or On the wish to outlast your own death, and the true shape of the largeness you are looking for.

This is the deepest hunger and the most human, and I have saved it for last because every other longing is a version of it. We do not want to vanish. We want to belong to something that goes on after we are gone, something large enough to make our small life mean more than its small span. The bloodline. The nation. The thousand-year reach. A name that survives inside the immortal group.

Power offers exactly this, and it is the most seductive thing it has. Give yourself to the nation, the race, the movement, and you will not really die, because the thing you gave yourself to will not die. The catch is in the giving. The immortal collective is always, in the end, hungry for the actual bodies of the people who believe in it. It promises to outlast your death and then arranges your death to feed its outlasting. The abstraction eats the very lives it offered to preserve.

Young’s answer is not to deny the hunger but to locate its true object. You already belong to something vast. You are made of the dead, of their language and their griefs and their choices, deposited in you like silt carried downriver and set down somewhere new. And you are making the ground the not-yet-born will stand on. The line of transmission is real, and it runs straight through you. You are the place where what was received crosses into what is passed on. You are the crossing point.

The eleventh pillar offers that real largeness in place of the murderous abstract one. You wanted to be part of something that outlives you. You are, already, with no leader required and no enemy to purge. The obligation it asks is not to die for the nation but to tend the actual generations, the ones in the ground behind you and the ones in the unformed ground ahead. It is humble, and it is located, and it does not need your blood. It needs your care.

You were looking for immortality. What you have is better, because it is true. You are a moment in a long act of carrying, and the carrying does not stop with you.
creative-03-11-pillar-eleven-the-crossin:
Pillar Eleven: The Crossing Point

← Pillar Ten: The Sacred is Here · The Creative Radical Collection · The Longing →

Pillar: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point · Across every book

Or, Why You Are the Center of Time

There is something the first ten pillars have been circling without naming.

Look back at what we have built. A self made of crowds. A reality that is constructed. Grief as permanent weather. The discipline of witnessing. The open structure, the unfinished work, the view from the edges, the sediment beneath our feet, the located language, the sacred ordinary. Ten pillars, each one a refusal of a different lie that tyranny depends on.

They stand. They hold weight. But when you step back from the architecture and look at it whole, you notice something: they are all rotating. They are rotating around a center that none of them, on their own, fully names.

That center is what this final pillar is about.

It is not a new rule added to the ten. It is not a bonus chapter or a coda. It is the hidden axis the entire structure has been organized around from the beginning, the point that was always already there, waiting for the rest of the building to make it visible. Young does not announce it directly in her novel. She never names it. But it is present in every sentence, in the way the narrator stands, in the way time moves in the book, in the way the past and future press simultaneously on every present moment.

You have been standing at this axis the entire time you have been reading.

What you have not yet done is look down and see what you are standing on. What you have not yet done is look up and understand what you are carrying. What you have not yet done is feel the full weight of the intersection itself: the place where everything that came before you crosses everything that will come after, where the sediment of history meets the unformed ground of the future, where the ancestors in your layers meet the not-yet-born who will walk on what you are forming right now.

You are not just a person living in the present. You are the crossing point itself.

That is the largest claim this philosophy makes. And it changes everything about where your power lives.

The Map Has a Second Axis

To understand this final pillar, we have to look at a basic geometry trick. Every single one of the first ten pillars described your life on a horizontal axis.

The horizontal line is the axis of accumulation. It tracks the wide, lateral spread of who you are right now in the present moment: your shifting inner crowd, your social relationships, and the daily weather of your grief. The horizontal axis is beautiful, and it is where we spend most of our daily energy.

But the horizontal axis cannot see the vertical axis.

The vertical line is the axis of transmission. It is the deep pipeline running straight through you, connecting the ancestors who came before you to the people who will inherit the earth long after you are gone.

Young's philosophy reminds us that we are alluvial. In geology, alluvial material is the rich soil and clay carried by a moving river and deposited in a delta to form a brand-new landscape.

You are a human river delta. You are made entirely of what was carried to you and deposited in you by the moving currents of time and human relation. The language you use to think, the cultural traditions you follow, and even the generational grief you carry were all deposited in your sediment by people who came before you.

You are not just a traveler walking down a straight timeline. You are the exact crossing point where the horizontal spread of today meets the vertical line of history.

The Ancestors under Your Boots, the Kids over Your Head

The eleventh pillar completely changes how we relate to the past and the future, stripping away abstract academic theories and making time feel intensely physical.

First, look downward. The ancestors are in the sediment.

Secular philosophy usually treats the dead like an ancient archive, a collection of old texts and data to look up if we feel like it. But Young says the dead are present as a literal, geological weight. They are in the soil that grew your food, the water flowing through your local aquifer, and the mental grooves that shape your thoughts. You are walking on top of their choices, and you are made of their deposits.

Now, look upward. The not-yet-born are in the ground you are forming.

We often talk about the future as a sentimental concept, but the eleventh pillar treats the future as a structural reality. Every single decision you make today, whether you are paying attention or not, acts as a fresh geological deposit. You are actively packing down the dirt that the next seven generations will have to stand on.

The Stable Center of a Turning Wheel: Boethius

To show us what it feels like to experience this, the text looks back at a famous moment in history. In the year 524 AD, a brilliant statesman and philosopher named Boethius was thrown into a prison cell and sentenced to death.

Before prison, Boethius was at the absolute top of the world. He held power in the court of a king. He was oriented on the horizontal axis: spreading his influence wide, accumulating honors, offices, and social power. He was a public man, connected to the machinery of the state, dependent on the wheel of fortune turning in his favor.

He wrote books. He held office. He commanded respect. He lived for the horizontal expansion of his status and his work.

Then his luck ran out. The king turned against him. He was accused of treason. He was imprisoned in a tower, stripped of his offices, separated from his family, waiting for execution. The medieval "Wheel of Fortune" turned him upside down.

Sitting in that cold cell with all of his lateral success stripped away, with nothing but a blank wall and the certainty of death, Boethius could have broken. Instead, he experienced a total rotation.

He was forced off the horizontal axis of accumulation and dropped straight onto the vertical axis of transmission. He stopped asking what he could build or acquire, and started asking what he was truly made of and what he was carrying forward. He began to write The Consolation of Philosophy, a work that asked: when everything external has been taken from you, when you have no office, no status, no power to spread horizontally, what remains? What is the ground beneath you?

In prison, Boethius discovered a beautiful secret: the crossing point does not move. The wheel of life can spin, your fortune can rise and fall, and the systems around you can erupt into total chaos. But the axis at the center holds perfectly stable.

He realized that he was not his office. He was not his status. He was not the accumulation of honors and influence. He was something deeper: he was a human being standing at the intersection of past and future, carrying something infinite, responsible to something vast.

When he dropped his attachment to the horizontal axis, when he stopped trying to climb back onto the wheel, he discovered a stability that no wheel could take from him. He was the still point around which the wheel turned. He was the crossing point where the weight of the past met the responsibility of the future.

He was enough, exactly as he was, stripped down to nothing but his mind and his mortality.

Jamming the Playbook: The Ultimate Accountability Shield

So, how does standing at the crossing point help us fight back against authoritarian control?

Tyranny relies on two major lies, and the eleventh pillar exposes both of them:

The Lie of the Neutral Ground: Authoritarian systems love to pretend that the current setup of society is neutral and natural. They want you to believe that poverty, exclusion, and their own massive power are just "the way things are". But a sedimentary mindset reads the ground honestly. It proves that the current landscape is actually an alluvial deposit created by specific historical choices, systemic extractions, and the long con of past regimes. Once you see the layers, the dictator can no longer lie to you about the soil.

The Lie of the Present Moment: Destructive systems operate entirely inside a short-sighted present-moment frame. They accelerate extraction, dismantle public institutions, and burn up resources because it benefits their current horizontal power, treating the future as if it doesn't exist. The crossing point enforces an unyielding intergenerational accountability. It forces us to ask: what kind of layer are we depositing into the ground for the kids who come next?

When you live at the crossing point, your obligations are no longer optional commitments you can pick up and drop for political convenience. They are built directly into your constitution. You recognize that you are a temporary carrier of an infinite human transmission, making you fiercely protective of the sediment beneath you and deeply responsible for the ground that will be built above you.

A person who understands that they stand at the crossing point of past and future cannot be bribed with short-term power. A person who recognizes that their children's children will walk on the ground they are forming today will not burn it for immediate profit. A person who feels the ancestors in their sediment and the unborn in their choices becomes unyieldingly protective of what matters.
creative-03-02-pillar-two-reality-is-con:
Pillar Two: Reality is Constructed

← Pillar One: Not One Self · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Three: Grief Doesn't End →

Pillar: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed · Across every book

Or, Why Seeing the Magic Trick Protects Your Mind

We are brought up to believe that the world is divided into two distinct categories: hard reality on one side, and silly illusions or daydreams on the other. We are told that reasonable people live in the real world and leave fantasies behind.

But Marguerite Young steps in with something that changes everything: the line between reality and illusion is completely made up.

The Fish in the Water

Young argues that illusion is not a fake escape from the real world. It is the very medium we live in. She suggests that human beings live in illusions the way fish live in water. What we choose to call "consensus reality" is really just one specific illusion that enough people have agreed to treat as true.

Think about the grand ideas that shape our daily lives: money, borders, social status, laws, and political frameworks. None of these things are physical objects you can dig up out of the earth. They are stories, agreements, and constructs that we built together from the materials available to us.

For centuries, traditional thinkers have used the old story of Plato's cave to explain life. In that story, people are trapped looking at shadows on a wall (illusions), and the goal is to escape into the bright, sunlit world outside (reality). But Young says there is no sunlit world outside the cave. There is only a larger cave, more beautifully lit, where everyone has simply agreed to call their specific shadows real.

Pulling the Rug Out From the Tyrant

So, why is this realization such a massive problem for authoritarian control?

Every oppressive system and dictator depends on a giant trick: they try to "naturalize" their own setup. They want you to believe that the way things are arranged (their power, their hierarchies, their exclusions) is simply the natural order of the universe. They want you to look at their cruel rules and think, "Well, that is just how the world works."

Young's philosophy shatters this illusion.

It exposes the setup: When you understand that all reality is constructed, you realize the dictator's authority is a fragile human performance, not a law of nature.

It returns power to you: If the current reality is an invention rather than an unchangeable truth, it means the political choices keeping things this way can be challenged, dismantled, and remade.

It creates automatic immunity: As Young herself directly noted, if you truly understand how illusion and hallucination work, you will never blindly follow any leader. You immediately see right through the political magic trick.

The very first act of political resistance is the simple refusal to mistake a dominant, man-made system as a natural occurrence.

The Map That Became the Territory: Jorge Luis Borges

To understand what it actually looks like to live inside the invention, to build an entire practice around the knowledge that reality is a human construction, consider Jorge Luis Borges, who spent his career doing exactly that and drawing out its political implications with quiet precision.

Borges was an Argentine writer who worked primarily in short fiction and essays. He was also a librarian, which is not incidental. He spent decades surrounded by the accumulated records of human invention: maps, encyclopedias, histories, taxonomies, legal codes, theological systems. He understood from the inside that these structures do not describe the world. They construct it. A map is not the territory. A legal category is not a natural fact. A nation is not a geological formation. They are all human agreements, maintained by repetition and enforcement, held together by the willingness of enough people to keep treating them as real.

His fiction made this visible. He wrote about a cartographers' guild that builds a map so detailed and so precisely scaled that it covers the entire territory it represents, one to one, a full-sized map of the empire laid over the empire itself. The map eventually falls into ruin, and travelers find its tattered remnants in the desert. The story is barely two paragraphs long. It does not explain itself. It does not need to. The image alone is enough to make the point: we have mistaken our representations for reality for so long that we cannot always tell which one we are walking on.

He wrote about a fictional encyclopedia, the Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, that describes a planet where reality is organized around idealism rather than materialism, where objects only exist when someone perceives them, where there is no concept of cause and effect, where nouns are replaced by verbs and adjectives because nothing holds still long enough to be named as a thing. The encyclopedia begins as a fiction. By the end of the story, the world it describes is bleeding into the actual world. Objects from Tlön are appearing in Argentina. The invented reality is displacing the one people took for granted. The story does not treat this as horror. It treats it as the logical outcome of how reality works: whoever controls the description controls the ground.

This is what Young means when she says that illusion is the medium we live in. Borges demonstrates it with precision. The systems we call real, the nations, the laws, the hierarchies, the categories, persist not because they are natural but because they are maintained. They require continuous enforcement, continuous agreement, continuous investment in keeping them visible and legible. The moment enough people stop agreeing, the system begins to dissolve. Not because it was fragile, but because it was always a construction, and constructions require builders.

The political implication is direct. An authoritarian system is a map that insists it is the territory. It claims that its categories are natural, its hierarchies inevitable, its power simply the way things are. It depends on you never noticing the cartographers. It depends on you walking on the map without ever looking up to check whether the territory matches.

Borges spent his career pointing at the cartographers. His fiction makes it almost impossible to finish reading and return to the assumption that the world you inhabit is the natural, neutral, only possible world. Once you have read him carefully, you carry a permanent awareness that someone drew these lines, that someone wrote this encyclopedia, that someone decided what counted as real and what did not. That awareness is not nihilism. It is clarity. And clarity, in the face of a system that depends on your confusion, is the beginning of everything.

Pulling the Rug Out From the Tyrant (Continued)

Young's own prose enacts the same refusal. Her sentences loop, circle back, resist settlement. She treats reality not as a fixed backdrop but as something continuously invented through the act of narration. When you read her carefully, you realize that what she is describing is not separate from how she is describing it. The form is the philosophy.

This brings us to a crucial point: understanding that reality is constructed is not the same as believing nothing matters or that you can wish things into being. Rather, it means understanding that the current arrangement is one specific choice among many possibilities. It means you cannot be gaslit into thinking that the way things are is the only way things could be.

When you live in this understanding, you become immune to a tyrant's greatest power: the power to convince you that your oppression is natural, inevitable, and impossible to change. Because you know the magic trick. You have seen the machinery. You understand that the construct is held together by agreement, and agreements can be withdrawn and re-made.

The Practice

Pick one thing in your daily routine that feels like an unshakeable, mandatory "reality" (like a rigid social expectation, a corporate habit, or a political narrative you see on the news). Pause and remind yourself: This is an invention. Someone built this story. Once you realize it is a constructed shadow on the wall, it loses its power to terrify or control you. You get to decide what stories are actually worth building.

Try a small experiment with language. Take a statement that feels like a fixed truth ("I am not creative," "people like us don't do that," "that's just how things are"). Now rewrite it in a way that emphasizes process and change instead of fixed identity.

Instead of "I am not creative," try "I have not yet given myself permission to create." Instead of "that's just how things are," try "that is what we have agreed to call normal, and we can agree to something different."

Notice how quickly the "reality" becomes fluid again when you change the grammar. That fluidity is where your power lives.

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar: Pillar 1 Not One Self · Across every book

Where did you try to be one person today, and what did it cost you?

The hunger is to be single and consistent, with the contradictions ironed out. Power offers one clean identity in exchange for the noise inside you. The plural self refuses the trade. You are many, and the contradiction in you is not a defect. It is what a person is.

Notice

For one day, catch the moments you feel pressure to be consistent. This might be smoothing over an opinion so it matches what you said yesterday, or hiding a want because it does not fit the version of you that other people expect.

Write down two or three moments you noticed this pressure today.

Practice

List the different people you are. The version of you at work, the version with your parents, the version alone at eleven at night, the version with an old friend. Do not try to reconcile them. Just name them, side by side.

Reflection

Where did you feel most tired today trying to hold yourself together as one person?

What happened in your body when you let two contradictory things be true about yourself at once, even for a moment?
creative-05-05-pillar-4-witnessing-is-th:
Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

← Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary →

Pillar: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Across every book

What did you look away from today, and what were you offered instead?

The hunger is to look away, because witnessing is heavy. Power offers spectacle, a designated enemy, or the feeling of being seen, anything but the steady burden of seeing what is actually in front of you. The witness stays in the room. Staying present, without fixing or flinching, is itself a refusal.

Notice

Name one thing today you wanted to look away from, whether it was a news story, a person's pain, or something true about your own life. Notice what you reached for instead, whether that was a screen, an argument, or a distraction.

Practice

Choose one hard thing you have been avoiding. Set a timer for five minutes. Stay with it. No fixing, no solving, no explaining it away. Just look at it and let yourself feel whatever comes up.

Reflection

What came up when you stayed past the point where you usually leave the room?

What is easier to look at when you are not trying to solve it first?

Longing 3: Grief Doesn't End

← Longing 2: Reality Is Constructed · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act →

Pillar: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End · Across every book

or On the loss that will not close, and what power does with our refusal to mourn.

We are bad at grief now. We want it to move through tidy stages and arrive at something called acceptance, after which we are restored to normal. The grief that does not cooperate, the kind that simply stays, embarrasses us. We treat it as a wound that has failed to heal on schedule.

Power is very interested in unmourned grief, because grief that cannot rest goes looking for somewhere to put itself. So power offers your loss a destination and a face. Your pain has a cause, it says, and the cause is them. The migrants, the elite, the unbelievers, whoever has been chosen. Let me remove them and you will be whole again. This is grievance turned into a weapon, and it works because the promise underneath it is the one we most want to hear: that the hurt can be ended, that someone can be made to pay, that you can be made new.

Young will not offer that. Her book is full of people carrying losses that never close. A mother lost inside her own dreams. A nursemaid lost to the sea. A search that finds no clean ending. Grief in that novel is not an event you get over. It is the climate you live in. It accumulates, layer on layer, like sediment, until it becomes the ground you walk on rather than a hole in the road.

The third pillar names grief as permanent weather. Not a problem to be solved, not a debt to be collected, but a condition you learn to live inside. And here is its political weight. If you can carry your loss without needing it avenged, without needing someone to pay, you cannot be recruited by the man who promises to heal you by harming somebody else. The unmournable grief that he wants to aim is, in you, simply being carried.

This is the hardest pillar to live, and I will not pretend otherwise. Letting grief stay, without the consolation of a culprit, asks a great deal of a person. But the alternative is to hand your sorrow to someone who will spend it on cruelty and call that healing. Better to carry it yourself. The weather does not have to clear for you to keep living under it.
creative-02-01-chapter-1-the-nostalgia-t:
Chapter 1: The Nostalgia Trap

← The Captured Mind: How Cults, Strongmen, and Algorithms Stea · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 2: The Logic of the Zealot →

"Memory sometimes provides the one flower more than ever blossomed. Memory sometimes omits the only flower there really was."

Before a demagogue can control your future, he has to rewrite your past.

This is always the first move. Not policy. Not theology. Not even fear. The first move is a photograph, held up like an icon: a factory town in 1958, smoke rising from the mill, a clean street, a family walking out of church. "This is who you were," the strongman says. "And they took it from you."

It doesn't matter that the photograph is a lie. It doesn't matter that the air in that town was killing people, that the church enforced the silence of women, that the prosperity on that street was built on systematic exclusion. None of that survives the edit. The strongman doesn't need the full picture. He only needs your hunger for one.

Every high-control system begins here. The political movement that promises to restore a golden age. The evangelical community that demands a return to original, uncorrupted faith. The end-times congregation that tells you the world you remember was pure and the world you live in now is fallen. The sales pitch is identical across all of them: the present is a disaster, the past was paradise, and only submission to this leader, this doctrine, this movement will take you back.

Your brain is not helping you resist this. Human memory is not a recording. It is an editing suite, and it runs constantly, softening pain, amplifying warmth, and cutting the complicated middle. When you are exhausted and the present feels loud and unnavigable, the edited past feels like oxygen. Manipulators understand this. They step into the exhaustion and hand you a story that makes the panic stop. Your brain does not care that the story is false. It only cares that it works.

The political machinery that runs this operation has been documented, tested, and refined. In Hungary, Viktor Orbán has spent fifteen years building a cultural and educational apparatus designed to produce a single, approved version of Hungarian history, one in which national greatness is always interrupted by foreign corruption, and in which the restoration of that greatness requires the suspension of democratic inconveniences. In the United States, the "Make America Great Again" framework did not describe a real historical period. It described a feeling, specifically the feeling of white male industrial centrality, and it weaponized nostalgia for that feeling into a political program. The facts of the actual postwar decades, the segregation, the Cold War terror, the violent suppression of labor, were not part of the image. They were the part that got cut.

At the intimate scale, the same mechanic runs with the same precision. NXIVM, the organization Keith Raniere built over two decades before his 2019 federal conviction on charges including sex trafficking and racketeering, was a masterclass in manufactured nostalgia. New members were wrapped in intense admiration. They were told they had a gift. That they could be leaders. That they had finally found the place where they truly belonged. That early period of warmth was not accidental. It was documented. It was the bait. As former member Sarah Edmondson has said publicly: no one joins a cult. They join something they believe in. What NXIVM sold in its first act was a memory of your best self, a period of clarity, purpose, and belonging that felt more real than anything you had experienced before. Once that memory existed, it became a leash. Every demand, every escalating act of submission, every piece of "collateral" extracted from members, was framed as the price of returning to that original feeling. The golden age of your membership was always just ahead, recoverable, if only you went deeper.

This is the structure. Create a paradise. Then sell it back to you piece by piece.

The action: The next time you feel the pull of a political movement, a religious community, or any group that asks you to long for something you've lost, write down two columns. First, write the feeling they're selling. Second, write who was not in the photograph. Not as an argument. As a discipline. The past is never as clean as the pitch. If it feels simple, it has been edited.
creative-05-09-pillar-8-the-past-doesnt-:
Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

← Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible →

Pillar: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away · Across every book

Are you gilding your past into a golden age, or trying to wipe it clean and start at year zero?

The hunger is to fix time, either to restore a golden past that never was or to wipe the slate at year zero. Power uses whichever lie is closer to hand. This pillar says the past is accumulation, not a paradise to recover and not a slate to clear. You carry all of it, layered, without gilding or erasing it.

Notice

Notice, over the next few days, when you reach for a story about your own past that is either too golden or too erased. A version where everything used to be better, or a version where you have supposedly moved past something completely.

Practice

Draw or describe a simple timeline of your life as layers, like sediment, rather than a straight line. Note what still presses upward from underneath, the old griefs and choices that are still active in you now.

Reflection

Where are you tempted to mythologize your past as better than it was, or to pretend you have wiped a part of it clean?

What would it mean to just carry it, unedited, as ground rather than as a verdict?

Longing 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Across every book

or On the comfort of the natural order, and the vertigo and freedom of knowing it was built.

There is a deep relief in believing that the way things are is simply the way things are. The hierarchy is natural. The arrangement is ancient. This is how it has always been, and your only job is to find your place inside it. The given order asks nothing of you except acceptance, and in exchange it lifts two heavy weights: the weight of responsibility, and the dizziness of having to decide.

Power adores the given. Every cruelty is easier to keep if it can be called natural, traditional, ordained, the way of things. The appeal to how it has always been is among the oldest tools there is, because it turns a choice somebody made into a fact nobody is allowed to question.

Young’s imagination runs the other way. She spent years on the story of New Harmony, two utopias built deliberately on the Indiana frontier by people who believed the order of life could be drawn up fresh. They failed, and Young does not hide the failure. But the point survives the failure: the arrangements people live inside were arranged. They are constructions, made and remade, not facts of nature. Even the self, in her work, is recursive, built out of older buildings, assembled rather than found.

The fifth pillar holds that everything is constructed, including the things that present themselves as eternal. This is vertigo at first. If nothing is simply given, then nothing carries you, and you are responsible after all. But the vertigo is also the door. What was built by hands can be understood, questioned, and built differently. The natural order, looked at closely, turns out to be a set of decisions wearing a costume.

You did not consent to most of what you live inside, but somebody made it, and what was made is not sacred. That is not a license for chaos. It is the return of a power that the word natural was quietly taking from you. The order is not the weather. It is architecture. And architecture can be redrawn.
creative-03-10-pillar-ten-the-sacred-is-:
Pillar Ten: The Sacred is Here

← Pillar Nine: Language Shapes What's Possible · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Eleven: The Crossing Point →

Pillar: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here · Across every book

Or, Why The Sacred Is Ordinary

When life gets incredibly difficult, chaotic, or confusing, almost every major religious and philosophical tradition makes the exact same move. They tell us to look up and out. They point toward a transcendent beyond, an unshifting sky, a distant deity, or a future utopia to anchor us and make sense of our current suffering. We are trained to look past the messy, ordinary world in search of a higher, absolute truth. The thinking goes: this world is broken and painful, but somewhere else, somewhere beyond, there is something that is perfect and whole. Hold on. Endure. Transcend. That is where meaning lives.

But Marguerite Young refuses that move at every single level of her system. She brings us a message that is profoundly comforting and fiercely radical: the sacred is here, or it is absolutely nothing.

The Magic of the Ordinary

The word immanence is just a philosophical way of describing what is right here, entirely present within our actual, day-to-day experience. When you add the word radical to it, it means this idea goes all the way down to the bedrock. There is no outside escape hatch. There is no secret baseline reality hiding underneath the world. There is no external guarantee to fix things for us. What is here is what there is.

But far from being cold or empty, Young shows us that this immediate world is absolutely bursting with depth. When we attend to our surroundings with the unblinking focus of a true witness, the ordinary landscape lights up with immense significance. The bus route becomes sacred. The dresser with the forgotten wig becomes sacred. The person sitting across from you becomes sacred. Not because we have decided to treat them that way. Not because we have projected meaning onto them. But because they are here, they are real, they are irreplaceable.

To illustrate this, Young's pillar connects with the work of indigenous scientist and author Robin Wall Kimmerer. Kimmerer teaches that the natural world is not a collection of dead, objective items for us to use and extract value from. It is a vibrant community of living subjects. The plants are not resources. They are persons. The water is not a utility. It is a subject with its own agency and its own gift to offer. The soil is not an inert medium. It is alive with millions of organisms working together.

This is what it means to find the sacred in the ordinary. It means recognizing that the ordinary world is not dead matter waiting for us to impose meaning on it. It is alive. It is conscious. It is already sacred. We do not make it sacred. We simply finally notice that it always was.

Young practices this exact mindset in her writing. In her world, everything around us becomes deeply sacred: the daily bus routes, the old wig resting on a dresser, our permanent grief, and our beautifully constructed, changing lives. Meaning is not handed down to us from a distant throne. It is carefully, lovingly crafted right here by plural selves building provisional structures together. It lives in the accumulation of small acts of attention and care. It lives in the choice to keep showing up, to keep witnessing, to keep building, even though nothing is perfect and nothing will be finished.

Starving the War Gods of Their Power

So, how does finding the sacred right under our feet deliver the ultimate blow to authoritarian control?

Throughout history, tyrants and oppressive movements have almost always relied on an appeal to a grand, distant beyond to justify their violence. They command people to sacrifice their lives, look away from immediate cruelty, and march to war by invoking abstract, absolute ideals. A mythical golden age. A supreme leader. A grand national destiny. A holy cause. A thousand-year empire. A glorious future. They use a fake, elevated sky to make regular human lives feel small, disposable, and cheap.

The appeal to transcendence is the dictator's greatest weapon. When you teach people that meaning lives somewhere else, somewhere better, somewhere that requires sacrifice in the present moment, you can get them to accept almost any amount of suffering here and now. You can get them to hurt others. You can get them to destroy. All in the name of some distant goal that will supposedly make it all worth it.

Young's final pillar completely starves that strategy of its power. It insists that there is nowhere else. There is no beyond.

It eliminates the excuse for violence. When you believe the sacred is found only in the ordinary world and the living beings right in front of you, you can never be talked into destroying real people for the sake of a distant, abstract ideology. You cannot sacrifice your neighbor for the glory of the nation. You cannot accept their suffering for the promise of a better tomorrow. Because the person in front of you is not a means to an end. They are the end. They are the sacred. They are the whole point.

It breaks the leader's spell. Dictators try to set themselves up as external gods or absolute anchors. They claim to represent something beyond, something transcendent, something that justifies their power. Young’s philosophy reminds us that there are no absolute anchors outside of human relationship and human place. It exposes the leader's performance as a fragile human invention. Once you see that the emperor has no clothes, the spell is broken. You cannot be controlled by someone who is just like you, unless you agree to treat them as more than human.

It grounds true collective power. When we realize that bus routes, town halls, community gardens, and school buildings are already filled with all the significance we will ever need, we stop waiting for a political savior to arrive. We stop looking for a leader who will rescue us and deliver us to the promised land. We find our power right under our feet, in the places we already are, with the people we already know. We realize that the sacred is not something that is coming. It is something that is already here, and we are already standing in it.

When we look at each other and our ordinary world with the full attention of a witness, we realize that here is the whole of it. We are already enough, and we have everything we need to stay free.

The Whole Point Is Here: Fannie Lou Hamer

To understand what it means to locate the sacred entirely in the ordinary world, in the specific bodies and specific ground of the people immediately around you, consider Fannie Lou Hamer, who never stopped pointing downward.

Hamer was born in 1917, the twentieth child of Mississippi sharecroppers. She spent the first forty-four years of her life working other people's land in Sunflower County, one of the poorest and most violently enforced counties in the Mississippi Delta. She did not have a platform. She did not have an education the system recognized. She had the ground under her feet and the people standing on it with her, and she treated both as sacred without ever using that word.

In 1962, she went to a meeting and heard for the first time that she had the right to register to vote. She did not experience this as an abstraction. She experienced it as something that was already true, already hers, being withheld from her by a system that depended on her believing the withholding was natural. She went to the courthouse the next week. She was turned away. She went back. She was evicted from the plantation where she had worked for eighteen years. She kept going back.

What drove her was not a vision of a distant future. It was the specific faces of the specific people she lived among, whose lives were being ground down right now, on this ground, in this county, by this specific arrangement of power. She was not working toward an arrival. She was insisting that the people in front of her were already the whole point. Their lives, ordinary and difficult and irreplaceable, were already the sacred thing. There was nothing beyond them worth more.

When she testified before the Credentials Committee at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, she did not speak in the language of ideology or grand national destiny. She spoke from her body, from a specific night in a Winona, Mississippi jail where she had been beaten so severely the damage was permanent. She named what had been done to her. She named where it happened and who did it and what it felt like. She did not abstract the violence upward into a symbol. She kept it right here, in her specific flesh, in the specific ground of Mississippi, among the specific people whose names she knew.

President Johnson was so threatened by the directness of her testimony, by the way it refused to be managed or softened or pointed toward a more comfortable elsewhere, that he called an emergency press conference to pull cameras away from her. He understood, even if he could not have named it this way, that a woman speaking from that location, refusing transcendence, insisting that what was happening right here to these people right now was the whole of the moral question, was more dangerous than any abstract political argument. You cannot negotiate with someone who will not look away from what is directly in front of her.

She was offered paths out. She could have left Mississippi. She could have taken her national profile and her extraordinary gifts and built something in a larger arena. She stayed. Not out of limitation but out of commitment to the ground she was standing on, to the people whose lives were the reason she had started in the first place. The Delta was not a stepping stone. It was the sacred place. The ordinary people in it were not a constituency to be managed toward a better future. They were the future, right now.

Authoritarian systems and the plantation economy she fought her whole life both depended on the same fundamental lie: that the lives of the people in front of you are preparation for something, instruments toward something, acceptable casualties of something more important happening elsewhere. Hamer refused that lie every time she opened her mouth. She kept pointing at the people directly around her and saying: these lives. This ground. Right now. That is the whole of it.

She died in 1977, in Mississippi, having never left. The ground she is buried in is the same ground she was born on, the same ground she refused to abstract into a symbol, the same ground she spent her life insisting was already sacred. She did not transcend it. She stayed in it, fully, until she was done.

The Practice

Begin to pay attention to the moments in your day when you are tempted to look past what is actually in front of you. When you are having dinner with someone you love, notice if you are thinking about how this moment will look in memory, rather than actually tasting the food and listening to the person. When you are walking through your neighborhood, notice if you are thinking about a better place you would rather be, rather than noticing the light on the buildings and the smell of the air.

Try this: for one day, try not to improve anything. Do not plan. Do not fix. Do not try to make your life better. Just notice. Just witness. Just be present to what is there. Pay close attention to a cup of coffee, or a conversation, or the way light falls through a window. Notice how much depth becomes visible when you stop trying to transcend the present moment and actually arrive in it.

Also notice when you are being offered a false transcendence. When a system tells you to sacrifice now for a better future. When a leader promises you something beyond if you will just comply. When an ideology asks you to treat abstract ideals as more important than the real people in front of you. Pause. Remember Young. Remember that the sacred is here. Starve that appeal to a distant beyond. Keep your attention on what is real, what is present, what is right in front of you. That is where your power lives.
creative-04-01-longing-1-not-one-self:
Longing 1: Not One Self

← The Longing · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 2: Reality Is Constructed →

Pillar: Pillar 1 Not One Self · Across every book

or On the self that refuses to be a single thing, and why that refusal keeps you free.

There is a tiredness that comes from being asked to be consistent. To be the same person on Monday that you were on Sunday, to want one thing and not its opposite, to have a story about yourself that holds together. Most of us cannot do it, not honestly. We are several people in one coat, and we spend a great deal of energy pretending otherwise.

Power understands that tiredness better than we do. Its first and kindest-seeming offer is relief from it. Be one thing, it says. You are a patriot. You are one of the real people. You are of the blood, the faith, the nation. Step into the single self we have cut for you and the argument inside you goes quiet. There is enormous comfort in that quiet. It is the comfort of no longer having to hold your own contradictions.

Marguerite Young builds the opposite person. Her narrator goes looking for one solid self, the dependable nursemaid who seemed made of pure reality, and finds instead that even she was many, masked, unfinished. Everyone in that book is more than one. The mother is a dozen women inside a single opium dream. No one resolves into a type. The novel runs past a thousand pages partly because a person does not reduce, and Young refused to pretend otherwise just to make the book shorter.

The first pillar is that refusal made into a stance. You are plural, and the contradiction in you is not a flaw waiting to be ironed out. It is the texture of being someone. When you stop treating your own multiplicity as a problem, the single clean identity loses its pull. There is no one you for the machine to enlist, no smooth surface for the slogan to stick to.

This is not a grand act of resistance. It is small and daily. It is letting yourself want two things, hold two truths, be tender and furious in the same hour, and not reaching for the person who promises to make you simple. The plural self cannot be marched in a single direction, because it was never marching as one.

You were never only one. That was never the failure. It was the whole of you.
creative-06-conclusion-to-this-collectio:
Conclusion to this Collection

← Closing Page · The Creative Radical Collection

You have reached the end of the collection, which means you carry something you did not have when you started.

You have seen the mechanisms taken apart, the ways a mind gets pried loose from its own perception. You have met the eleven pillars, the ways of standing that a captured mind cannot hold. You have followed me through the more personal reckoning, where the target moved from the strongman to the hunger he feeds on. And you have done the exercises, or you will, or you will come back to them, catching that hunger while it is still small and practicing the alternative until it becomes a habit. I want to be honest, at the end, about what all of it can and cannot do.

It cannot make you invulnerable. The hungers are real, and they do not disappear because you have named them. You will still be tired. You will still grieve losses that refuse to close. You will still, some evening, want one clean answer and someone to follow, want to be lifted out of the ordinary grey into something that finally means more. That wanting is not a flaw in you. It is the most human thing there is, and every system in these books was built by people who understood it well enough to engineer against it at scale.

What changes is not that the wanting stops. What changes is that you now have somewhere to put it other than the hands of whoever is selling a cure.

That, in the end, is the whole of Young's medicine. She did not offer a better paradise or a truer leader. She offered the refusal of the entire structure, and the discovery underneath the refusal that the ordinary, unfinished present is enough to stand on. She said, more or less, that once you have looked at every illusion and understood there is no solid reality waiting beneath them, and you go on living anyway, you have become a grown person. Not arrival. Not rescue. You see that it is all a mask, and you stay, and you keep living in the here that is left.

The defense these books describe is not dramatic, and it will not save you all at once. It is the opposite of the thing it resists. Where capture is fast, this is slow. Where capture promises arrival, this stays in the present. Where capture wants you certain, this asks you to hold your doubt carefully, as a tool rather than a wound. It looks like writing down what you saw before the authorized version arrives to replace it. It looks like sitting with a question you were told not to ask. It looks like staying in the room with a person rather than reaching for the phone and the facts. It looks like leaving a thing unfinished on purpose and calling that honesty. Small, daily, unglamorous, and yours.

The systems arrayed against your attention are large and patient and well funded. They win the way water wins, through small surrenders that each seem reasonable in the moment and only add up in the dark. The good news, the only news these books have really been carrying, is that the defense works the same way. It is also incremental. It is also daily. And unlike the machinery on the other side, it asks no one's permission but your own.

There is one more thing, and it is the reason for the last line of every piece in this collection.

You are not the end of this. You are a place it passes through. The language you think in, the griefs you carry, the capacity to stay present in your own mind, all of it was handed to you by people who came before, and all of it can be handed on. That is the real version of the largeness the strongman counterfeits. He offers you a kind of immortality through the crowd, and then asks for your life to feed it. Young offers something smaller and true. You are a moment in a long act of carrying, and the carrying does not stop with you.

So do the small things. Keep your mind unfinished. Refuse the clean story that would flatten it. And when you meet someone standing at the edge of something they cannot name, the way you once were, tell them a truer story, and hand them the tools.

Here is enough. Here is enormous. The sentence has not ended.

Pass it on.

Visit coralrussell.substack.com for 800+ free posts exploring Radical Immanence and Marguerite Young’s work.
creative-05-03-pillar-2-reality-is-const:
Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

← Pillar 1 Not One Self · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End →

Pillar: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed · Across every book

What are you still hoping someone will hand you the real story about?

The hunger is for the one explanation that makes the chaos cohere, the secret underneath the surface. Power arrives as the one who tells it like it is. This pillar holds that there is no bedrock story, it is masks the whole way down, and you can live anyway, without grabbing the totalizing myth that promises to steady you.

Notice

Catch a moment this week when you feel the pull toward one explanation for something confusing, a person, a piece of news, your own situation. Notice the specific relief that comes with the phrase now it all makes sense.

Practice

Pick something confusing you have been trying to solve, a person's behavior, a current event, a decision you cannot settle. Instead of searching for the hidden truth underneath, write down every surface version you actually know. Then stop. Do not dig further tonight.

Reflection

What did it feel like to stop before you found the real answer?

Who has offered you a bedrock explanation recently, and what did they want from you in exchange for the relief of certainty?
creative-03-04-pillar-four-witnessing-is:
Pillar Four: Witnessing is the Core Ethical Act

← Pillar Three: Grief Doesn't End · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary →

Pillar: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Across every book

Or, Why Simply Staying in the Room is a Revolutionary Act

We are a society obsessed with quick fixes and immediate action. Marguerite Young offers a different kind of heroism: the quiet, stubborn power of refusing to look away.

Pillar Four is where the real ethical work of Young's system begins. The first three pillars describe what the world is, but the fourth pillar tells us exactly what to do about it: we witness.

Our culture loves a fixer. We celebrate the decisive leader, the hero who charges into a problem, resolves it, and delivers a clean, happy ending where everyone can move on. We are trained to look at a complicated situation and immediately ask, "How do we fix this?"

But Young warns us that rushing to "fix" or "solve" a deep contradiction is often just a sneaky way of making ourselves feel comfortable at the expense of the truth.

What Does It Mean to Witness?

To witness doesn't mean to fix, judge, or resolve things. It means choosing to stay in the room with what is actually there, seeing it without flinching and without rushing to a neat conclusion. It means being able to look at a messy, painful reality without needing one to be truer or more real than the other.

This might sound passive at first, but it is actually the most demanding ethical stance we can take. In a standard story, the hero acts, the problem is solved, and the book ends. But the witness stays while the problem remains, the story keeps going, and the witness keeps staying. There is no final arrival; there is only the quality of attention you bring to the ongoing journey.

In Young's world the ones who suffer are the ones who stop witnessing. They are the people who get uncomfortable, get tired of the mess, and replace the reality in front of them with a neat, comfortable frame that makes things manageable at the cost of their actual complexity.

And here is the beautiful twist: Young reminds us that we don't just owe this deep attention to other people. We also have to witness ourselves: our own inner crowd, our permanent grief, and our own constructed realities, holding it all with compassion and zero judgment.

Stopping the Propaganda Machine Dead in Its Tracks

So, why does the simple act of witnessing jam the authoritarian playbook?

Our political culture is obsessed with constant action, decisive leaders, and the fantasy of a permanent arrival where a problem is finally solved forever. But Young points out that political action not grounded in genuine witnessing is incredibly dangerous.

Authoritarian movements absolutely depend on the refusal of witnessing. They survive and grow by executing a very specific strategy.

They erase complexity: They reduce complex, plural human beings into simple, sorted categories like "us" versus "them".

They enforce a single script: They replace genuine, close-up attention with a rigid ideology.

They hide the damage: They decide that whatever doesn't fit their pre-made political frame simply doesn't need to be seen.

When you choose to be a witness, you break this entire machine. By stubbornly staying in the room and keeping your eyes wide open, you refuse to let a political ideology distort the human being standing right in front of you. You refuse to look away from institutional cruelty just because it is politically convenient or uncomfortable to face.

Witnessing creates a space for honest appearance. It is a quiet, unyielding veto against the lies a regime tells to justify its power.

The Cost of Clarity: Hannah Arendt

To understand what witnessing actually requires, it helps to look at someone who dedicated her entire intellectual life to it.

Hannah Arendt was a political theorist who refused to look away from totalitarianism, even when that refusal made her deeply uncomfortable, even when it contradicted what others wanted to believe, even when it meant sitting with ideas that had no easy resolution.

Arendt fled Nazi Germany and spent her life trying to understand how totalitarianism worked. She refused to offer her readers the comfort of a simple moral story. Instead, she insisted on paying close attention to the actual mechanics of power, to how ordinary people became complicit, to how systems of control operated not through crude force alone but through the subtle destruction of human plurality and the public realm.

Her most famous book, The Origins of Totalitarianism, is not a book that offers solutions. It does not tell you how to fix totalitarianism or what the good society looks like. Instead, it demands that you stay in the room with the full complexity of how totalitarianism emerges, how it destroys the conditions for human freedom, and how difficult it is to resist once it has taken hold. She refused to simplify the problem or offer false hope.

This made her unpopular. Readers wanted her to tell them that totalitarianism was the fault of evil men, or of a single flaw in human nature, or that it could be prevented by following the right political path. But Arendt refused those comforts. She insisted that totalitarianism was a genuine danger to human freedom, that ordinary people participated in it, that the systems were more durable and more subtle than most people wanted to admit, and that understanding it required sustained, difficult attention.

Later, when she witnessed the trial of Adolf Eichmann, she had to do something even harder. She had to stay in the room with a man who had orchestrated the Holocaust and try to understand him not as a monster but as a human being. The result was a book, Eichmann in Jerusalem, that refused the comfort of seeing evil as something alien and incomprehensible. Instead, she argued that Eichmann was an ordinary bureaucrat who had stopped thinking, who had accepted the regime's language and categories without question, who had disappeared into the machine.

This was not a comfortable argument. People wanted Eichmann to be evil in a way that was easy to recognize and reject. Arendt's refusal to offer that comfort, her insistence on staying in the room and looking clearly at what had actually happened, made her controversial. But that discomfort is exactly the point. A witnessing that makes us comfortable is not witnessing. A witnessing that allows us to feel superior to the people who did harm is not witnessing. True witnessing requires that we look at the mechanisms of evil, at how ordinary people become complicit, at how systems work to destroy human judgment and responsibility.

Arendt modeled something crucial: the refusal to rush toward a solution, a judgment, or a comfortable moral frame. Instead, she stayed in the room with the hardest questions. She paid attention to language, to how totalitarian regimes used words to erase meaning. She refused to sort people into simple categories. She held the complexity without trying to resolve it.

This kind of witnessing is not passive. It is the hardest work there is. It requires that you give up the comfort of quick judgment and instead stay present with what is difficult to understand. It requires that you resist the impulse to look away when things get uncomfortable. It requires that you refuse the false solutions and easy narratives that allow most people to sleep at night.

But this kind of witnessing is also the ultimate form of resistance. Because a person who will not look away, who will not accept the regime's simplified categories, who will not be rushed into premature judgment, is a person who cannot be manipulated by propaganda. That person becomes a threat to any system that depends on people accepting easy narratives and refusing to see what is actually in front of them.

The Practice

When you find yourself in a difficult conversation, a moment of personal anxiety, or reading a complex news story, notice the urge to jump in with a quick fix, an easy judgment, or a neat political label.

Catch that impulse and try this instead: just stay in the room. Keep looking. Tell yourself, "I am not going to rush to a conclusion right now. I am just going to witness this fully." Notice how much courage it takes to let the complexity exist without trying to force it into a tidy box.

This applies to how you witness other people as well. When someone tells you something difficult, resist the urge to offer advice or to sort them into a category. Instead, try to see them fully: in all their contradiction, their complexity, their incompleteness. Hold all of it without needing to fix them or make them simpler. That full attention is witnessing, and it is the greatest gift you can offer another human being.
creative-04-06-longing-6-unfinished-is-h:
Longing 6: Unfinished Is Honest

← Longing 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth →

Pillar: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest · Across every book

or On the dream of arrival, and why the most dangerous promise is that the work can be done.

We are taught to love completion. The finished project, the closed list, the goal reached, the story that ends well. Incompletion feels like failure, like something we did not get around to. We want to arrive.

The largest version of this longing is the one power reaches for. It promises arrival on a vast scale. The completed nation. The purified people. The end of history, the final stage, the promised land at the close of the long march. Almost every catastrophe of the last century was committed in the name of a finished state that was only one more push away. The most dangerous sentence in any language is the one that imagines the work can finally be done, because once you believe in the finished world, the people standing in the way of it stop looking like people.

Young wrote a book that refuses to end. The sentences run long, the search does not resolve, the answers do not arrive, and this is not a flaw in the design. It is the design. Her lifelong subject was the lost utopia, the perfect ending that was promised and never came, at New Harmony, in the dream of a redeemed politics, in the longing of every character for a completion the book denies them. She knew exactly what the dream of arrival costs.

The sixth pillar makes incompletion into an ethic. There is no final state, and that is not a tragedy to be overcome. It is the condition of anything still alive. The unfinished is the living. The completed is the embalmed. A person who has stopped needing the work to be done cannot be sold a final solution, because they no longer believe such a thing exists.

So you do not finish. You do not arrive. You keep the list open, the question open, the future open, and you call that openness the point rather than the problem. The promised land is always one purge away. The actual land is here, unfinished, and it is the only place you get to live.
creative-02-05-chapter-5-the-machine-tha:
Chapter 5: The Machine That Knows You

← Chapter 4: The Closed Loop · The Creative Radical Collection · Chapter 6: Why Facts Aren't Enough →

"She had cried outside many gates of stillness where only her own voice had cried back to her, bouncing like the echo."

We have been waiting for the wrong enemy.

For decades, warnings about mind control described a charismatic figure: a man on a podium, a preacher on a screen, a demagogue at a rally. We learned to look for the human face of manipulation. While we were looking, the most effective behavior modification system in history was built into a rectangle of glass and placed in our pockets. It has no face. It has no ideology. It has only one objective: to keep you looking at it as long as possible.

The modern social media feed is not a communication tool that sometimes manipulates people. It is a manipulation system that sometimes facilitates communication. The distinction matters because it changes what you are dealing with. You are not making choices about how to use a neutral platform. You are navigating an environment that has been precision-engineered, using your own behavioral data, to override your judgment.

The mechanism is straightforward. Every pause, every reread, every share, every angry comment you leave is a data point. The algorithm accumulates these data points and constructs a detailed map of what makes you afraid, what makes you angry, what makes you feel vindicated, and what makes you feel alone. It then uses that map to build a feed calibrated specifically to keep your nervous system in a state of aroused engagement. Not happiness. Not information. Engagement. Outrage and anxiety produce more engagement than contentment. Fear produces more engagement than reassurance. The feed learns this about you personally and acts on it continuously.

This is not a conspiracy. It is an engineering decision, and the internal documents prove it was made with full knowledge of the consequences.

In 2021, former Facebook data scientist Frances Haugen leaked thousands of internal company documents to the Wall Street Journal. The documents revealed that Facebook's own researchers had spent years studying Instagram's effect on teenage users and had reached conclusions the company chose not to disclose publicly. According to their own internal findings, thirty-two percent of teen girls said that when they felt bad about their bodies, Instagram made them feel worse. The company's own researchers concluded: "we make body image issues worse for one in three teen girls." A separate internal presentation found that among teens who reported suicidal thoughts, thirteen percent of British users and six percent of American users traced the desire to kill themselves to Instagram.

The company had this information in 2019. It did not change the algorithm. It did not disclose the findings. Internal memos showed the company was simultaneously concerned about losing teenage users, with one memo stating: "If we lose the teen foothold in the U.S. we lose the pipeline." The pipeline was more important than the harm. This was not an accident or an oversight. It was a choice made by people who had read their own research.

What the documents expose is not a failure of the system. It is the system working as designed. The feed does not care whether the engagement it produces is healthy or destructive. It cares only that it continues. A teenager spiraling into body dysmorphia is spending more time on the platform. More time on the platform is the metric that determines success. The harm is, from the algorithm's perspective, a feature.

Understanding this changes your relationship to the device in your hand. You are not a user exercising free choice. You are a behavioral profile being actively optimized. Every time you open the app out of boredom or anxiety, you are handing the system another data point it will use to tighten its hold. The pull you feel toward the screen is not curiosity. It is a response to an environment that has been designed, using everything it knows about you, to produce exactly that pull.

The political consequences of this system are not incidental. A feed optimized for outrage and tribal engagement will radicalize, gradually and invisibly, because outrage at an outgroup and fear of an enemy are among the most powerful engagement drivers the system has found. You do not join an extremist position the way you join a political party. You drift into it through a series of recommendations, each one slightly more extreme than the last, each one selected because your prior behavior indicated you would not look away. By the time the position feels like your own deeply held conviction, you have no memory of the drift. You remember only the certainty.

The solution is not willpower. You cannot outthink a system that has studied your behavior more carefully than you have. The solution is structural.

The action: This week, remove the social media applications from your phone. Not forever. One week. Keep the accounts if you want them; access them only from a desktop browser where the experience is slower and less engineered. Notice what happens in your body during the first two days. The discomfort you feel is not boredom. It is withdrawal from a system that has been dosing your nervous system with calculated stimulation. Notice what returns in the space: longer thoughts, slower attention, the ability to sit with an unresolved feeling without immediately reaching for distraction. That returning capacity is what the feed has been quietly consuming. It belongs to you.
creative-04-09-longing-9-language-shapes:
Longing 9: Language Shapes What's Possible

← Longing 8: The Past Doesn't Go Away · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 10: The Sacred Is Here →

Pillar: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible · Across every book

or On the word that ends thought, and the language that keeps the world open.

The most useful word to power is the one that settles the matter. The slogan, the clean phrase, the line you can repeat without thinking, the name that forecloses the argument before it starts. We reach for these words because ambiguity is tiring and a good slogan relieves the tiredness. It tells you what to feel and saves you the labor of working it out. That relief is exactly the opening.

Propaganda is built for this appetite. It renames things until the new name covers the old reality. It repeats a phrase until the phrase begins to feel like a fact. War becomes security. Cruelty becomes order. A whole false world can be assembled out of words and then closed over the real one, and the closing is the point. The finished phrase is a door swinging shut on thought.

Young was a writer who refused the closed phrase on principle. Her sentences open and open and open, qualifying, doubling back, declining to land on the tidy summary. People find the book difficult for exactly this reason, and the difficulty is the argument. She knew that language builds the world, and she refused to build a world that pretended to be finished. Her prose stays accountable to how much it is leaving out.

The ninth pillar holds language as construction, always, and that honest language is the kind that knows it. If you understand that words make worlds, you can hear a slogan as a piece of construction rather than a piece of reality. You can notice the door swinging and put your foot in it. The renamed thing keeps its old name in your mind. The repeated phrase does not harden into fact, because you can see the hands that are doing the repeating.

Honest language keeps the world open, which is tiring, and that is the cost of it. The closed phrase is a rest you cannot afford. Keep the sentence open. The open sentence is where you are still allowed to think.
creative-05-01-how-to-use-this-workbook:
How to Use This Workbook

← The Longing Under Each Pillar: A Workbook · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 1 Not One Self →

Each of the eleven essays names a hunger that power feeds on, and a pillar of Radical Immanence that answers it. Reading about the shift is one thing. Feeling it happen in your own body and your own week is another. This workbook is for the second kind of knowing.

The chapters describe an idea. The exercises here ask you to catch the hunger while it is active, usually in something small, and to practice the alternative until it stops being a concept and starts being a habit.

A few ways to work through it

  • One pillar a day, or one a week. Eleven pillars, eleven sessions. There is no prize for finishing fast, and the ethics of incompletion is one of the pillars, so take that as permission.

  • Read the short recap at the top of each section, then move straight into the exercises. You already read the full essay. This is the part where you test it against your actual life.

  • Each exercise has two parts. A Notice exercise, which asks you to catch the hunger in daily life before you try to answer it. And a Practice exercise, which is something to actually do, not just think about.

  • Write by hand if you can. The lines are there for that. If a question does not fit your week, skip it and come back later.

  • Nothing here needs to be shown to anyone. The only person this workbook is accountable to is you, on the page.

One last note before you start. Power's whole strategy in each pillar is to offer relief from a real ache. The exercises will not make the ache disappear. They will just show you that there is a way to hold it that does not require handing yourself over to someone selling a cure.
