creative-04-04-longing-4-witnessing-is-t:
Longing 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

← Longing 3: Grief Doesn't End · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary →

Pillar: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Across every book

or On the urge to look away, and the quiet power of refusing to.

It is exhausting to keep looking. There is too much, it is too much, and the most natural thing in the world is to turn the eyes somewhere easier. Power knows this and offers you several ways not to look. It offers spectacle, an endless bright churn of things to watch instead. It offers a single enemy, so that all your looking can be aimed in one safe direction. And it offers, at the rally, in the feed, the rare and intoxicating feeling of being seen yourself, which is its own way of stopping you from seeing.

What it cannot survive is a person who stays in the room and keeps their eyes open.

Young’s narrator is a witness above all else. She does not solve the people she loves. She does not look away from the mother in her drugged paradise or the nursemaid in her concealment. She stays, she watches, she keeps faith with what is actually in front of her, even when it offers her no resolution and no reward. The whole book is an act of refusing to leave the room.

The fourth pillar is that refusal. The witness is the one who does not flinch, does not change the channel, does not accept the spectacle in place of the thing, does not let the designated enemy absorb the whole of their attention. It sounds passive. It is not. To witness clearly, over time, without looking away, is one of the few things a person can do that power cannot easily undo, because you cannot be argued out of what you saw with your own eyes. The lie needs you to have not been looking.

You do not have to fix what you witness. That is a different pillar, and a relief. You only have to stay, and see, and refuse the comfort of the turned head. Most of what gets done in the dark is done counting on the fact that we would rather not look. Be the one who looks. Stay in the room.
creative-01-introduction-to-this-collect:
Introduction to this Collection

The Creative Radical Collection · The Captured Mind: How Cults, Strongmen, and Algorithms Stea →

This is a collection of short books about how a mind gets captured, and how it stays free.

They were written across a stretch of time, though the thing they describe has been arriving for a long time. The forms it takes look different from the outside. A cult. A strongman at a podium. A high-control church. The algorithm running quietly inside the phone in your pocket. The movement that takes someone you love and, gradually and then completely, makes them unreachable. From a distance these look like separate problems. Underneath, they run on the same mechanism. Something gets between a person and their own perception. Over time the person stops trusting what they see and starts trusting the authorized version. By the end they are not making choices. They are running a script that someone else wrote.

Every book in this collection is an attempt to interrupt that process. And every one of them is built from a single source that most people have never read.

Some years ago I picked up a novel called Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, by an American writer named Marguerite Young. It runs to nearly twelve hundred pages. Young worked on it every day for close to two decades. It was published in 1965 to a reception that was half astonishment and half bewilderment, admired by writers like Anais Nin and Kurt Vonnegut, and then it slipped out of the conversation and mostly stayed out. It is still in print. It is still almost never read.

I did not expect a difficult midcentury novel about a woman on a bus in Indiana to become a manual for the present moment. But the longer I read, the more I recognized. Young had mapped, decades early, the exact conditions that make a person easy to capture. The manufactured nostalgia for a past that never existed. The relief of being handed a world with no gray areas. The slow work of teaching someone to distrust their own memory. The permanent emergency that keeps a person too frightened to think. She wrote all of it into the structure of a novel, filtered through the mind of a woman searching for the one person who had once felt like solid ground.

For a long time I read the book as an answer to the dictator. I think I had the aim slightly wrong, and the correction is the reason this collection exists.

Young was not writing about the strongman. She was writing about the longing he feeds on. Before there is a regime, there is a personality that craves one clean answer and someone to follow. And before there is that personality, there is an ordinary human hunger, worn down by grief and contradiction and the exhausting work of being several people at once, that would hand all of it over for a single redeeming story. The dictator is not the beginning. He is what swallows the bait. Young spent her life inside the bait, naming it, mourning it, and refusing in the end to be consoled by it.

Her answer to that hunger was not a better story. It was not a truer leader or a corrected paradise waiting at the end of the march. Her answer was to stay here, in the ordinary and unfinished present, and to find it enough. I have come to call this Radical Immanence: the idea that meaning is not found by escaping ordinary experience but by going more deeply into it, into its contradictions, its incompletions, its refusal to resolve. That idea is the ground the whole collection stands on.

The books are arranged to be read in order, though you can move through them however you like.

The first, The Captured Mind, is the practical one. It takes the mechanisms apart one at a time, using documented cases from cults, political movements, and the technology companies whose own internal research told them what they were doing. It stays close to the evidence, and it ends each chapter with one concrete thing you can do, not to rescue the person you are worried about, but to protect and sharpen your own attention.

The second, The Creative Radical, goes underneath the mechanics to the philosophy that answers them. It lays out eleven pillars, eleven ways of standing in the world that a captured mind cannot hold. Each one is a refusal of a specific lie that control depends on, and each is carried by a real person who lived it.

The third, The Longing, is where I work out the correction I described above, the shift from writing against the strongman to writing against the appetite he exploits, and they take each pillar back down to the particular hunger it answers.

The Longing Workbook is unique to this collection. It turns the philosophy into practice. It is a set of exercises for catching the hunger while it is active, usually in something small, and for practicing the alternative until it stops being an idea and becomes a habit. Nothing in it needs to be shown to anyone.

A word about who this is for, since that is sometimes clearer than saying who it is not. It is not for people who are certain they are immune, because certainty of immunity is one of the first things these systems exploit. It is not for people who believe the captured are simply less intelligent or less informed than the free, because the evidence does not support that and one of these books explains at length why. It is for people who have stood at the edge of something they could not name and felt the ground shift. It is for people who love someone who has become unreachable. It is for people who have noticed something happening to their own thinking and want a language for it.

The cage that every control system builds is made entirely of stories. So is the key. These books are your permission to examine both.

Here is enough. The sentence has not ended.

Pillar Eight: The Past Doesn't Go Away

← Pillar Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Nine: Language Shapes What's Possible →

Pillar: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away · Across every book

Or, Why the Past Is Right Beneath Your Feet

We are trained to think of time as a giant, one-way conveyor belt. The future is ahead of us, the present is where we are standing, and the past is a distant land trailing out behind us. When bad things happen in history, or even in our own personal lives, people love to say: well, that is in the past now, or we need to look forward, not backward. We treat history like a book where the previous chapters are closed for good. Move on. Do not look back. The past has nothing to do with the present. This is the story we tell ourselves, and we tell it over and over, as if repetition could make it true.

But Marguerite Young looks at the clock and tells us that linear time is an illusion. The past does not recede. It does not float away into irrelevance. In her system, the past sediments. It accumulates right underneath our feet, layer upon layer, heavy and present.

The Geology of Our Minds

To understand this pillar, Young invites us to look at the earth itself. Think about a geological cross-section of rock layers beneath a riverbed. You have layers from millions of years ago, layers from ice ages, layers from recent floods. You have compressed shells from ancient seas. You have the ash from volcanic eruptions that happened long before humans walked the earth. None of those past eras have magically vanished into thin air. They are all physically present right now, stacked on top of one another, heavily pressing down on the surface we walk on today.

The weight of those layers shapes everything about the present moment. The river flows the way it does because of the rock layers beneath it. The soil composition in one place differs from another because of what sedimented there millions of years ago. The mineral content of the groundwater, the stability of the bedrock, the likelihood of earthquakes or floods in any given area: all of this is determined by the sedimentary layers beneath our feet. You cannot understand the present landscape without understanding its geological history.

Young argues that time works exactly like geology. The past does not float away. It layers up. Every joy you have experienced, every historical event, and every collective trauma is still right here, forming the invisible substrate of our current reality. The joy of your childhood does not disappear; it sediments into who you are now. The trauma that happened to your grandparents does not vanish; it shapes the nervous system you inherited. The slavery that built wealth for certain families does not fade into history; it compounds into the economic inequality we see today. The land theft that displaced indigenous peoples does not resolve itself; it shapes the property arrangements, the water rights, and the resource access that create the landscape of our present moment.

To bring this point home, Young's ideas connect with the philosopher Walter Benjamin and his famous image of the angel of history. Benjamin describes a painting by the artist Paul Klee, and in this painting, there is an angel. The angel is being pushed backward by a violent wind, a storm that is blowing it forward into the future. But the angel is not looking ahead toward the future. It is facing backward, looking at the past. And what does the angel see? Not a chain of linear events. Instead, it sees one single, massive catastrophe that keeps piling wreckage upon wreckage right at its feet. The past is always right there, loudly demanding our full attention. It is not behind us. It is beneath us, accumulated and pressing.

Benjamin wrote this in 1940, as the Nazi regime was destroying Europe. He was trying to make sense of how this catastrophe was possible, how humanity could perpetrate such violence. The answer, he suggested, is that the catastrophe was not some aberration. It was sedimentary. It had layers upon layers beneath it: centuries of colonialism, of slavery, of dehumanization, of the treatment of certain people as disposable. All of that sediment had accumulated, and the genocide was its eruption. You cannot understand the present catastrophe without understanding what sedimented beneath it.

Why Tyrants Want You to Forget the Sediment

So, how does shifting from a straight-line view of time to a layered view of time help us resist authoritarian power?

Authoritarian movements and dominant political systems absolutely love the straight-line progress narrative. They want you to believe that the past is a separate country that has nothing to do with today. That was then, this is now. We have progressed beyond those problems. That was a different era. This ideology allows them to cover up their tracks. It tries to convince you that the current setup of society is natural, fair, and neutral. It was not created by anyone. It just is.

When we embrace sedimentary time, we bust this narrative. We expose what was hidden beneath the straight-line story.

We expose the roots of wealth and power. We realize that things like the wealth extracted from centuries of enslaved labor are not just past events to be glossed over in a textbook. They are active, heavy layers in the current sediment, directly shaping today's economic and property arrangements. The fact that certain families own most of the land in certain regions, that certain cities have concentrations of wealth while others are disinvested: none of this is accidental or natural. It is sedimentary. It accumulated through specific historical choices that were made by specific people, and those choices are still shaping the landscape today.

We stop falling for fake progress. When a politician says we have moved past that era, a sedimentary mindset reminds us that you cannot just paint over a deep geological layer. The wreckage is still in the soil. The sediment is still pressing down. Building a just society requires attending to what is in the substrate rather than pretending the ground is neutral.

We protect collective memory. Authoritarians want a blank slate so they can rewrite history to fit their propaganda. They want you to believe that the regime is building something completely new, something unprecedented, something that has never been done before. This requires erasing all the layers that came before. Remembering that the past is always present beneath us prevents our collective memory from being erased. We refuse the blank slate. We insist on the layers.

Understanding time as a layered structure removes the mask from historical injustice. It shows us that the struggles of the past are not over. They are simply the ground we are standing on right now. Our job is not to move on from them. Our job is to understand them, to feel their weight, to acknowledge the people who suffered under those layers, and to take responsibility for the ground we are forming for those who come after.

The Archive and the Uncovered Ground: What We Found in the Swamp

To understand what sedimentary time means in practice, consider what happened when archaeologists and historians began to seriously study the Great Dismal Swamp: a vast wetland that spans the border between Virginia and North Carolina.

For centuries, this swamp had been treated as a barrier, a wasteland, a place to be drained and developed and turned into profitable land. But when historians began to look closely at what was actually in the swamp's sediment, they discovered something that the straight-line progress narrative had erased: the swamp had been a place of refuge for enslaved people. For over two hundred years, people fleeing slavery had found hideouts in the swamp's hidden channels and islands. They had built communities. They had maintained their dignity and their freedom in a place that the system wanted to treat as empty, uninhabitable wasteland.

The ground itself had been carrying that history. The swamp was not a blank slate waiting to be developed. It was a palimpsest of resistance and refuge, of struggle and survival. But the straight-line progress narrative had erased it. It had been treated as empty, as nothing, as worthless.

When archaeologists began to dig, to look at the sediment carefully, the layers began to tell their story. They found pottery fragments. They found the remains of structures. They found evidence of long-term habitation. They found archaeological proof that people had been living on that ground with intention and dignity, even though the official historical record had simply erased them.

This is what sedimentary time does. It refuses the erasure. It says: even though the system wanted to forget this, even though it was not written in the official history books, the ground itself carries the memory. The sediment knows. And when we pay close attention to the sediment, we recover what was taken from us.

A straight-line progress narrative would say: the past is past, slavery is over, we should move on. A sedimentary approach says: slavery is not over. Its effects are still in the economic structure, still in the laws, still in the trauma passed down through generations, still in the land arrangements, still in who owns what and who has access to what. The swamp's history of refuge is not a quaint historical detail. It is information we need right now to understand who we are and what ground we are standing on.

The Practice

Pick a physical place in your town or city. It could be an old building, a park, a street name, or even your own neighborhood. Do a little mental digging. What are the historical layers beneath it? Who lived there before? What built the economy of that space? Who benefited from those arrangements? What sediment is pressing down on the ground you are standing on?

Remind yourself that those older layers have not disappeared. They are actively pressing on the present moment. They are in the water table. They are in the property arrangements. They are in who has access to resources. They are in the inherited trauma and the inherited wealth. Practice standing on the ground with an awareness of everything it carries. Notice what changes when you stop treating the past as behind you and start treating it as beneath you.

Also apply this to your own body and your own history. The childhood you lived is not safely behind you. It is sedimentary in your nervous system. The losses you have suffered are not past events to move on from. They are compressed into your capacity to love and to be cautious. The family patterns, the cultural inheritances, the traumas passed down through generations: all of this is sediment. When you pay attention to it, when you refuse the straight-line progress narrative and acknowledge the layers, something shifts. You stop blaming yourself for your reactions. You start understanding them as sedimentary. And you start asking: what kind of sediment am I creating for those who come after me?

creative-03-07-pillar-seven-the-margins-:
Pillar Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Pillar Six: Unfinished is Honest · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Eight: The Past Doesn't Go Away →

Pillar: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · Across every book

Or, Why the Margins Are an Anti-Fascist Blueprint

From the time we are small, society loves to organize the world into neat, tidy boxes. We have rigid categories for almost everything: boy or girl, sane or crazy, productive worker or outcast, citizen or criminal, the person who belongs and the person who does not. We are taught to look at the center of these categories to understand what is normal, and we treat anyone who does not fit into the pre-made slots as a weird exception, an awkward remainder, a problem to be managed or corrected or hidden.

But Marguerite Young flips the script completely. She populates her entire world with characters who live right on the ragged edges of social expectation. And she does not treat them as cautionary tales or tragic exceptions. She treats them as the most reliable witnesses to the truth.

Where the Categories Show Their Seams

Young focuses her deepest attention on people who refuse to fit neatly into the system's boxes. They are not dismissed as eccentric side notes or colorful background characters. Young insists that these people are not distractions at all. They are the absolute center of her philosophical message.

Why? Because the margins are exactly where the categories show their seams. When you look closely at the edges of any box, you see the glue, the staples, the artificial joins, and the enormous amount of pressure required to hold the construction together. The person who does not fit the social mold is not a broken exception. They are the living evidence of how the mold was made, and who made it, and what it costs to maintain it.

This is a profound claim about what actually exists and what is real. Young is arguing that the margins are not outside reality. They see more than the center sees, precisely because they are not inside the system looking out. They are outside the system looking in, and from that vantage point the whole machinery becomes visible in a way it never is to those it was built to accommodate.

Think about what it means to fit perfectly into a social category. It means the category was built with you in mind. The doors are the right width for your body. The forms have a box for your name. The language has words for your experience. The history books include people who look like you doing things that matter. When the system fits you well, you tend not to notice the system at all. It feels like reality. It feels like the natural order of things.

But when the system does not fit you, you notice everything. You notice the width of the doors. You notice which boxes on the form do not apply to you and which ones erase you. You notice whose experience the language was built to hold and whose it was built to make unspeakable. You notice the gap between what the system claims to be and what it actually does to the people it cannot accommodate.

That noticing is not a wound, though it often feels like one. It is knowledge. It is the clearest possible view of how power actually operates, what it protects, what it discards, and where its seams are showing. Young builds her entire philosophy on that view. She trusts the margins more than the center because the margins have seen the construction from the outside. They know it is a construction. They have the evidence in their own bodies.

The Moving Bus

To illustrate what a community built on this principle actually looks like, Young gives us a beautiful and deceptively simple image: the passengers on a cross-country bus.

They are not a group of people who share the same background, the same politics, the same story, or the same destination. They are a collection of different, complex individuals, each carrying their own unique realities, their own permanent grief, their own inner crowd of contradictory selves. They did not choose each other. They are not bonded by ideology or agreement or shared identity. They are together because they are all, for this particular stretch of road, in transit through the same complicated world.

What holds them together is not forced sameness. It is the shared condition of movement, of being on the way, of witnessing each other's differences without demanding that those differences be resolved or erased. The bus does not require you to be the same as the person sitting next to you. It only requires that you share the road for a while.

This is Young's model for genuine community: not a group of identical people unified around a single identity, but a collection of irreducibly different people held together by the honest condition of being alive in the same world at the same time. The margins are not a threat to that community. They are its most essential members, because they are the ones who can see where the road actually goes and where the system's promises fall apart.

Why the System Needs You to Look Away from the Edges

So how does shifting our gaze to the margins help us resist authoritarian control?

Authoritarian movements grow by executing a very specific strategy: they destroy plurality. They demand that every person become legible, sortable, and if possible identical in their loyalty and their silence. They need the center to hold, which means they need the edges to disappear. They need the people who do not fit to be invisible, institutionalized, criminalized, or dead. Not because those people are dangerous in themselves, but because their existence is dangerous to the fiction the system depends on.

The fiction is this: the categories are natural. The boxes were not built by anyone. The people who fit inside them are normal, and the people who do not are aberrations. If you can keep that fiction intact, you can keep the center from asking why the boxes were built the way they were, who benefits from the current arrangement, and what would happen if the walls came down.

The person at the margin blows the fiction apart simply by existing visibly. They do not have to say anything. They do not have to make an argument. Their presence alone is evidence that the box is a construction, that normal is a choice, that the categories require maintenance and enforcement and the constant, exhausting work of making the seams invisible.

This is why authoritarian systems spend so much energy on the margins. They do not ignore them. They obsess over them. They pass laws against them. They build institutions to manage them. They invest enormous resources in making sure the people who do not fit stay out of sight, because the sight of them is destabilizing to everyone the system has convinced that the current arrangement is natural and inevitable.

When we center the margins, when we look at the edges and take seriously what is visible from there, we protect our communities from being captured by that fiction. We build a way of seeing that cannot be taken in by the system's claim to naturalness. We build people who know, from direct evidence, that the boxes are built and can be rebuilt differently.

The Ground That Knew Her: Harriet Tubman

To understand what it means to live at the margin and use that position as a source of power rather than a site of defeat, consider Harriet Tubman, who spent her entire life operating at the edges of every category the system tried to enforce, and who used that position to see things the center could not see and do things the center could not imagine.

Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland sometime around 1822. From the beginning, she existed at the intersection of every category the system used to control people: she was Black, she was a woman, she was enslaved, she was considered property. The law did not recognize her as a person. The social order did not have a box for her humanity. She was, in the system's terms, entirely outside the category of those whose lives counted.

She also had a neurological condition, likely narcolepsy caused by a severe head injury inflicted by an overseer when she was a child, that caused her to lose consciousness without warning and experience vivid, involuntary visions. By any standard the system recognized, this made her less valuable, less reliable, less predictable. It marked her further outside the category of the useful and the normal. It was one more way the system had of dismissing her.

But from the margin where all of this placed her, Tubman could see things that the center was structurally incapable of seeing.

She knew the land. She had worked it, moved through it, slept on it. She knew which swamps were passable and which were not, which roads were watched and which were forgotten, which farms were safe and which were dangerous. She knew the geography of the system from the outside, from the position of someone the system had never bothered to hide itself from, because it had never imagined she would use what she saw.

In 1849 she escaped north, alone, through nearly ninety miles of hostile territory. She arrived free. And then she went back.

She went back thirteen times. She led approximately seventy people out of slavery through the network that became known as the Underground Railroad. She used the landscape the system had built to contain people as the very infrastructure of their liberation. She used the darkness, the swamps, the forgotten roads, the edges of the map where the system's attention did not reach. She operated entirely in the margins, in the spaces the center had decided were not worth watching, and from those spaces she dismantled the system's hold on person after person after person.

The center could not have done this. A person operating from inside the system's categories, trusted and legible and accommodated by the existing order, would not have known where the seams were. Would not have known which roads were unguarded. Would not have had the intimate, embodied knowledge of how the system actually operated as opposed to how it claimed to operate. The margin was not a disadvantage. It was the source of everything Tubman knew and everything she could do.

The visions the system used to dismiss her, the involuntary losses of consciousness that marked her as unreliable, she understood as guidance. She trusted them. She said she never lost a passenger, and she credited those visions as part of how she navigated. What the system read as a defect, she read as information. What the center saw as the evidence of her limitation, she used as a tool.

This is what Young means when she focuses on the margins. It is not that suffering is good, or that exclusion is a gift, or that the violence of the margin should be romanticized. It is that the margin produces a specific and irreplaceable kind of knowledge that the center cannot generate. It is that the people the system has placed outside its categories are the people who can see the categories most clearly, who know where the walls are and how they were built and where the gaps are large enough to move through.

Tubman did not wait for the center to invite her in. She did not petition the system to recognize her humanity or revise its categories to accommodate her. She used what she knew from where she stood and she moved. She kept moving. She treated the margin not as a place of defeat but as a position of clarity, and from that clarity she did what the center had declared impossible.

After the Civil War, she continued. She worked for women's suffrage. She established a home for elderly African Americans in Auburn, New York, where she had settled. She kept operating at the edges of what the system recognized as legitimate political action, and she kept making things happen that the center had not authorized and could not fully account for.

She died in 1913, surrounded by people she loved, having spent her entire life using the view from the edges to see what the center refused to look at. She is buried in Auburn, on the ground she chose, in the place she made her own.

The system never found a box for her. That was never the point. The point was that she could see the boxes from the outside, and seeing them clearly was what made her free.

The Practice

Pay close attention to the places in your own life, your workplace, or your community where you or someone else does not fit into a standard social box. Instead of treating that mismatch as an awkward problem to fix, look at it as a moment of clarity. The edge is where the artificial seams of the system are showing. The person who does not fit is not the problem. They are the evidence.

Notice also when you are being asked to look away from the margins. When a system or a culture directs your attention toward the center, toward the normal, toward the people and stories that fit neatly into the established categories, ask what is being kept out of frame. Ask who is at the edge and what they can see from there that the center cannot.

And notice the knowledge you carry from your own experience of not fitting. The places where the system's categories did not hold you, where the boxes were the wrong shape for your life, where you had to find your own way through terrain the map did not acknowledge. That knowledge is not a wound to be healed. It is information. It is a view of the seams that most people never get. Treat it as the irreplaceable resource it actually is.
creative-03-01-pillar-one-not-one-self:
Pillar One: Not One Self

← The Creative Radical · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Two: Reality is Constructed →

Pillar: Pillar 1 Not One Self · Across every book

Or, Why Your Inner Crowd is an Anti-Fascist Superpower

We live in a culture that is absolutely obsessed with consistency. From the time we are kids, we are told to find our "true self," lock down our personal brands, and stay predictable.

Mainstream society treats a change of mind as a weakness, and holding contradictory feelings is often viewed as a moral flaw. We are under constant pressure to trim away our rough edges so we can fit neatly into a single, easily digestible box.

But Marguerite Young looks at all that pressure and tells us we are looking at identity completely backwards.

You Are a Verb, Not a Noun

Young's first big claim is wonderfully liberating: you are not a single, solid, unchanging object. You are a living, breathing crowd of different selves all navigating the world at the exact same time.

This inner multiplicity is not a problem to be solved or a mental health crisis to fix; it is the absolute, healthy condition of being alive. Think about it: the version of you that sits at a holiday dinner with your family is vastly different from the version of you that collaborates on a creative project, which is different again from the quiet voice inside your head when you are grieving a loss.

Traditional philosophy has spent centuries trying to protect the idea of a single, unified "I" ruling over our minds. But Young invites us to look at the actual experience of being human. As she beautifully demonstrates, the self is a verb, not a noun. It is an ongoing process of becoming a winding stream that flows in multiple directions at once.

Breaking the Sorting Machine

So, how does acknowledging your inner crowd protect you from tyranny?

The demand for a single, simple identity is not just an irritation: it is a highly effective political technology used to control populations.

Authoritarian movements and dictators thrive on a population that can be easily sorted. They need clean, rigid boundaries to build their power: us versus them, the loyal patriot versus the dangerous outsider, the productive worker versus the citizen who does not belong.

The more complex your inner world is, the harder you are for a regime to manage. When you accept your own internal multitudes, you actively jam their sorting machine.

When you are honest about your own complexity, you cannot be neatly filed away as just an enemy or just a loyalist. You become fundamentally un-sortable.

Because you recognize the diverse, shifting voices inside yourself, you are far less likely to fall for propaganda that tries to turn other human beings into flat, one-dimensional monsters. Your inner crowd becomes your ultimate shield against total control.

The Refusal: James Baldwin

This is not an abstract principle. The stakes of refusing to be sorted become clear when we look at what happens to people who actually do it.

The American writer James Baldwin spent his entire career holding contradictions that the dominant system wanted to reduce to a single label. He was a Black man writing in a literary tradition that had tried to erase Black presence. He was a gay man in an era when homosexuality was treated as a perversion to be hidden or fixed. He was an American writer living much of his life in exile in France. He was a literary artist who wrote essays of scorching political clarity. He was a man shaped by Christian faith and fierce atheism at the same moment.

The machinery of control wanted to file him away in a single box: "the gay writer," or "the Black writer," or "the protest novelist." Any single label would have made him manageable, his work categorizable, his threat containable.

But Baldwin refused. He wrote directly about this refusal, insisting that he would not reduce himself to fit the system's categories. In his essays and novels, he held all of these identities at once, refusing to apologize for the contradictions or to choose one over the others. His very refusal to be sorted made his work almost impossible to control. The system could not pin him down, could not use him as a symbol to settle a single debate, could not make him serve a single political narrative.

His inner crowd was not hidden or ashamed. It was on display, complex and irreducible, on every page. That complexity is what gave his work its devastating power. Because Baldwin would not simplify himself, his readers could not simplify the world he was describing to them. When you read Baldwin, you cannot sort people into clean categories. You cannot look away from the full humanity of those the system tries to reduce.

The regime does not love this. It cannot tolerate people who refuse to stay in a single box, because those people cannot be used as reliable tools. They become un-predictable, un-manageable, and contagious. Their refusal gives others permission to refuse as well.

The Practice

Try to pay close attention to the different "characters" that wake up inside you depending on where you are and who you are with. When a contradiction pops up (like feeling deeply lonely while surrounded by friends, or feeling incredibly brave and terrified at the exact same moment), do not try to fix it or force yourself to choose just one emotion.

Let the contradictions sit in the room. Releasing the demand to be perfectly consistent is the very first act of creative resistance.

Pay attention to when external systems or people try to flatten you into a single identity. Notice the pressure to choose: are you the caregiver or the person with your own needs? Are you the professional or the person with a messy inner life? Are you the victim of a loss or the person who is healing and moving forward? Notice that these forced choices are always a form of control.

The truth is that you are all of these things at once. Your refusal to pick one and discard the others is not a failure of clarity. It is a form of freedom.
creative-05-12-pillar-11-the-crossing-po:
Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

← Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here · The Creative Radical Collection · Closing Page →

Pillar: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point · Across every book

What are you carrying forward, and who is it for?

The deepest hunger is to belong to something that outlasts you. Power offers immortality through the bloodline or the nation, and asks you to give yourself away for it. This pillar offers the true version of the same largeness. You are made of the dead, and you are making the ground the not yet born will stand on. You are already the crossing.

Practice

Write down the names of people, living or dead, whose language, grief, or care you know you are carrying. They can be family, teachers, strangers, writers.

Practice

Now write one specific thing you are handing forward, to a child, a student, a friend, or someone not yet born. Make it concrete, not abstract, a habit, a phrase, a way of paying attention.

Reflection

What does it feel like to belong to something vast that does not need a leader or an enemy to hold it together?

What is one small, located act of care you can do this week that tends the actual generations around you?

Pillar: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End · Across every book

What loss have you been waiting to see paid back, rather than letting it simply stay?

The hunger is to be done with a loss, to have it explained, redeemed, or avenged, so you can be whole again. Power offers your grief a destination and a face. This pillar lets grief be weather, something you live inside rather than something you resolve. Carried without needing it paid back, it cannot be aimed at anyone.

Notice

Name one grief you carry that has not closed, and probably will not. It can be small or large. Notice, without judging it, whether any part of you has assigned it a cause or a culprit.

Practice

Write a letter to that grief. Do not ask it to leave and do not aim it at anyone. Describe it the way you would describe weather, something present, something that changes day to day, something you are learning to live under rather than something owed to you.

Reflection

Who or what have you wanted to blame for a grief that never found a proper target?

What changes in you when you set down the need for it to be avenged, even without the grief itself going away?

Longing 2: Reality Is Constructed

← Longing 1: Not One Self · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 3: Grief Doesn't End →

Pillar: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed · Across every book

or On the hunger for the secret truth, and the freedom of living without one.

We are told, constantly, that there is a real story under the visible one. That the news is a cover, that the official account hides the actual machinery, that if you could just pull back the curtain you would see the thing as it truly is. Some of this suspicion is healthy. Most of the time, though, it is a door.

Through that door walks the figure who says he has the real story. He tells it like it is. He names the hidden hand, the cabal, the enemy you could not see. The relief is immediate, because the worst feeling is not being lied to. It is not knowing, and he has cured the not-knowing. He has handed you one explanation that makes the whole churning mess cohere. This is how conspiracy works on a person. It is the hunger for bedrock, answered by a man with a shovel and a story.

Young’s whole novel is built to starve that hunger. Her narrator chases the one person who seemed entirely real, entirely without illusion, and discovers that the realist was masked too, that under the plain practical surface was another concealment. There is no figure in the book who turns out to be the solid ground. It is illusion the whole way down. And the strange thing Young insists on is that you can know this and still go on. You do not need the floor to be real in order to keep walking on it.

The second pillar is exactly that. There is no secret story that will finally explain everything, no curtain that pulls back on the real. It is masks, and construction, and appearance, and you live anyway. Once you have made your peace with that, the man with the shovel has nothing you need. You can sit inside uncertainty without grabbing the totalizing myth he is selling, because you are no longer desperate for bedrock. You have learned to stand on water.

The terror of no floor and the freedom of no floor are the same fact. Which one you feel depends on whether you are still waiting to be saved by the truth, or have decided to live without that particular rescue.

Longing 10: The Sacred Is Here

Pillar: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here · Across every book

or On the longing to be lifted out of the ordinary, and the danger in the height.

The ordinary is hard to bear sometimes. The grey Tuesday, the unremarkable life, the sense that the real and shining thing is happening elsewhere, higher up, and that you are stuck down here in the small and the dull. Into that ache comes the oldest offer of all. Let us lift you out. Here is a cause larger than your little life, a height worth climbing toward, a glory worth dying for.

And, in the same breath, worth killing for. This is where the longing turns. Power sacralizes itself. The nation becomes holy, the movement becomes a higher purpose, and once the cause lives up there in the sacred, any cruelty down here can be justified by it. The bodies become acceptable because the thing they are spent on is so exalted. Every transcendent cause keeps a ledger of the ordinary lives it burned to reach the height. The promise to lift you out of the grey is also a permission to do terrible things in the grey, for the sake of the bright thing above it.

Young points the other direction, downward and inward. The sacred in her work is not above the ordinary. It is inside it. It is in the dim room, the long bus ride, the unredeemed afternoon, the grief that does not resolve and the self that will not simplify. She called the central scene of her great book an opium addict’s paradise, a heaven located inside a small bedroom, and the irony is exact. The transcendence people reach for is right here, misrecognized, in the very life they are trying to escape.

The tenth pillar collapses the height into the present. If the sacred is already here, in the grey, then you do not need the cause to lift you to it, and no one can hand you a glorious reason to harm the actual life in front of you. There is nothing higher than this Tuesday to sacrifice this Tuesday for. The bus is not the waiting room for the sacred. The bus is where the sacred turned out to be.
creative-03-06-pillar-six-unfinished-is-:
Pillar Six: Unfinished is Honest

← Pillar Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth →

Pillar: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest · Across every book

Or, Why the Perfect Ending is a Trap

We live in a culture that is absolutely obsessed with the finished product. We want the clean resolution, the tied-up loose ends, and the satisfying final chapter. We treat an unfinished project like a failure, and an unresolved argument makes us deeply uncomfortable. From corporate milestones to our personal lives, there is a massive amount of pressure to cross the finish line, stamp a project as done, and move on. We celebrate the completed memoir, the solved problem, the person who has moved on from their trauma. We are trained to believe that a life well-lived is one where the chapters resolve properly, where closure is achieved, where you can finally say: I am finished with that.

But Marguerite Young steps in with a radical reality check. She argues that demanding everything be perfectly wrapped up and completed is actually a form of violence against our real, day-to-day human experience. It is a violence we commit against ourselves, against others, and against the work itself.

The Masterpiece of the Unfinished

Young's philosophy accepts the unfinished as the natural, honest state of things. Why? Because a philosophy that requires everything to be finished is a philosophy that can only describe a world that does not actually exist. The world does not resolve. Our inner selves do not stop changing. Our grief does not just vanish once we have processed it properly. Our work remains forever provisional. Our communities remain forever under construction. Our understanding deepens and then shifts again.

To insist that life must be finished is to insist that we must lie about this. It is to force ourselves and others to pretend that closure exists when it does not, that final answers are possible when they are not, that we can ever truly be done with anything that matters.

Young draws this insight from observing something crucial about human making. When we look at the work that lasts, the work that continues to matter across generations, it often carries the mark of incompletion. It does not pretend to be final. It does not close the door on further thinking. It leaves itself open to interpretation, revision, and deepening.

To help us understand this, consider Walter Benjamin, the German philosopher who spent years gathering thousands of notes, fragments, and reflections for a massive study on modern culture and the development of capitalism. The work was called The Arcades Project. Benjamin was obsessed with the great shopping arcades of Paris, those magnificent covered passageways that had just come into being during the nineteenth century. He wanted to understand what they meant: how they revealed the logic of modern desire, how they transformed urban space, how they embodied the fantasies and alienations of a new kind of human world.

Benjamin died in 1940, on the run from the Nazis, before he could assemble all those raw materials into a finished book. He left behind thousands of notes: observations, quotations from other texts, photographs, reflections, fragments of analysis. For decades, readers approached this work as an unfortunate incompleteness. If only Benjamin had lived, the thinking went, he would have organized all this material into a proper book, with a clear argument and a systematic structure. Then we would truly understand what he was trying to say.

But when you actually read the Arcades Project as Benjamin left it, you realize something startling: its incompleteness is its greatest strength. If Benjamin had forced all those raw, chaotic pieces of history into a neat, polished, systematic textbook, he would have ruined the entire point. The fragments needed to stay fragments to be honest to real life. The quotations needed to accumulate without being resolved into a single argument. The incompleteness was not a failure. It was total integrity.

The form of the Arcades Project mirrors its content. It is a book about capitalism, about the way modern systems promise coherence and resolution while actually delivering fragmentation and endless desire. To write about fragmentation while pretending to coherence would be a lie. To write about endless accumulation while organizing everything into a tidy conclusion would be dishonest. Instead, Benjamin's incompleteness says something that no finished argument could: this is what it actually feels like to live in this world. This is how knowledge actually accumulates: in fragments, in layers, in unresolved observation. This is what honesty looks like.

When we finally encounter the Arcades Project as it actually exists, we have to do something harder than reading a finished book. We have to engage with the thinking itself. We have to let the fragments work on us. We have to sit with the tensions and contradictions. We have to resist the urge to resolve everything into a single, clean meaning. And in doing that, we become part of the work's ongoing process. We become collaborators in its incompletion. The book does not tell us what to think; it invites us to think alongside it, to find our own connections, to build our own understanding.

This is what Young means by the ethics of incompletion. It is not laziness. It is not a failure to finish. It is, instead, a commitment to honesty about the nature of knowledge, human relationships, and the work itself. It is refusing to compress lived experience into a false finality.

Busting the Political Long Con

So, how does celebrating the unfinished protect us from authoritarian control?

In daily life, the demand for a perfectly finished product can feel like standard social pressure. But at a political scale, Young warns us that this demand is exactly what produces the long con: the confidence scheme that authoritarian movements depend on to maintain their power.

Authoritarian movements and deceptive leaders pull off this con by claiming they have the absolute, perfectly completed answers to all of society's problems. They present rigid platforms, unshakeable positions, and flawless policy statements to project total authority. They want you to believe their system is entirely finished, entirely thought through, and therefore beyond question. A demagogue does not say: here is my preliminary thinking on this problem, and I will revise it as I learn more. That would invite scrutiny and revision. Instead, the authoritarian says: I have the perfect solution. It is complete. It is unshakeable. You simply have to trust me and follow it.

This finished, perfect, unquestionable system is the entire basis of totalitarian control. It leaves no room for adaptation. It admits no error. It demands absolute compliance because to question any part of it would be to question the whole thing, and the whole thing is, by definition, perfect.

When we embrace the ethics of incompletion, we dismantle this trap.

We unmask the false promise: We recognize that any political leader pretending to have a flawless, permanent fix is running a manipulation tactic. No human being has finished answers to complex problems. Anyone claiming they do is lying, and the lie is the whole con.

We keep power adaptable: A policy that claims to be finished is incredibly dangerous because it cannot be revised or corrected when it starts causing real-world harm. It is frozen in place. It becomes a weapon. An institution built on the principle that it is forever unfinished, forever open to revision, forever willing to ask if it is causing harm, remains responsive to the actual needs of actual people.

We treat rules as active conversations: Instead of viewing founding political documents as sacred, untouchable monuments, we see them for what they truly are: ongoing, living arguments that must change as we learn more about what works and what does not. The original architects of a system are not prophets. They are human beings with limited perspective, shaped by the particular moment they lived in. Their work deserves respect, but not veneration. It deserves revision.

By building the unfinished directly into our mindsets and our institutions, we protect our communities from becoming frozen into tools of tyranny. We ensure that power remains transparent, accountable, and open to revision. We create a structure where every person in the system has the responsibility and the right to say: this is not working, we need to change it. And the system can actually respond and change, rather than demanding that reality itself conform to the finished blueprint.

The Cost of Closure: The Archive Wars

To understand what it actually costs to demand closure, it helps to look at how archives work as a site of political struggle. The historical archive is never complete. It is always fragmentary. It is always shaped by what was preserved and what was destroyed, by whose voices were recorded and whose were silenced. The official history that gets written in textbooks is actually a curated selection from a much messier, more contradictory body of material.

What happens when a regime demands that history be finished, organized into a clean narrative, resolved into a single official story? What gets left out? Whose experiences become untellable because they do not fit the narrative arc?

The answer is always the same: the people who were already on the margins. The women whose labor built a movement. The artists whose visions did not serve the new state. The dissidents who wanted something different. The complex, contradictory human beings who could not be reduced to a single role in the official story. All of them have to be compressed into a finished narrative, or erased from it entirely.

What protects us from this erasure is the refusal to finish the archive. It is the commitment to preserving the fragments, the letters that do not fit, the photographs that complicate the official record, the voices that were not supposed to survive. An archive that stubbornly remains incomplete, that resists easy narration, that forces readers to sit with contradiction and ambiguity, is an archive that cannot be used for propaganda. It cannot be turned into a finished justification for power.

The fragments remain difficult. They remain unglamorous. They remain hard to turn into an inspiring national story. But they remain true. And in remaining true, they preserve the possibility of a more honest future: one that is not built on the lie of a finished past, but on the honest weight of everything that actually happened.

The Border That Would Not Close: Gloria Anzaldúa

To understand what the ethics of incompletion actually demands of a person, consider Gloria Anzaldúa, who spent her life refusing to let the wound close on command.

Anzaldúa grew up on the Texas-Mexico border, in a family that had worked that land for generations before a line was drawn across it and half of what they knew became a foreign country. She grew up between languages, between cultures, between the identity her community expected of her and the desires and visions she could not suppress. She was Chicana and queer and a mystic and a scholar and a poet, and none of those things resolved neatly into the others. The border was not just geography. It was the permanent condition of her inner life.

When she wrote Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza in 1987, she made a formal choice that most editors and academics found uncomfortable: she refused to finish it. Not in the sense that she ran out of time, but in the sense that the book's form enacts its argument. It moves between Spanish and English without translation, trusting the reader to sit with what they cannot fully parse. It moves between scholarly essay and poetry and memoir and myth without signaling which register is primary. It circles back. It contradicts itself. It leaves threads hanging. It refuses to arrive at a single, clean thesis that a reader can extract, summarize, and shelve.

This was not a failure of craft. Anzaldúa was a meticulous writer who revised obsessively. The incompletion was the point. She was writing about a wound, and she understood that a wound that closes too quickly does not heal. It festers. The honest thing, the only ethical thing, was to leave the border open on the page the way it remained open in her body. To force a tidy conclusion onto that material would have been to lie about what the border actually does to a person. It would have been to perform recovery she had not achieved and could not honestly claim.

She called the consciousness that lives in this unresolved space the new mestiza consciousness, a way of thinking that holds contradiction without demanding resolution. It is not comfortable. It is not efficient. It does not produce clean arguments or settled identities. But it is honest, and in its honesty it is more durable than any finished system. A person who has learned to live in the borderland, to tolerate the open wound, to work from the unresolved center, is a person who cannot be captured by any ideology that promises to finally sort them out.

Authoritarian systems cannot tolerate the open border. They need the wound to close, the identity to settle, the edges to be declared and defended. A person who insists on living in the unresolved space between categories is a person the sorting machine cannot process. Anzaldúa's refusal to finish, her insistence on leaving the book and the self permanently open to revision, was not a personal limitation. It was a structural refusal of the demand for completion that power depends on.

She died in 2004 with several projects unfinished. The scholars who came after her found the fragments and the drafts and the notes. Some tried to assemble them into finished arguments. Others understood that the fragments were already doing their work exactly as they were, the same way Benjamin's arcades kept speaking through their incompletion. The unfinished work was not waiting to be completed. It was complete in its incompletion. It was telling the truth about what it cost to live at the border, and the truth required the open form.

The Practice

Find one thing you are currently working on or worrying about that feels frustratingly incomplete. It could be a messy creative draft, a house project that never quite gets finished, or a complicated relationship dynamic that never quite resolves. It could be your understanding of a historical event, or your relationship to a loss that just refuses to fully heal.

Instead of stressing over how to force a quick ending, take a deep breath and give yourself permission to leave it unfinished for a moment. Tell yourself: this messiness is not a failure; it is honesty. Notice how much breathing room opens up when you stop demanding an immediate arrival.

Also notice the language you use when you talk about unfinished things in your life. Do you call them failures? Do you apologize for them? Do you rush to fix them before anyone else notices? What if you reframed the incompletion as integrity instead? I am still working on this. This is more complex than I can resolve right now, and that is okay. I do not have the answer yet, and I am learning as I go.

When you hear a political figure claim to have all the answers, all the finished solutions, the perfect plan, pause. Remember Benjamin's fragments. Remember that anyone claiming to have finished the work is lying. The only honest politics is one that admits: we are building this together, we will get it wrong, we will need to revise, and that is where our actual power lives.

What are you still waiting to finally finish, and what have you been told it will give you?

The hunger is to arrive, to reach the finished nation, the completed project, the end of the long march. This pillar refuses the final state and calls the refusal a virtue. The unfinished is the living. A person who has stopped needing the work to be done cannot be sold a final solution.

Longing 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Longing 6: Unfinished Is Honest · The Creative Radical Collection · Longing 8: The Past Doesn't Go Away →

Pillar: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · Across every book

or On the wish to be at the center, and the contempt it quietly requires.

Everyone wants to matter. To be in the main story, part of the real action, one of the people who count. It is a clean and human wish, and power knows precisely how to use it. It builds a center and a margin. It tells you that you belong at the center, with the real people, the true citizens, the heartland, the core. And the price of that belonging, never stated but always understood, is your contempt for whoever has been placed at the edge.

That is the quiet machinery of it. To be told you are central, you must agree that someone else is not. The us is manufactured out of the them. Every politics of purity runs on this exchange, offering you the warmth of the center in return for your willingness to despise the margin.

Young’s attention goes the other way, almost stubbornly. Her novel is full of people the world would file under minor. A waitress, a spinster cousin, a small-town nursemaid, an addict in a dim room. She treats them not as background but as the place where reality is densest. The overlooked figure, in her hands, carries as much being as any great man. She grants full reality to exactly the people a politics of the center would tell you do not finally count.

The seventh pillar is that grant. The marginal is not lesser being. The person at the edge is as real as the person at the podium. Once you hold that, the whole architecture of center and enemy loses its floor, because you cannot be sent to clean out a margin you know to be where life actually lives. The contempt the bargain required of you is simply no longer available.

You wanted to matter. You do, but so does the person you were being invited to look down on, and exactly as much. That symmetry is inconvenient for anyone trying to build a pure center. Which is precisely why it is worth keeping.
creative-05-11-pillar-10-the-sacred-is-h:
Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

← Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible · The Creative Radical Collection · Pillar 11 The Crossing Point →

Pillar: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here · Across every book

Where have you been waiting to feel lifted out, when the thing you wanted might already be here?

The hunger is to be lifted out of the grey ordinary into something glorious, a cause worth dying for and worth killing for. Power sacralizes itself and any present cruelty is justified by the height of the cause. This pillar puts the sacred here, in the ordinary afternoon, so no one can hand you a transcendent reason to harm the actual life in front of you.

Notice

Notice one truly ordinary moment today, a bus ride, doing the dishes, waiting in line. Notice any impulse to rush past it toward something more meaningful.

Practice

Sit inside one ordinary moment for a few minutes on purpose. Do not use it to plan or scroll or escape. Look for what is actually here, without needing to leave it for something higher.

Reflection

What have you been waiting to feel somewhere else that might already be available in this Tuesday?

What cause or ideal have you been tempted to place above your actual, ordinary life?
creative-02-07-chapter-7-the-machine-tha:
Chapter 7: The Machine That Speaks for You

← Chapter 6: Why Facts Aren't Enough · The Creative Radical Collection · The Creative Radical →

"he was the counterfeit of himself — this face which passed for his face and yet was not his identical face — though others should recognize him and torment him by their mystified recognition"

Every control system described in this book required human labor. A demagogue had to give speeches. A cult leader had to run meetings. An abuser had to be in the room. The reach was always limited by the hours in a day and the number of people one person could touch.

Artificial intelligence removes that limit entirely.

We are not yet living in the science fiction version of this threat, the sentient machine with its own agenda. We are living in something more mundane and more dangerous: a technology that allows human agendas, including the most destructive ones, to scale beyond anything previously possible. The question is not whether AI will become malevolent. The question is who is already using it, for what purpose, and what legal or social infrastructure exists to stop them.

The answer to the last part, as of now, is: very little.

On the evening of January 21, 2024, thousands of registered Democrats in New Hampshire began receiving a phone call. The call opened with the phrase "What a bunch of malarkey," a common Biden expression, and the voice told recipients not to vote in Tuesday's presidential primary, claiming that voting would only enable Republicans. The voice was indistinguishable, to most listeners, from the voice of the sitting President of the United States. It had been artificially generated. The call was spoofed to appear on caller ID as coming from a prominent Biden supporter, to make it appear sanctioned.

The New Hampshire attorney general opened an investigation the following day. A political consultant named Steven Kramer was eventually charged with thirteen felony counts of voter suppression and thirteen misdemeanor counts of impersonating a candidate. In 2025, he was found not guilty. His lawyers argued that the use of deepfake technology was protected speech rather than voter suppression, and that he had not impersonated a candidate because Biden's name was never spoken and he was not on the primary ballot.

Read that outcome carefully. A synthetic presidential voice was used to tell Democratic voters to stay home. The person who created it was acquitted. The legal system could not find language sufficient to name what had happened.

This is where we are. The technology for generating a convincing clone of any public figure's voice costs almost nothing and requires no specialized knowledge. A 2024 report by the cybersecurity firm Recorded Future documented 82 pieces of AI-generated deepfake content targeting public figures across 38 countries in a single year, with a disproportionate number focused on elections. These are only the cases that were identified and tracked. The ones that were not detected left no record of themselves.

The deeper threat is not any single deepfake. It is what the existence of deepfakes does to your relationship with all media. When you know that any voice can be cloned, any image fabricated, any video altered with no visible seam, you face a version of the gaslighting described in Chapter 3, but now operating at civilizational scale. You can no longer trust your ears. You can no longer trust your eyes. The rational response to this environment is epistemic paralysis: the feeling that it is simply impossible to know what is real, and that the effort of trying is not worth the exhaustion.

Epistemic paralysis is enormously useful to people in power. A population that has given up on the possibility of shared truth is a population that can be managed through whatever story is most aggressively distributed. If nothing can be verified, then the loudest voice wins by default. This is not an accident. The liar's dividend, as researchers have named it, means that the existence of deepfakes allows real footage of genuine events to be dismissed as fabricated. A politician caught on video committing a crime says: that's AI. The burden of proof, which used to rest on the person making the accusation, now rests on the person presenting the evidence.

The cognitive offloading problem runs alongside this. When AI can answer any question, summarize any document, and generate any text in seconds, the brain does what brains always do when a shortcut is available: it stops doing the work. This is not laziness. It is the same energy-conservation instinct that makes every other cognitive shortcut appealing. But the consequence of outsourcing your thinking to a system trained on existing data, shaped by the incentives of its creators, and incapable of genuine uncertainty is a gradual narrowing of your own analytical range. You stop cross-examining sources. You stop sitting with ambiguity. You stop developing the tolerance for complexity that is the only real defense against a simplified, manipulated world.

The defense is not to refuse all technology. It is to refuse to let any technology do your thinking for you.

The historical parallel worth sitting with here is the printing press. When Gutenberg's press made text reproducible at scale in the fifteenth century, it produced two things simultaneously: the democratization of knowledge and the industrialization of propaganda. Bibles and pamphlets. Scientific treatises and forgeries. The same technology that made the Reformation possible also made the systematic manufacture of religious disinformation possible. Europe spent the next century and a half in a series of catastrophic conflicts that were fueled in significant part by the weaponization of the new medium.

We are inside a similar moment now, compressed into years rather than centuries because the technology moves faster. AI has already democratized the production of persuasive text, realistic synthetic media, and automated disinformation at a scale that would have been unimaginable five years ago. The same tools that allow a novelist to work through structural problems at midnight or a researcher to synthesize a literature review also allow a political operative to generate ten thousand personalized pieces of targeted misinformation and deploy them before breakfast.

The question that the printing press eventually forced, after considerable violence, was not whether the technology could be controlled. It could not be, entirely, and attempts to control it through censorship mostly entrenched the powerful and suppressed the inconvenient. The question it forced was how citizens develop the capacity to navigate an environment saturated with reproducible text, some true, some false, some weaponized, without a reliable external authority to sort it for them. The answer, worked out slowly and imperfectly over centuries, was a set of practices: source evaluation, cross-referencing, institutional verification, the cultivation of a reading public with enough critical apparatus to make independent judgments.

We are going to have to work out the AI equivalent of those practices. They do not exist yet in anything like a stable form. What we have are instincts, and the most important one is this: your uncertainty is a feature, not a malfunction. A mind that remains genuinely uncertain about AI-generated content, that treats its own first reaction to a synthetic voice or a generated image with suspicion rather than acceptance, is a mind doing exactly what the moment requires. The systems described in this chapter are designed to produce certainty, compliance, and the comfortable feeling of having understood something quickly. Resist the comfort. The discomfort of not knowing is where your judgment lives.

The other instinct worth cultivating is specificity. Generalized distrust of all media, of all technology, of all institutions, is not a defense. It is paralysis, and it is exactly the condition that makes a person susceptible to whoever speaks with the most confidence into the void that distrust creates. Specific, targeted, evidence-based skepticism is different. It asks not "can I trust anything" but "what is the specific chain of verification for this specific claim." That question is harder and slower. It is also the only one that leads anywhere useful.

When a claim is alarming or convenient, find the primary source. Not a summary, not a clip: the full, unedited original. When a voice or image seems designed to produce an immediate emotional reaction, pause before that reaction becomes a conviction. When AI generates an answer that resolves your uncertainty cleanly and quickly, notice the relief you feel and treat it with suspicion. Clean, quick resolution is not a feature of complex reality. It is a feature of systems designed to keep you moving without stopping to look.

The action: This week, choose one topic you have been relying on AI or social media to interpret for you, whether that is a political situation, a medical question, or a historical claim. Find one primary source on that topic: a government document, a peer-reviewed paper, an unedited transcript, a physical book. Read it slowly. Notice how different it feels from the version you had been carrying. The difference between those two versions is the gap that every manipulative system, human or automated, lives inside.

Chapter 5: The Recursive Phrase The phrase as an infinite spiral (Pillar 5)

← Chapter 4: Witnessing the Raw Gesture Working the sacred ord · Art When Here Is Enough · Chapter 6: Stumbles, Spasms, and Lost Balance The truth at t →

I. The Philosophy: You Build on Sand, So Build Anyway

Dance culture sells the set piece. Learn the choreography, clean it, run it, and you arrive at the finished work, identical night after night. The piece is handed to you as a fixed truth that exists before you and outlasts the performance. Your job is to execute it without deviation. A mistake is a betrayal of the work.

Radical Immanence works the other way. You build phrases, ideas, projects, knowing they have no solid foundation and will need to be rebuilt, and knowing that dance more than anything vanishes the moment it is made. That is not a failure. It is the only honest way to work. What you build teaches you something, and you use that lesson to build again. The self is not a fixed thing waiting to be expressed. It is an ongoing process, made and remade in the doing, and unmade the instant it is done.

In the studio this becomes the recursive phrase. Each movement sits on the temporary ground of the movement before it, still moving, still falling forward. Nobody hands you a foundation. You make a provisional one, you learn what it can hold, and you make the next one out of what you learned. The honest shape of the work is not the closed loop that returns to its start and seals shut. It is the spiral, which comes back near where it began but never to the same point, always one turn further out, always carrying the last turn inside the muscle memory. The phrase does not exist before you make it. The phrase is what your body is learning as it goes.

II. Deep Journal Prompts

The Style You Outgrew. Write about a technique or a style you once trained faithfully and have since left behind. Do not frame it as a phase you were too naive for. Frame it as a foundation that did its job: it held you up long enough to teach you the thing that let you leave it. What did that outgrown training give you before you set it down? What are you standing on right now that you will eventually outgrow the same way?

The Next Turn. Recall your most recent piece, or the one you are making now. Without judging it, write down the single most interesting thing it taught your body: a weight shift, a fall, a mistake that felt alive. Now write the first instruction for the next piece using only that lesson. You have just made the spiral visible: the new work growing directly out of the old, with no set choreography in between.

III. Studio Exercises

The Spiral That Feeds Itself

Move a piece with no plan and one rule: every new movement must be generated by feeling the movement before it. You begin with a single small gesture, a shift, a fall, a reach, chosen freely. After that you are not allowed to invent. You may only respond.

Phase 1. The seed. Make one small, honest beginning. Do not plan past it. Come to stillness and feel it settle in the body as if someone else had moved it.

Phase 2. The reading. Ask the last movement a plain question with your body: what does this need next? Maybe it left you off balance, so the next movement has to catch the fall. Maybe it wound you up, so the next one unwinds. Let the momentum you already made give the order.

Phase 3. The turn. Move the next phrase as the answer. Then feel again, and answer again. Keep spiraling outward. The dance grows by self-reference, each movement shaped by the momentum of the one it came from, never by a set combination.

The Teaching Fall

Deliberately try a movement you expect to fail. Push past what your body can control, a balance that will topple, a turn you cannot land, a drop you cannot catch. When it fails, and it should, do not throw it out and do not fix it. Repeat it and study it. Feel and then write the one thing the failure taught you. Then build a new phrase whose entire design comes from that one lesson. The failed movement is not waste. It is the temporary ground the next phrase stands on.

IV. Cross-Medium Interference

The Score Made of Questions

Write a score for the next dancer, except it contains no instructions. Every line is a question instead of a command. Not travel downstage in four counts, but where would you go if no one were watching from the front? Not repeat the phrase twice, but what does your body want to repeat right now, and how long until it gets bored? Hand this question-score to a friend, or pin it in the studio. A score made of questions cannot be obeyed, only answered, and every answer turns the spiral one more time.
