Chapter Five. Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary: The End Is the Beginning Renamed

← Chapter Four. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act: The Awe Is · Be Bak in a Whale · A Closing Note. Where the Philosophy Meets the Person →

Pillar: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Across every book

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The novel ends where it begins.

Not literally. Not in the way that circular narratives return to their opening sentences and close the loop. Young’s ending is not the same as her beginning. But the ending contains the beginning, the way the Earth contains everything it has been given: present, layered, transformed but not gone. Vera is still on the journey. Esther is going back into the whale. The sentence hasn’t ended. The question the novel opened with, what do you do when the solid ground turns out to be a construction, has not been answered so much as deepened, turned over, returned to from a different angle with everything the journey has taught, and found to contain more than it appeared to on the first pass.

Young does this again and again across 1,198 pages. The images return. The grief accumulates rather than resolving. The characters circle back through their own histories and find them changed by the circling. The end is the beginning renamed. The beginning is the end approached from the other direction. The novel moves the way memory moves and grief moves and the plural self moves: not forward in a line but recursively, each pass finding what the previous pass had walked past, each returning to the beginning discovering that the beginning contains more than it appeared to the first time through.

This is not a formal experiment for its own sake. It is Young enacting the fifth pillar in the structure of the novel itself, before the reader has the language to name it.

You build anyway.

⁂

The fifth pillar of Young’s philosophy is this: you build anyway. Knowing the building is provisional. Knowing the map is wrong before the ink dries. Knowing the finished structure will be less than you imagined and more than you expected and already in need of revision by the time it is complete. You build because the recursive attempt is the only form of integrity the system allows. Because building is what it means to keep going, and keeping going is what the witness does after it has stayed in the room long enough to understand what the room actually contains.

This is where Young’s philosophy becomes livable. The first four pillars are descriptions of a world that is genuinely difficult to inhabit: the self is plural and unstable, reality is constructed and contested, grief is permanent, and the only honest ethical stance requires a quality of attention that most of us cannot sustain for long without relief. It would be reasonable, having followed Young this far, to ask what exactly is being offered.

The fifth pillar is the answer. Not a consolation. Not a resolution. The answer: you build. You return to the beginning with what you learned on the last pass. You build again. The structure is always under construction and that is not its failure. That is its honesty. The recursive attempt is not the second-best version of a finished thing. It is the only form available to a self that is honest about its own condition.

⁂

I didn’t realize it until I wrote this book that my Substack is the personal recursive construction.

The early writings were spaghetti thrown at the wall. I knew I was doing it. I threw them anyway because the alternative was to wait until I understood enough to write with authority, and waiting would have meant not writing, and not writing would have meant not finding out what I understood. The throwing was the thinking. The wall was the test. What stuck was the kernel, and the kernel was the thing worth keeping even when everything around it was imperfect.

I thought about deleting the early work. The impulse is understandable because the early attempts are visibly imperfect, the thinking is incomplete, the language is reaching for something it hasn’t found yet. A reader coming to the Substack now would find the early posts and see the distance between where the work began and where it is.

I let it pile up.

Not because I couldn’t see the imperfections. Because the pile is the argument. The early attempts with three volumes of To All My Darlings and then revising that into a second edition that I thought would make it more manageable that instead expanded it with more information I had mined from multiple readings to taking volume three and expanding each of those into its own book and then exploding my Substack with multiple posts a day because there was so much I needed to get out of my head, just dump it, to try to clarify, until finally settling on a simpler, shorter (still 500 pages) of A Guide to Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling and then AND: The Philosophy of Marguerite Young then to this book are all part of the same construction, and the construction only makes sense as a construction, as a thing that is visibly being built rather than a thing that arrived complete. The early kernels are the foundation the current understanding stands on. To delete them would be to pretend the current understanding arrived without the foundation, which would be the same dishonesty Miss MacIntosh committed when she insisted the solid world had always been solid.

The pile is the sediment. The layers are the geological record of a thinking mind working through a problem that keeps revealing itself to be larger than the previous pass had accounted for. Nothing erased. Everything present. The early imperfections and the later precision and all the readings between them, layered, carrying each other forward the way the Earth carries everything it has been given.

⁂

The word recursive is precise and worth unpacking.

A recursive process is one that calls itself as part of its own operation. That uses its own output as part of its input. That loops through its own structure in order to proceed. The recursive story is the one that keeps returning to its own beginning, not to repeat it but to find something new in it on each return, to discover that the beginning contains more than it appeared to the first time through.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is a recursive novel. The wig appears and reappears. The grief accumulates rather than processing. Vera’s journey circles through itself. The novel does not move from beginning to middle to end in the linear sense. It moves the way Young’s mind moves, returning to what it cannot let go of, finding new layers on each return, deepening rather than resolving. The end is the beginning renamed because the journey has changed what the beginning means. Vera arriving at What Cheer, if she arrives, will not find the What Cheer she imagined when she set out. She will find what the journey has made of it, which is always more complicated and more honest than the destination imagined before the journey began.

This is what my five readings of the novel are. Five passes through the same recursive structure, each one finding what the previous pass had walked past, each one arriving at a different What Cheer than the last. The first reading produced drowning and the last line and the knowledge that I would come back. The second produced characters and the beginning of the philosophy. The third produced the wig sentence and Roe and the personal foundation collapsing. The fourth produced Jonah’s whale and Esther and the geological carrying. The fifth produced the system, the five pillars, the understanding that Young had built something complete whose completeness was not the destination but the building.

And there will be a sixth reading. There will always be a next pass. The novel keeps generating new surfaces because it was built that way, recursively, each layer placed with the knowledge that the next reader’s return would find something the current reader had walked past. The excitement is real because the discoveries are real.

⁂

Young spent eighteen years building the novel and she did not stop there. Harp Song for a Radical, the Debs biography, grew to 2,400 pages of manuscript at the time of her death. She was still building. Still returning to the beginning with what she had learned on the last pass. Still finding that the territory was larger than the previous map had accounted for.

She did not finish.

That is not a tragedy. It is the fifth pillar enacted at the scale of a life. The building that knows it is building. The map that knows it is wrong before the ink dries and draws itself anyway. Young did not stop when the novel was published because the novel was not the destination. It was the pass. The next pass was already beginning. The sentence had not ended. It had not ended because the world that made it necessary had not ended and the self that was writing it was not singular and stable and therefore finished but plural and ongoing and therefore always in the middle of the next return.

This is what Young means when she says the sentence hasn’t ended. Not that the novel is incomplete. That the recursive construction is the condition of honest work and honest work does not end when a particular structure is finished. It ends when the worker does, and even then the Earth carries what was built into the next pass made by the next witness who finds the thread and pulls it.

⁂

Maybe this book is the final touch.

Finally having the language to express the journey with this book. The reading guide that holds the reader’s hand through the novel’s considerable demands. The philosophy named and placed in conversation with the thinkers it anticipated and surpassed. And now this, the inside account, the record of five readings and what they built. The story of the reader who drowned the first time and came back and kept coming back and found in the coming back the only method adequate to what Young had built. The story of how long it takes to learn a language in order to express what was found and experienced while reading a book.

Maybe this is it.

Maybe there is still more.

Both of those sentences are true simultaneously and Young’s system is the only one I have encountered that does not require me to resolve them into one. The fifth pillar holds them together: the building that names what it has built and leaves the door open and puts it out there and trusts the carrying. Not as a failure to commit. As the honest acknowledgment that the territory keeps revealing itself to be larger than the current map, and the revelation is not a problem. It is the condition of genuine work.

I am perfectly willing to receive more from anyone who starts this journey.

That sentence is the fifth pillar stated as a personal practice. The building released into the carrying. The work is put out there for the next witness who arrives with different tools and a longer reach and finds in the pile the kernel that the current pass had not yet known what to do with. The door left open not from uncertainty but from the understanding that the room is larger than any single occupant, that the work is larger than any single life, and that what you build with full attention and release into the world’s keeping will be carried further than you can follow.

⁂

The five pillars build on each other in a specific direction.

The plural self is the ground: the honest account of what selves actually are, which dismantles the demand for the singular acceptable self and the threat that enforces it. Illusion as primary is the epistemological consequence: if the self is plural then reality is constructed, and if reality is constructed then the question of whose construction dominates is the central political question. Grief as permanent weather is what you live in when you have accepted the first two pillars honestly: the climate of a world where nothing holds still and everything you love is always already changing and the Earth carries what you cannot. The witness is the ethical response: the only honest stance available to a plural self living in constructed reality in the permanent weather of grief is to stay in the room and keep looking and not conclude. And recursive construction is what the witness does with what the room contains: builds anyway, knowing the building is provisional, returning to the beginning with what the last pass taught, finding that the beginning contains more than it appeared to, building again.

The fifth pillar is where Young’s philosophy becomes a life. Not a theory about life. The actual practice of living honestly inside the conditions the first four pillars describe.

Young built a novel across eighteen years. I have been building around that novel across years of reading and writing and returning. The Ohio series (currently in progress) are five fictional novels whose architecture grows directly from the five pillars. The reading guide, chapter by chapter through all eighty-two chapters. Young’s philosophy named and argued for the first time. And this book, the inside account, the record of the journey that the other books were preparing for without knowing it.

Each of those was a pass. Each one found something the previous pass had walked past. Each one is a layer in the sediment, early kernels and later architecture all present simultaneously, none of it deleted, none of it resolved into a cleaner version of itself, all of it the record of a mind working through a problem that keeps revealing itself to be larger than the previous accounting.

That is the recursive construction. That is Young’s fifth pillar enacted in a life rather than argued in a treatise.

⁂

Vera never arrives at What Cheer in any simple sense.

Or rather: what she arrives at is not what she was traveling toward, because the traveling changed what the destination means. What Cheer at the end of the journey is not What Cheer at the beginning. The place is the same. The self arriving at it is not. The journey has built a different reader for the destination, and the destination has to be read again now with the self the journey made.

That is what happens to every honest reader of this novel. You arrive at the last page a different reader than the one who opened the first page, and the difference means the first page needs to be read again, and the reading will produce something the first reading could not have found because the self doing the reading is not the same self. The end is the beginning renamed. The recursive construction has already begun before you know you are inside it.

Young built that into the novel deliberately. She built a novel you have to read more than once not because it is deliberately withholding on the first reading but because it is genuinely larger than any single reading can hold. The first reading gives you what you are ready for. The second gives you what the first prepared you to see. And so on. The novel is the recursive construction made into a reading experience: you keep returning to the beginning and finding it has more in it than it appeared to have the last time you were there.

⁂

The sentence hasn’t ended.

Young said this about her own work and she was right in the way she was right about everything: not as a metaphor for incompleteness but as a precise description of the condition of honest building in a world that does not resolve. The sentence hasn’t ended because the world that made it necessary hasn’t ended. The plural self is still being demanded to simplify. The constructed real is still being presented as the natural order. The grief is still the climate. The witness is still in the room. The building is still under construction.

This book is a pass. It is the pass that finally had the language for the journey, that could stand inside the novel and the philosophy and the personal history and the political present simultaneously and show how Young built the system that holds all of it. It is the pass that found Esther’s last line as the key the other passes had circled without entering. It is the pass that understood the baby rabbits and the unmarked grave and the crab and the geological carrying as Young’s own argument made visible in her own images.

It is not the last pass.

The door is open. The pile is visible. The early kernels and the later architecture are all present and available to the next witness who arrives with different tools and a longer reach. The work is in the world’s keeping now. The Earth has it. The carrying continues.

You build.

You return.

You build again.

The sentence hasn’t ended yet.

Chapter Four. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act: The Awe Is the Witness Recognizing the Witness

← Chapter Three. Grief Doesn't End: The Earth Took Them Comple · Be Bak in a Whale · Chapter Five. Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary: The End →

Pillar: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

I started chasing the philosophy in the novel.

Not because I had a philosophy background. I didn’t. Philosophy had been noise to me, occasional sound bites rising above the static, nothing that cohered into a system I could use. But something in Young’s novel kept pulling at me and I knew, the way you know things before you can prove them, that the pulling was philosophical. That the novel had embedded in it a way of thinking about the world that was not incidental to the fiction but structural to it, woven into the sentences and the images and the formal decisions so completely that you could not extract the philosophy without destroying the novel and you could not fully read the novel without the philosophy.

So I bought the books. I gathered the resources. I went out of my depth and I knew I was out of my depth and I stayed anyway because the alternative was to stop following the threads, and stopping felt like a betrayal of what the novel was asking of me.

What I didn’t know yet was that what I was chasing was the fourth pillar. That I was already doing what Young’s philosophy names as the only honest ethical stance available in a world built the way this world is built.

I was witnessing.

⁂

The fourth pillar of Young’s philosophy is this: the only honest ethical stance available in a world where the self is plural and reality is constructed and grief is permanent is the witness. The one who stays in the room with the contradiction and does not flinch and does not conclude. The one who brings the full weight of attention to what is actually there without the distortions of projection or the desire to make the thing more manageable than it actually is.

This sounds passive. It is not.

The witness is the most demanding ethical stance Young’s system makes available, and it is demanding precisely because it refuses the satisfactions that make ethical action feel complete. The hero acts and the problem is solved and the story ends. The witness stays and the problem remains and the story keeps going and the witness keeps staying. There is no arrival. There is only the quality of attention brought to the continuing.

Young builds this into the novel’s form before she builds it into its content. The 1,198 pages are not excess. They are the time required to witness properly. You cannot witness in summary. You cannot witness at a distance. Witnessing requires duration and proximity and the willingness to keep looking after the looking has become difficult, which it becomes almost immediately in a novel that is committed to not looking away.

Young spent eighteen years in the room with this novel. That is not a metaphor for dedication. It is the literal enactment of the fourth pillar. She stayed. She kept following the threads. She kept giving the novel more than any conventional measure of sufficiency would have required because the witness does not calculate the minimum attention necessary. The witness gives the full attention the thing deserves, which is always more than anyone expected, which is why the novel is the length it is.

⁂

The novel itself is an act of witnessing.

Young’s narrator does not judge Catherine Cartwheel. She does not diagnose her, does not position her opium world as inferior to the world outside it, does not offer the reader the comfort of a clinical or moral frame that would explain Catherine and thereby contain her. She witnesses Catherine. She gives Catherine’s world the full weight of her attention and renders it with the same density and care she gives everything else and she does not conclude. This is Young’s formal ethics made visible in the prose before the reader has the language to name what they are seeing.

And Young does not judge Miss MacIntosh either. This is the harder thing to see and the more important one. Miss MacIntosh is the character who failed to witness. She drew the boundary of her attention at the wig and refused to see what was underneath it, refused to allow the subordinate self its visibility, threatened annihilation when the visibility was forced on her. She is the novel’s clearest example of what happens when the witness stops witnessing: when the quality of attention becomes selective, when some things are seen and others are decided in advance not to be.

And yet Young does not condemn her. She gives Miss MacIntosh the same fullness of attention she gives everyone else. She witnesses the woman who failed to witness with the same care and density and refusal to conclude that she brings to Vera and Catherine and Mr. Spitzer and Esther. The witness does not exclude the people who have refused to witness. The witness stays in the room with the contradiction of that too.

That is the most demanding thing Young asks of the reader: not to follow the philosophy, not to understand the system, to bring to the novel the same quality of attention Young brought to writing it. To stay in the room with all of it, the beautiful and the compromised and the failed and the grieving and the threatened, and not look away and not conclude.

⁂

I was in awe of what Young had packed into the novel.

The awe came from recognizing an encyclopedic mind at work. Young had studied philosophy and came close to her PhD before deciding it took too much time away from her novel, and you can feel that in every page: she knew Descartes and Hume and James and Whitehead and she had thought through them and past them and built a system that their work pointed toward but could not complete because their form could not hold what the system required. She packed all of that into the fiction not as a performance of knowledge but because the knowledge was structural. Because the novel could not do what it needed to do without it.

I knew when I felt the awe that it had to mean something. Something big. Something important. And I hoped, something original, because no other book had made me feel this way, and the feeling was the kind that belongs to genuine discovery rather than recognition of something already known.

So I did the work. I built A Guide to Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. I built AND: The Philosophy of Marguerite Young. I named the five pillars and placed Young in conversation with the thinkers her work had anticipated and surpassed. And at the end of all of it, after all the work, my instinct was not, I have solved this. It was: I’ll put it out there and hope someone smarter will come along. Maybe someone with a philosophy degree who would know more about it than I ever could and would want to give it the same attention. I hoped it was at least original enough for that.

I want to stay with that for a moment because it is the most important thing I have said in this book and I said it without recognizing what it was.

That is the witness stance taken to its fullest expression. Not the awe, though the awe was necessary. Not the work, though the work was necessary. The release. The understanding that you do your portion with complete attention and then you put it out there and you trust that the attention you brought will call forth more attention. That the work is larger than any single person’s capacity to complete it. That completion is not the point. The quality of attention brought to the continuing is the point.

Young did the same thing. She put the novel out there in 1965 and it was filed and ignored and occasionally praised and largely unread and she kept going. Harp Song for a Radical reached 2,400 pages of manuscript at the time of her death. She did not stop witnessing because the witnessing was not being recognized at the scale it deserved. She stayed in the room. She kept following the threads. She put it out there and trusted the carrying.

The Earth carries what we put out there. That is the thread from Chapter One and Chapter Three arriving here as the crab, the rabbits, the unmarked grave, and now this. The work you do with full attention and release into the world’s keeping. The Earth carries it. The witness carries it. The next reader who comes along and pulls the thread carries it. The carrying is not yours to complete. It is yours to begin.

⁂

Simone Weil argued that the foundation of ethics is not duty or utility or virtue but attention. The capacity to truly see the thing in front of you, to give it the full weight of your regard without the distortions of self-interest or the desire to make it into something more manageable than it actually is. For Weil, attention is an act of love. Not a feeling but a practice. The practice of keeping your eyes open when everything in you wants to look away or simplify or conclude.

Young arrives at the same place through fiction rather than philosophy. The witness in Young is practicing Weil’s attention whether Young named it that way or not. The 1,198 pages are 1,198 pages of practiced attention: keeping the eyes open, refusing the simplifications that would make the novel shorter and the ethics easier, staying in the room with what is actually there.

The difference between them is instructive. Weil’s attention operates between persons as you attend to the other, the one in front of you, the one whose suffering makes a claim on your regard. Young’s witnessing operates at every scale simultaneously. You witness yourself, your own plurality, your own grief, your own constructed reality. You witness the other. You witness the system that shapes what is possible for both of you. And you witness the natural world that carries what neither of you can hold alone.

Young’s witnessing is Weil’s attention made systemic: attention not as an individual ethical act but as a philosophical stance, a way of being in the world that shapes everything the self does and makes and builds and releases.

⁂

The characters who fail in Young’s novel are not the ones who suffer. Suffering is not failure in Young. The characters who fail are the ones who stop witnessing. Who replaces genuine attention with a frame that makes the thing in front of them manageable at the cost of its actual complexity.

Miss MacIntosh fails this way. She witnessed the solid world with tremendous attention and refused to witness anything else. Her pragmatism was a witnessing of one reality and a deliberate not-witnessing of everything that reality couldn’t contain. The wig was the boundary of her attention. What was underneath it she had decided in advance not to see. And deciding in advance is the failure: not the wig, not the baldness, not the false teeth or the one breast, but the threat issued to protect the boundary. The - I will kill you that stands behind every selective attention and enforces it.

Mr. Spitzer fails differently. He fails from the outside, from the institutional side: the man who arrives with the apparatus of reason and law and social legitimacy and still cannot see what Catherine and Cousin Hannah already know. His failure is not selective attention but the specific blindness of the person whose construction of reality is so dominant and so unexamined that it cannot perceive what falls outside its frame. He is not threatening. He is simply unable to witness what the women in the room are witnessing because his frame was built to exclude it.

Together they triangulate the failure. Miss MacIntosh wigs herself into certainty and threatens annihilation when the certainty is disturbed. Mr. Spitzer cannot find certainty even with the full apparatus of institutional reason behind him. One builds the frame too tight and enforces it with violence. The other cannot build a frame adequate to what is actually there. Between them is the witness: the one who sees without the frame, who stays in the room without the protection of the wig or the institution, who bears the full weight of what is actually present.

That figure is Vera. Imperfect, grieving, plural, unable to arrive at the destination she has been traveling toward for 1,198 pages. And yet witnessing. Staying on the bus. Keeping the journey going. Bringing the full weight of her attention to everything she passes through without the protection of the wig or the institution or the stage model of grief that would tell her the loss is processed and the forward motion can resume.

⁂

I want to say something about what it cost to witness Young’s novel across five readings without the validation of a tradition that had decided the novel was worth witnessing.

The critical tradition filed Young away. The academic apparatus had decided she was a difficult woman writer who didn’t quite fit, and that filed away things don’t get reconsidered easily, and so the attention that the novel deserved and demanded had not been given. The reading community that would have recognized what Young had built did not have a visible center. There was and is no institution behind the work I was doing. No publisher, no academic affiliation, no peer review, no conference, no tenure case that required someone to engage seriously with Young’s philosophy. Just the novel and the threads and the feeling that the threads led somewhere important.

The witness does not require institutional validation to continue witnessing. This is the political dimension of the fourth pillar that the tradition has never fully recognized because the tradition is itself the institution. It rewards the witnesses it has already decided are worth rewarding and ignores the ones working outside its frame.

Young was outside the frame. I was outside the frame. The work we were both doing, each in our own time and form, was the work of the witness who stays in the room because the room contains something true, not because the staying will be recognized.

I publish exclusively on Substack and in free PDFs because the philosophy this book is built on does not permit me to do otherwise. Serious ideas belong to everyone. The witness who charges admission to the witnessing has already compromised the attention. You cannot give the full weight of your regard to something and simultaneously manage the economics of who gets to receive it. Young understood this. She gave the novel everything. She held nothing back for a more manageable version.

The awe I felt reading her was the awe of recognizing that quality of attention in someone else’s work. The recognition that something had been given everything and held nothing back. That the encyclopedic mind behind the novel had stayed in the room for eighteen years and given the room everything it had.

The awe is the witness recognizing the witness.

⁂

There is one more thing that needs to be said about the witness before we move to the fifth pillar, and it is the thing that connects all four pillars into a coherent ethical stance rather than a collection of philosophical positions.

The witness can only do what the witness does because of the first three pillars. You cannot witness from a unified self because the unified self is already managing what it will and will not see, already enforcing the boundary of its attention, already prepared to threaten what threatens it. The witness requires the plural self: the self that has stopped demanding that one of its selves kill the others into silence, that can hold the wig and the baldness simultaneously without resolving them into a judgment.

You cannot witness from inside the belief that consensus reality is the only reality because the belief has already decided what is worth seeing. The witness requires the understanding that all reality is constructed, that the frame you are looking through is a frame and not a window, that what falls outside your frame is not therefore less real.

And you cannot witness without the capacity to stay in the permanent weather of grief. The witness sees loss. Constantly. The things that are being lost while they are still being lost. The beauty that is inseparable from the grief of the natural world that Mr. Spitzer embodies. The losses built into the foundation of the collective life that the political system demands be called resolved. The small losses, the rabbits, the unmarked grave, the stick that the Earth took along with everything else. The witness does not look away from any of it. And that requires the third pillar: the understanding that the looking will not resolve, that the grief is the climate, that the honest life is the one that stays in the weather.

The witness is what the first three pillars make possible. It is the ethical stance that follows honestly from the philosophical ground. If the self is plural and reality is constructed and grief is permanent, then the only honest response is to witness: to stay in the room with all of it, to bring the full weight of attention to what is actually there, to not look away and not conclude and not replace the difficulty with a consolation that would require pretending the difficulty isn’t there.

Young stayed in the room for eighteen years.

I have been in the room since 2019.

The room is larger than either of us. It contains the novel and the philosophy and the reading guide and this book and everything that will come after this book when someone smarter pulls the thread further. The room is the Earth that carries what we put into it. The room is the witness that outlasts any individual witness.

Stay in the room.

Keep looking.

Do not conclude.

Put it out there and trust the carrying.

Pillar: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

I loved horror as a kid. Not the idea of it. The actual thing. I had a closet full of it. While other girls read romance I read horror, and especially Stephen King, because King understood something about the world that the sanitized version of childhood was not allowed to say: that the thing in the dark is real, that the structure holding everything together is more fragile than the adults want you to know, that fear is a form of honesty.

I stopped at Gerald's Game.

The premise was a woman handcuffed to a bed with a man on top of her who has just died. I read the setup and thought, now that is horrifying. And then I thought, this is ugly and nasty and not what I want to read from a man's point of view. I didn't have the language yet for what I was feeling. I just felt the wrongness of it, the specific quality of wrongness that comes when you understand, below the level of articulation, that the woman in the story is not the subject. She is the situation. Her constraint is the spectacle. Her interior life, whatever it contains, is the setting for someone else's horror, framed for someone else's consumption.

I put the book down and started looking at the shelves.

Everything I had been consuming over decades (books, movies, television). The directors. The authors. The critics who told me what was worth reading and watching. All men. I had been surrounded by women in my actual life, women who were the texture and substance of my daily reality, and none of them were anywhere in my interior life. The interior life I had built, the one stocked from years of reading and watching and absorbing what I had been told was the best, had been curated entirely by men and I had received that curation in good faith because I had no framework yet for questioning it.

That had to stop.

The decentering took years and it came in layers. The shelves first, then the directors, then the deeper discovery, the one that cut the deepest was eighteen years of formal education, the best pedagogy money could buy, built almost entirely on studies of men and boys. The curriculum I had trusted as rigorous and complete had been constructed from half the species and handed to me as universal. I had received it in good faith. I had taught from it in good faith. And then the wig came off and I understood that the solid ground of my entire intellectual formation was a construction, a very specific curation of what counted as knowledge and what counted as the best, and the curation had never been neutral.

I recentered. I went looking for what the curation had left out.

Marguerite Young was what was waiting at the end of the search.

⁂

The second pillar of Young's philosophy is this: illusion is not the distortion of reality but its medium. Human beings do not live in the world and sometimes retreat into illusion. They live in illusion the way fish live in water, and what we call reality is one particular illusion that has achieved consensus.

This is more radical than it sounds and Young knows it. The Western tradition has organized itself around the real and the illusory as a foundational opposition since Plato's cave as the shadows on the wall are illusion, the sunlit world outside is reality, and the philosopher's task is to drag people toward the light. The entire project of epistemology, of figuring out how we know what we know, is built on the assumption that there is something to know and that knowing it means getting past the distortions that stand between the mind and the real.

Young answers this differently: the sunlit world outside the cave is not reality. It is a larger cave, more elaborately lit, whose inhabitants have agreed to call their shadows real. Consensus reality is not less constructed for being agreed upon. It is just more crowded.

The vehicle for this demonstration is Catherine Cartwheel.

⁂

Catherine is Vera's mother. She lives in an opium world in her mansion on the eastern seaboard while Vera is raised by Miss MacIntosh. The critical tradition has read her as the novel's negative pole: the deluded one, the absent mother, the cautionary example of what happens when you abandon consensus reality for interior fantasy. Young refuses that reading at every turn, and the way she refuses it is through the catalog.

Young does not sketch Catherine's world. She does not gesture at it or summarize it or give the impressionistic outline of a dream sequence. She catalogs it. Object by object, detail by detail, with the same obsessive specificity she brings to everything else in the novel. Catherine's interior world has geography, population, history, and internal logic. It has the weight of accumulated specific reality. Young gives it the same density as the Indiana plains, the same insistence on its own existence, the same refusal to be treated as secondary or derivative or less than.

I want to be honest about what I did with the catalog in the early readings. I thought that if I dig into it far enough I will find the answer. I followed it the way you follow a difficult argument, looking for the point where the meaning would crystallize, where Young would finally say what the catalog was for.

The answer is not at the end of the catalog. The answer is the catalog itself.

The accumulation is the argument. Young is not building toward a revelation about Catherine's world. She is demonstrating, through sheer density and specificity, that Catherine's world has as many things in it as the solid world, as much weight, as much insistence on its own reality. The catalog is Young saying: count the objects. Count the details. Count the specific gravity of what Catherine inhabits. And then tell me which world is real.

You cannot. That is the point. The catalog makes the question unanswerable not because it is evasive but because it is honest. The question of which world is real presupposes a framework for adjudicating between them, and that framework is what Young is dismantling. You cannot stand outside both worlds and judge them from neutral ground because there is no neutral ground. There is only the world you are living in, which is as constructed as Catherine's and as real as Catherine's, and the belief that yours is the standard against which hers should be measured is itself the illusion the novel is built to expose.

⁂

The war on drugs was a war on Catherine.

Not literally, not exclusively, but structurally. The criminalization of substances that alter consciousness is the political expression of the second pillar's refusal, of the insistence that consensus reality is the only legitimate reality, that the interior life built outside its boundaries is not a world but a pathology, and that the people who inhabit those interior worlds must be brought back into line or destroyed. The threat was made so high that one step out of place meant falling to the bottom, and in this country the bottom is a literal hell. Not a metaphor. Incarceration, poverty, death, the permanent mark of a record that follows you out of every door you try to open.

I didn't smoke marijuana until it was legal in my state. And my reaction when I finally did was wondering what exactly the fuss was about. And I knew immediately. The fuss was never about the substance. It was about the interior life the substance made possible. The relaxation that allowed the questioning. The relaxation that gave one the ability to step outside the productive arrangement. The self that refuses to be only legible and useful to the system that requires it to stay in place. Catherine's opium world is not the failure of a self that couldn't cope with reality. It is the interior life of a person for whom the exterior world as constructed offered insufficient reality, and the system that criminalized it was the same system that handcuffed the woman to the bed and called it horror for the reader's entertainment.

Young understood this in 1965. She built Catherine's world with the full weight of her attention because she understood that the interior life of a woman is not the setting for someone else's story. It is a world. It has a catalog. The catalog is the proof.

⁂

I was a daydreamer. I checked out by listening to music and reading continuously, and later by watching films, and I was conscious and careful about what I consumed. I looked for what was considered the best. I followed the lists and the critics and the syllabi and the canon because I trusted the curation. I believed the best was the best because the people telling me it was the best were the people the system had designated as the authorities on bestness.

What I was doing, though I didn't have the language for it yet, was exactly what Catherine does. Building an interior world from the materials available. Stocking it as carefully and specifically as Young stocks Catherine's opium world. The difference is that my materials had been pre-approved. My interior world was built from the canon and the canon had been built by men and called universal, and I had received it as universal because the construction of it as universal was so complete and so long-standing that it had achieved the status Young identifies as consensus reality: not less constructed for being agreed upon, just more crowded.

Gerald's Game was the moment the catalog failed. Not King specifically, not horror specifically, but the specific image of a woman whose interiority is the setting for a man's premise, framed for a male reader's consumption, handed to me as part of the best that the genre had to offer. And I felt it before I named it. This is not my world. This catalog does not contain me. The consensus reality of this interior life that I have been building from approved materials does not have room for what I actually am.

That feeling is what Young calls the recognition that there is no single reality.

Not the philosophical argument. The felt experience of the argument landing before the argument has been made. The moment you understand that the world you have been living in is a construction and you have been mistaking the construction for the world.

⁂

The political consequences of the second pillar are where Young's philosophy becomes most dangerous to the systems that depend on the naturalization of their own construction.

Every dominant system depends on appearing not to be a system. On appearing to be simply the way things are, the natural order, the obvious truth that doesn't require defense because it is just reality. The literary canon is the best literature because it is the best literature. The curriculum is rigorous because it is rigorous. The drugs are dangerous because they are dangerous. The woman handcuffed to the bed is horror because horror is horror. None of these require examination because they are not constructions. They are facts.

Young's second pillar removes the ground from under all of it.

If all reality is constructed, then the natural order is always already a political choice, and the political choice can be named and challenged and remade. The canon is not the best literature. It is the literature that the people with power to define the best decided what was the best, and that decision encoded their interests and their blind spots and their specific construction of what interiority looks like and whose interiority counts. The curriculum is not rigorous. It is the knowledge that the people who built the curriculum decided was worth knowing, and they built it from studies of men and boys and called it universal because calling it universal was more convenient than calling it partial.

This is why Young's insistence on Catherine's catalog is not just an aesthetic choice. It is a political act. Giving Catherine's world the same density as Miss MacIntosh's world, the same weight of accumulated specific reality, is Young refusing to participate in the hierarchy that decides which interiors count as real. It is Young saying: I will not write Catherine thin. I will not make her world decorative or derivative or secondary. I will give it the full weight of my attention and let the reader count the objects and decide for themselves which catalog is real.

That is the same act I performed when I stopped trusting the curation. When I looked at the shelves and the syllabi and the lists and understood that what had been handed to me as universal was particular, as neutral was interesting, as the best was a construction built by people who had decided in advance whose interior life was worth the catalog.

Men had their writing poured over for decades. Young had been filed under difficult women writers and left there. There was no reason I couldn't do what the tradition had done for the writers it valued. I would pour the attention over her work until it yielded what it actually contained rather than what the filing system had decided it contained.

That decision was itself the second pillar enacted as a scholarly practice. The realization that the constructed real of the literary canon was a political choice, not a natural order. The refusal to mistake the dominant construction for the only construction. The decision to build a different catalog.

⁂

Young's formal choices in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling are themselves an argument about illusion that goes deeper than content.

The novel does not distinguish between Catherine's interior world and the exterior world in its prose. The sentences that move through Catherine's opium visions have the same texture, the same density, the same commitment to specificity as the sentences that describe the Grey Goose bus or the Indiana landscape or Miss MacIntosh's belongings left on the beach. Young refuses the formal signals that literary fiction conventionally uses to mark the boundary between interior and exterior, between dream and waking, between illusion and reality.

This is not a stylistic choice. It is a philosophical position built into the craft. If the prose treated Catherine's world as thinner, as marked by the conventional signals of unreality, it would be reproducing the hierarchy it is dismantling. The form would be saying what the argument denies. Young is too rigorous for that inconsistency.

The result is the disorientation of the early chapters, which I experienced as drowning. I could not find the boundary between what was real and what was Catherine's opium world because Young had removed the boundary. Not hidden it. Removed it. Philosophically. Because the boundary was the construction the novel was built to expose.

The disorientation was not a failure of communication. It was the communication. Young was doing to the reader what the second pillar does to the concept of reality: making the boundary unstable, and then asking you to live in the instability with your eyes open.

I had spent years reading toward this without knowing it. Every daydream, every album listened to in the dark, every film chosen because someone had called it the best, every hour with my closet full of horror novels. I had been building an interior world from the materials available and I had been doing it because the exterior world as constructed was insufficient. Not wrong, not evil, not to be rejected entirely. Insufficient. It did not have room for the full complexity of what I was, and so I went somewhere else, and the somewhere else was as real as anything I was being told was real, and Young was the first writer I encountered who built a novel that said so in its bones.

⁂

There is something Young says in the Friedman and Fuchs interview that I return to every time I teach this pillar to myself:

When you have examined all the illusions of life, and know that there isn’t any reality, but you nevertheless go on, then you are a mature human being. You accept the idea that it is all mask and illusion and that people are in disguise. You see the crumbling of reality and you accept it.

Maturity, in Young's system, is not the achievement of certainty. It is the willingness to keep going after the certainty has crumbled. Not because a new certainty will replace it. Because going on is what an honest life requires when you have stopped pretending that the mask is the face.

The people who are most damaged by the refusal to examine illusion are the people whose lives have been most thoroughly organized by someone else's construction of reality. The woman in Gerald's Game. The people whose interior worlds the war on drugs criminalized. The students who are educated on a curriculum built from half the species and presented as universal. Young understood this. She saw that the demand to accept consensus reality as the only reality was not a philosophical position. It was a political mechanism for keeping the constructed order in place by making the construction invisible.

Catherine's catalog is the refusal of that mechanism. It is Young pouring the full weight of her attention onto an interior world that the mechanism had decided did not count, and insisting, object by object, detail by detail, that it counts.

The catalog is the argument. The accumulation is the proof. The density is the politics.

⁂

I said in the prologue that I never belonged anywhere until I read this book. The second pillar is part of the reason why.

The interior world I had built across decades of reading and listening and watching and dreaming had always felt, at some level, like a confession of inadequacy. Like evidence that the exterior world as given was sufficient for normal people and I was the anomaly who kept retreating from it into music and books and film and daydream. The culture that handed me Gerald's Game as horror also handed me the implicit message that the woman who needed a richer interior life than the approved catalog provided was the problem, not the catalog.

Young's second pillar says: the catalog was always the problem. The interior world you built was not a retreat from reality. It was a reality. It had objects in it. It had weight. It had the specific gravity of everything you brought your full attention to, and the full attention was itself the proof that the world was real.

Catherine is not the cautionary example. Catherine is the witness to what happens when the interior life is given room. When someone refuses to make it secondary or derivative or thin. When someone catalogs it with the same obsessive care that the tradition reserves for the exterior world it has decided is real.

Young catalogs Catherine. I catalog Young. The act is the same. The politics are the same. The refusal is the same.

There is no single reality.

The beauty of it is that you nevertheless go on.

Walking toward the catalog.

Counting the objects.

Finding that the world you were told was not real has more things in it than the world you were handed.

Chapter Three. Grief Doesn't End: The Earth Took Them Completely

← Chapter Two. Reality Is Constructed: Count the Objects · Be Bak in a Whale · Chapter Four. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act: The Awe Is →

Pillar: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

I was a child when I understood what the Earth does with what it takes.

I had found baby rabbits. I took them home because I should not have, because the wanting to care for them was stronger than the knowledge that I shouldn’t, and I tried to keep them alive. Then I had to go to camp. I called my grandmother to come get me rather than stay overnight because I needed to go home and make sure the rabbits lived. I came home and they had died.

I buried them sobbing. I placed a stick on the grave and walked away.

And then I turned around.

I went back to check. Terrified that I had made a mistake. That I had buried them alive and they were still under there and I could still save them if I could just find the place. I dug for the stick. I dug for the hole. I found nothing. The Earth had taken them completely. No marker. No evidence of the grave. No confirmation that what I had buried was truly gone and not still alive underneath waiting for me to find them in time.

The Earth had taken them completely.

I did not know it then but that was the moment I began to understand what Young spends 1,198 pages demonstrating: that grief does not resolve. That the Earth does not give you back the marker. That the turning around is not weakness but the honest response of a self that loved something and cannot simply walk away from the site of the loss, and that the love and the loss and the terror of having made a mistake and the inability to find the evidence and the ground that shows nothing: all of it is permanent. All of it is the weather you live in from that moment forward.

⁂

The third pillar of Young’s philosophy is this: grief is not a stage or a season. It is the permanent atmospheric condition of a world in which everything you love is always already changing into something you didn’t expect.

We have a story we tell about grief. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross gave us the stages and the stages became the normative prescription of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. The story of grief is the story of getting through it, of moving toward acceptance which is the destination, the place where grief becomes integrated and the self resumes its forward motion. Grief as temporary weather. Difficult while it lasts, bounded, finite, something that eventually passes.

Young does not believe this.

More precisely: Young does not believe it because it is not true, and she is too honest to reproduce a comfort that falsifies the actual experience it claims to describe. In Young’s system, grief is not temporary weather. It is the climate. The permanent atmospheric condition of a world in which nothing holds still, in which the people you need most are dying or absent or constructed differently than you understood, in which the self that does the loving is itself plural and unstable and not fully available to itself.

The character who carries this pillar most fully is not Vera, though Vera grieves on every page. It is Mr. Spitzer.

⁂

I never quite liked Mr. Spitzer the way I liked Vera and Miss MacIntosh. I want to say that plainly because it matters for what follows. Part of it was the conscious decentering I was doing when I came to Young’s novel of I had made the decision to stop organizing my interior life around men’s perspectives and Mr. Spitzer is a man and I carried that wariness into him.

The second reading changed something. The foreshadowing became visible that I had missed the first time: he is not who he says he is. Catherine knows. Cousin Hannah knows. The women in this novel see through the construction of Mr. Spitzer while he maintains it, and Young builds that dramatic irony carefully across the novel, laying the evidence in plain sight for the reader who is paying full attention.

But here is what Young does that the tradition has no category for: she gives the most breathtaking grief in the novel to the most compromised character.

Mr. Spitzer’s descriptions of the natural world are among the most beautiful passages in the book. His grief over what is lost, what the world has lost, what the natural world loses either through its own processes or through human intervention: it is genuine. It is embodied. It is more fully inhabited than almost anything else Young gives us, and she gives it to a man who is performing his own identity, who is not who he says he is, who the women around him see through.

Young does this deliberately. Grief is not a reward for virtue. It is not given to the characters who have earned it by being honest or good or singular. It is the weather. It falls on everyone. The person who is not who he says he is still loses things genuinely. The loss is real even when the self that carries it is constructed. The grief is among the genuine things even when everything else is performance.

That is the plural self and the grief pillar working together. You can be multiple things simultaneously, some of them false and some of them genuine, and the grief belongs to the genuine register even when the identity containing it is a construction. Mr. Spitzer’s grief over the natural world is real. The man performing the identity of Mr. Spitzer is not entirely real. Young holds both of those truths simultaneously without resolving them into a judgment about which one cancels the other.

⁂

I feel at home outside and in nature. I have always felt this. Camping, hiking, sports, playgrounds, a wild wooded ravine that was my backyard. The natural world has never felt like an escape from the real world. It has always felt like the more real world, the one that was here before the human arrangements and will be here after, the one that operates at a scale and with a patience that the constructed world cannot approach.

Mr. Spitzer gave me language for that feeling before I understood that Young was giving me language for anything. His descriptions of the natural world, the haunting beauty of nature encountered while going about ordinary business, moving through streets, living a circumscribed daily life while something vast and indifferent and gorgeous operates alongside it. I recognized that. I had been living inside that recognition since the baby rabbits. Since the Earth took them completely and left no marker and I stood at the place where the grave had been and understood that the Earth does not grieve what it carries.

It just carries.

That is the distinction Young builds into the novel through the natural world that runs through it constantly, underneath everything, never resolved. The grief in the novel is human. The carrying is geological. Vera grieves. Mr. Spitzer grieves. Catherine grieves in the way that the opium world is itself a form of grief, the interior life built to hold what the exterior world has lost or taken or refused. But the Earth does not grieve. The Earth sediments. It takes the wig and the crab carries it through the water. It takes the rabbits and closes over the grave without a marker. It takes everything that has been lost and carries it forward, transformed but not healed, present but not returned.

Young understood that the human self cannot hold the full weight of permanent grief alone. Individual life lasts decades. The grief she describes accumulates across centuries. The vessel is too small for what it is being asked to carry. But the Earth is not too small. The Earth has been carrying loss since before any human philosophical tradition existed to name what carrying means. The geological record is permanent cumulative grief made literal: layer upon layer, nothing resolved, everything present, the complete record of every loss the world has sustained, sediment by sediment, carried forward without ceremony, without conclusion, without the demand that any of it be processed into something more manageable.

We planted the crab at the end of Chapter One. The crab carries the wig through the water without knowing what it carries. That image is the beginning of this argument. Here is where it becomes explicit: the natural world in Young’s novel is not a backdrop or atmosphere or symbol. It is the original witness. The only archive large enough for what human selves cannot hold.

⁂

Vera Cartwheel is grieving from the first page.

She is grieving Miss MacIntosh, who walked into the water and did not return. She is grieving the childhood organized around a woman who turned out to be a construction. She is grieving Catherine, who is alive but absent in the way that a person absorbed into their own interior world is absent: present in body, unreachable in the ways that matter. She is grieving the self she was before the wig came off, the self that had a foundation even if the foundation was false.

And she cannot stop.

The grief does not process. It does not move through stages toward resolution. It accumulates. Each new understanding of what has been lost adds to rather than replaces the grief that preceded it. Vera at the end of the novel carries everything she has ever grieved, layered and present and unresolved, the way the Earth carries everything in its strata: the old losses and the new losses and the losses that are still in the process of being understood as losses, all of it present simultaneously, none of it gone.

Young presents this not as pathology but as accuracy. As the appropriate response to actual loss in an actual world where loss is permanent and cumulative and does not resolve. The alternative, the grief that resolves, the acceptance that integrates loss into a resumed life, requires at some level deciding that the lost thing was not so irreplaceable after all. Young finds something dishonest in that decision: the lost thing was irreplaceable. Life without it is not the same life. The self that loved it has not found its way forward so much as it has found a way of not looking back.

Not looking back is not the same as arriving somewhere better.

⁂

The turning around.

I keep returning to that gesture because it is the most honest thing I know about grief. You bury what you have lost. You place the marker. You walk away because walking away is what you are supposed to do, what the stage model of grief requires, what the people around you need you to do so that the loss can be categorized and filed and the forward motion resumed.

And then you turn around.

Not because you haven’t accepted the loss. Because the fear underneath grief is not the fear of losing. It is the fear of having made a mistake. Of having buried something alive. Of having walked away from something that still needed you and would have survived if you had stayed. That terror, the terror that you turned your back too soon, is the engine of the turning around, and it is the most honest account of what grief actually feels like from inside it. Not the sadness. The terror that the loss was your fault. That you could have prevented it. That the marker you placed was premature and underneath it something is still waiting.

Young builds this into Vera’s entire journey. The bus is moving toward What Cheer, toward the place Miss MacIntosh came from, and the movement is itself a turning around. Vera cannot stop returning to the loss. She cannot stop looking for the marker, the confirmation, the evidence that what she buried was truly gone and not still alive underneath waiting for her to arrive in time. The journey is the grief. The 1,198 pages are the grief. Not because the novel is depressing but because the turning around is what the honest self does, and Young refuses to abbreviate it into something more manageable than it actually is.

⁂

There is a political dimension to permanent grief that Young builds into the novel without stating explicitly, and it is the dimension that connects the third pillar to the world we are currently living in.

A society that cannot grieve honestly cannot reckon honestly.

The American relationship with its own history is a grief problem before it is anything else. The losses built into the foundation of this country, the theft of indigenous land, the centuries of enslaved labor, the systematic exclusion of women and queer people and immigrants from the promises the country made about itself. These are not losses that have been processed. They have been managed. Periodically acknowledged and returned to the category of the past, the thing that has been gotten over or gotten through, the grief that has supposedly resolved into the acceptance of a nation that has moved forward.

Young’s philosophy says: the grief does not resolve. The losses are permanent and cumulative and the demand that the people most directly descended from those losses perform a recovery they have not experienced is its own violence. The demand for performed recovery is Miss MacIntosh’s threat in a different register: I will kill you if you tell. Keep the wig on. Walk away from the grave and do not turn around. The marker is where we put it and the loss is processed and the forward motion has resumed and if you turn around you are the problem.

The Earth knows better. The Earth has been carrying what the political system demands be called resolved for longer than the political system has existed. The Mahoning Valley carries the grief of deindustrialization in its landscape, in the empty lots and the rusted infrastructure and the particular quality of light in a post-industrial city. It carries the grief of what was taken from the Wyandot people in the land itself, in the river, in the glacial formations that were here before any human arrangement and will be here after all of them. The Earth does not accept the political system’s timeline for grief. It sediments. It carries. It shows nothing where the marker was and that is not erasure. That is the honest account of how long loss actually lasts.

Mr. Spitzer grieves the natural world because the natural world is where the permanent record is kept. His grief over what has been lost to human intervention, the beauty that emerges from that grief, the haunting quality of nature encountered in the middle of ordinary life: Young gives him this because she understands that the grief of the Earth is the scale at which human grief has to be understood if it is to be understood honestly. The individual loss is real and specific and devastating. The Earth carries it alongside everything else it has been given, without hierarchy, without the demand that any of it be resolved before the next one arrives.

⁂

I want to be precise about what Young is not saying.

She is not saying that grief is simply permanent suffering. She is not arguing for despair or for the dissolution of the self into its losses. The third pillar is consistently misread as the novel’s melancholy, its beautiful hopelessness, its maximalist sorrow. That reading mistakes the refusal of false consolation for the refusal of consolation altogether.

What grief gives, in Young’s system, is depth. The self that has not grieved is thinner than the self that has, not morally thinner but experientially thinner, less capacious, less able to hold the full weight of what existence actually contains. Grief is the education that cannot be acquired any other way. It teaches the self the actual scale of what it loves, which is always larger than the self knew before the loss.

I understood this with the rabbits before I had language for it. The grief was proportional to the love, which was larger than I knew I had until the loss measured it. I didn’t know how much I loved those rabbits until I was sobbing at the grave. I didn’t know how much I needed the evidence of the grave until I turned around and went looking for it. The turning around was not a failure to accept the loss. It was the measurement of how real the loss was.

And then the Earth took the marker too, and I stood at the unmarked ground and understood something that I would not have language for until decades later when I read Young’s novel for the first time and drowned and read it again and found Mr. Spitzer and his grief over the natural world and his descriptions of the haunting beauty of what is being lost and understood that the beauty and the grief were the same thing.

You only see the haunting beauty of what is being lost when you have stopped pretending the loss will resolve. When you have turned around enough times to understand that the marker will not be there, that the Earth has taken it, that the carrying is the Earth’s work now and not yours, and that your work is to remain present to what is being lost while it is still being lost, which is always, which is the condition, which is the climate you live in if you are paying honest attention.

⁂

This memory is also what made me empathize with Esther.

I have been thinking about why for a long time and here is what I understand now, the child who sobbed at the grave and turned around to find nothing grew into the reader who recognized Esther as the person who keeps going back in. Who writes the note as best she can. Who cannot spell either, which means she cannot perform the acceptable version of the gesture, can only make the honest version, the one that shows the spelling and the limitation and the going-in-anyway simultaneously.

Esther’s note is the grief pillar compressed into a sign in a restaurant window. It does not resolve. It does not perform recovery. It acknowledges the going out and promises the coming back and admits the whale, which is Jonah’s whale, which is the creature that swallows you and keeps you alive in the dark and eventually returns you, transformed but not healed, to the world.

The whale does not resolve the grief of having been swallowed. It carries it. The way the Earth carried the rabbits. The way the Earth carries everything: without ceremony, without conclusion, without the demand that the carried thing be processed into something more manageable than what it actually is.

Young ends the novel with Esther because Esther is the most honest answer to the grief pillar available in the book. Not the most eloquent. Not the most philosophical. The most honest. The person who cannot spell, who writes the note as best she can, who goes back into the whale not because the whale is where she wants to be but because the whale is where she is and the honest life is the one that acknowledges where it is.

The grief is the climate.

The whale is the Earth that carries it.

The note is what you write when you have stopped pretending either of those things is temporary.

Bee bak in a whale.

For she could not spell either.

Neither could the child at the unmarked grave. Neither can any of us. We write the note as best we can and we go back in and the Earth takes the marker and we turn around anyway and the turning around is the honest life and Young spent 1,198 pages proving it.
