Chapter Thirteen: The Ten Pillars and Daily Life

← Part Five: Living in the Architecture · Radical Immanence Collection · Chapter Fourteen: What Cheer: The Youngian Polity →

Philosophy that cannot be lived is philosophy that has failed the test Young's system sets for it. The recursive attempt, the fifth pillar, is not a theoretical commitment. It is a daily practice. The witness, the fourth pillar, is not a philosophical position. It is a way of being in a room.

The ten pillars describe a way of living as well as a way of thinking, and the two cannot be separated in Young's system, because the system is built on the recognition that the form of the thinking and the form of the living are the same thing.

Living the plural self means releasing the demand for consistency as the primary virtue. It means allowing the self that is present in this moment to be different from the self that was present in the last moment, without requiring that the difference be explained or resolved. It means holding the plurality with honesty rather than managing it into the appearance of unity. This is harder than it sounds in a culture that treats inconsistency as a moral failure. The person who has changed their mind is suspected of weakness. The person who holds contradictory positions is suspected of dishonesty. The person who contains multitudes is suspected of containing too much. Young's plural self says: the multitudes are not the problem. The demand that they be reduced to one is the problem.

Living the witness means staying in the room when the room becomes uncomfortable. It means maintaining the quality of attention that the thing in front of you deserves, even when the thing in front of you is contradictory or painful or resistant to the simplifications that would make it easier to process. The witness in daily life is the person who does not look away from the difficult conversation, who does not rush toward resolution when the contradiction becomes uncomfortable, who can hold the wig and the baldness simultaneously without requiring that one of them be more real than the other. This is an ethical practice, not a passive one. The witness is not the bystander. The witness is the one whose presence changes the quality of what is happening, whose attention creates the conditions for honest appearance, whose refusal to conclude keeps the space open for the full complexity of what is there.

Living recursive construction means building without needing the building to be finished. It means returning to the beginning with what you learned on the last pass, incorporating what the previous attempt revealed, building again with the honest acknowledgment that this attempt will also reveal what it didn't know. This is the practice of the honest life: not the life that has found its foundation and built on it, but the life that has stopped looking for a foundation and started building with what is actually available. The plural self. The situated knowledge. The permanent grief. The quality of attention the witness brings. The language that knows it is a construction. The community that holds difference without erasure. The sedimentary time that carries the past forward.

The unfinished that is the only honest form integrity can take.

You build with all of this. You return. You build again.
collection-03-10-chapter-seven-youngs-ho:
Chapter Seven: Young's Horizontal Lady

← Chapter Six: The Medieval Wheel · Radical Immanence Collection · Chapter Eight: The Turn →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Marguerite Young spent eighteen years on the horizontal axis.

This is not a criticism. The horizontal axis is where the ten pillars live. It is where the plural self spreads its full width, where the sedimentary layers accumulate, where the permanent weather of grief moves through the atmospheric conditions of a life that refuses to resolve. The horizontal axis is where Miss MacIntosh, My Darling was built, page by page, sentence by sentence, the long recursive construction of a philosophical system that chose fiction as its only honest form.

But Young knew about the vertical. The novel is reaching toward it in every sentence that circles back on itself, every image that returns with the weight of all its previous appearances pressing down on the new encounter. The wig on the back of the crab is not only a horizontal image, a lateral spread of symbol and meaning across the surface of the text. It is also a vertical one: the weight of everything the wig has meant, all the layers of Miss MacIntosh's constructed solidity and Vera's childhood faith and the collapse of the opposition between Catherine's illusion and the solid world, pressing down through the image into the sediment of the novel, depositing something that will be in the ground of every subsequent reading.

Young's sentences are crossing points. They are the places where the horizontal spread of the plural self meets the vertical line of transmission, where the accumulation of the present moment is intersected by the weight of what came before and the weight of what will come after. The sentences that circle back and refuse to finish are sentences that are trying to hold both axes at once, to stay in the horizontal spread of the present moment while feeling the pull of the vertical line.

The novel never arrives at What Cheer. But it arrives, repeatedly, at the crossing point. It arrives at the place where Vera is most fully herself: not moving toward a destination, not accumulating toward a resolution, but standing at the intersection of everything she has received and everything she will deposit, holding the weight in both directions, witnessing without concluding.

The Wheel of Fortune turn in Young's work is the moment when a character who has been resting in the horizontal spread of consciousness is rotated into the vertical line of transmission. Miss MacIntosh's turn is the most dramatic: the wig comes off, the horizontal accumulation of her constructed solidity collapses, and she is suddenly visible as a vertical figure, a person constituted by what she received and what she deposited, a carrier rather than a destination. The solid world she represented was not solid. It was alluvial. It was made of what was carried to her and deposited in her and carried forward by her, and the wig was the pretense that the carrying had stopped, that she had arrived somewhere stable rather than being, like everyone else, in the middle of the transmission.

Catherine's turn is subtler and more philosophically interesting. Catherine is already on the vertical axis in a sense: her opium world is a world in which the horizontal accumulation of consensus reality has been suspended and the vertical line of what she has received and what she is depositing is more visible. Her interior world is not a retreat from the transmission. It is a different orientation within it, a way of being at the crossing point that the horizontal world cannot process and therefore pathologizes.

Young does not pathologize it. Young witnesses it with the same density and care she gives the Indiana plains. In doing so she is enacting the eleventh pillar before the eleventh pillar had a name: she is treating the vertical orientation as a legitimate way of being at the crossing point, not as a failure of the horizontal but as a different relationship to the same structure.

The Grey Goose bus is the crossing point made mobile. It is moving through the horizontal landscape of Indiana while carrying its passengers along the vertical line of their individual transmissions, each one oriented differently, each one at a different point in the rotation, each one carrying a different weight in a different configuration. The bus is not going to What Cheer in any simple sense. It is going to the crossing point, which is always already here, which is where the passengers already are, which is where the novel was from the first sentence.
collection-02-04-part-three-the-monday-m:
Part Three: The Monday Mirror

← Part Two: Common Questions · Radical Immanence Collection · Part Four: Short Meditations →

The Monday Mirror is a weekly practice of honest attention. Not self-improvement. Not reviewing your performance. Just turning and looking at what is actually here before the week carries you forward.

These thirty prompts are organized by theme. You can use one per week, one per day, or open the list wherever it opens. There is no order to complete. There is only the one you are in right now.

The question underneath every prompt is the same: what is actually here?

01 BODY

Notice where your shoulders are right now. Not where they should be. Where they actually are. If they are up near your ears, that is information. It is not a problem to fix. You have been carrying something. Your body already knows. You do not need to explain it. You can just let your shoulders drop a little, or not. Either way, something true is here.

What is here for you in this?

02 MORNING

You woke up today and the first feeling was not gratitude. Maybe it was dread, or a blank gray nothing, or the weight of what is still unresolved. That is not a failure of your morning. That is your morning. It is already happening. It counts. You are already in the day.

What is here for you in this?

03 GRIEF

The person you lost would have liked today's weather, or they would have hated it. Either way, you noticed. That noticing is not a wound to push through. It is a form of love that is still moving in you. It does not need to go anywhere. It is allowed to just be here, in the noticing.

What is here for you in this?

04 ORDINARY OBJECT

The mug on your desk is probably not clean. Or it has been sitting there long enough that the coffee left a ring. That ring is time. You were here yesterday, and the day before. You kept showing up, even on the days that did not deserve it. The ring is proof.

What is here for you in this?

05 INCOMPLETION

There is something you have not finished. Maybe many things. The list exists somewhere, maybe written down, maybe just living in your chest. You do not have to address it today. But you can look at it honestly. Incompletion is not the same as failure. Sometimes it is just the shape of a life being lived.

What is here for you in this?

06 RELATIONSHIP

Think of someone you love and have not called. You know who it is. The not-calling is not indifference. It might be exhaustion. It might be not knowing what to say. It might be that connection feels too large right now. That is allowed. The love is still there, even when the phone is not in your hand.

What is here for you in this?

07 SEASON

It is the season it is. Not the one you wish it were. The light is exactly this long today, and in your body something responds to that whether you think about it or not. You are an animal on a tilted planet. Something in you is adjusting. That is not poetic. It is just true.

What is here for you in this?

08 EVENING

At the end of the day you are counting what you did not do. That is a habit, not a verdict. The day happened. You moved through it. Some of it was good and some was barely manageable and some you would rather not look at. All of it was yours. All of it counts.

What is here for you in this?

09 MEMORY

Something from years ago has come up again this week. You recognize the shape of it. The feeling is older than the current situation. You are not broken for being back here. Some things circle. You can stand in the circle and just look at what is in the center.

What is here for you in this?

10 BODY

Your jaw is probably clenched. Not from anger, necessarily. Just from the effort of being a person today. Let it soften, if you can. If you cannot, that is fine too. Notice the effort itself. You have been working hard at something. It shows up in the body. The body is not wrong.

What is here for you in this?

11 GRIEF

You are grieving something no one else can see. A version of a relationship that did not become what you hoped. A door that closed quietly. No one sent flowers. There was no ceremony. But it was real, and the loss is real. You are allowed to grieve things that do not have funerals.

What is here for you in this?

12 MORNING

You did not sleep well. Or you slept too long and woke up feeling far from yourself. Either way, you are here now, in this body, on this particular day. You do not have to generate energy you do not have. You can just begin where you actually are.

What is here for you in this?

13 ORDINARY OBJECT

Look at your hands. Not to evaluate them. Just look. These are the hands that have done every hard thing you have done. They have reached out, held on, let go, made things, and sometimes done nothing at all when nothing was all you had. They are enough hands.

What is here for you in this?

14 INCOMPLETION

You started something and stopped. You meant to return to it. It has been longer than you planned. This is not a story about your character. This is a story about capacity, and seasons, and the way life interrupts itself. The thing you stopped is still there if you want it. And it is okay if you do not.

What is here for you in this?

15 RELATIONSHIP

There is someone you are not sure how to be around right now. Something shifted and it has not been named. You are carrying the weight of an unspoken thing. You do not have to speak it today. But you can notice the weight. It is real, and noticing it is not nothing.

What is here for you in this?

16 SEASON

Something is ending. Maybe slowly, maybe in a way you can only see in retrospect. Endings do not always announce themselves. Sometimes they are just a gradual quieting. You are allowed to feel the ending before you understand it. Understanding is not required for feeling.

What is here for you in this?

17 BODY

There is tiredness in you that sleep has not fixed. Not every tiredness is about sleep. Some of it is the weight of ongoing things: a situation with no resolution, a decision still unmade, a need that is not being met. You are not lazy. You are carrying something real.

What is here for you in this?

18 MEMORY

You remember a moment when you felt genuinely okay. Not happy, necessarily. Just okay, and present, and not braced against anything. That moment was real. You have been that okay before. You may be that okay again. You do not have to perform okayness now to remember it exists.

What is here for you in this?

19 GRIEF

Grief is not always loud. Sometimes it is just a Tuesday afternoon when everything is technically fine and you feel a weight you cannot name. The weight is not nothing. It is accumulated. It is real. You do not have to explain it to anyone, including yourself. You can just be under it for a moment.

What is here for you in this?

20 ORDINARY OBJECT

The photo on your phone that you keep coming back to. You know which one. There is something in it that you need. Maybe it is the person in it. Maybe it is the version of you that took it. Maybe it is just that particular afternoon. Whatever it is, it is still here, in that square of light.

What is here for you in this?

21 MORNING

You have things to do today and part of you does not want to do any of them. That part is not sabotage. It might be asking for something. Rest. Acknowledgment. A moment that belongs to no task. You might not be able to give it that today. But you can at least hear the asking.

What is here for you in this?

22 INCOMPLETION

You have been meaning to forgive yourself for something. It has been a while. Forgiveness is not a decision you make once. It is something that happens slowly, in layers, when you stop demanding that you already be on the other side of it. You are on this side. That is where the work is.

What is here for you in this?

23 RELATIONSHIP

There is someone who loves you in a way you find difficult to receive. Not because the love is wrong, but because receiving requires something open in you that is sometimes closed. You are not ungrateful. You are human. Let the love be there, even if you cannot fully take it in today.

What is here for you in this?

24 BODY

Your stomach. What is happening there right now. Tightness, or emptiness, or a low-grade hum of something unresolved. The gut knows before the mind does. It is not catastrophizing. It is tracking something real. You can check in with it, the way you would check in with a friend.

What is here for you in this?

25 SEASON

You are in a period of waiting. Not the romantic kind. The kind where you cannot move forward yet and you cannot go back and the middle is uncomfortable and slow. You are not behind. You are in a season that requires patience you did not plan to need. It is still a season. It will not last forever.

What is here for you in this?

26 EVENING

Before you go to sleep tonight, you will probably run through everything that went wrong, or almost wrong, or could go wrong tomorrow. That is the mind doing its job. You do not have to believe all of it. You can watch it the way you watch weather. Real, but not the whole story.

What is here for you in this?

27 MEMORY

There is a younger version of you who needed something they did not get. Not because no one cared, or maybe exactly because no one cared. Either way, the need was real and it is still in you somewhere. You can acknowledge that today without needing it to resolve. Some things we just carry, and that is allowed.

What is here for you in this?

28 GRIEF

You are not the same as you were before the thing that happened. You know that. Sometimes people want you to be, or you want yourself to be, and the gap between who you were and who you are now is the grief. You do not have to bridge it. You can just stand in it and look both ways.

What is here for you in this?

29 ORDINARY OBJECT

The plant in your window. The pile on your floor. The light coming in at this particular angle today. This is the texture of your actual life. Not the version you are building toward. This one. The mess and the light together. Here. This is where you live.

What is here for you in this?

30 INCOMPLETION

You are not finished becoming. That is not a promise that something better is coming. It is just the truth of being alive. You are mid-sentence. Most people are. The incompletion is not the problem. It is the condition. And within it, right now, you are enough.

What is here for you in this?
collection-01-08-chapter-six-build-anywa:
Chapter Six: Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

← Chapter Five: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Radical Immanence Collection · Part Three: The Five Extensions →

Pillar: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Across every book

Characters: Vera Cartwheel

The fifth pillar is where Young's philosophy becomes livable.

The first four pillars are descriptions of a world that is genuinely difficult to inhabit: the self is plural and unstable, reality is constructed and contested, grief is permanent, and the only honest ethical stance requires a quality of attention that most of us cannot sustain for long without relief. It would be reasonable, having followed Young this far, to ask what exactly is being offered. If there is no bedrock, no resolution, no arrival, no foundation that holds, then what is the point of building anything at all?

Young's answer is the fifth pillar, and it is the most quietly radical thing her system contains.

You build anyway.

Not because the building will last or because the foundation is solid or because the finished structure will be what you imagined when you started. You build because the recursive attempt is the only form of integrity the system allows. You build because building is what it means to keep going, and keeping going is what the witness does. The building is provisional. That is not a concession. That is the design.

The word recursive is precise here and worth unpacking. A recursive process is one that refers back to itself, that uses its own output as part of its input, that loops through its own structure in order to proceed. A recursive story is one that keeps returning to its own beginning, not to repeat it but to find something new in it on each return, to discover that the beginning contains more than it appeared to the first time through.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling by Marguerite Young is a recursive novel. It returns to its own images and characters and weathers in the way that a mind returns to what it cannot let go of, finding new layers on each return, deepening rather than resolving. The wig appears and reappears. Grief accumulates rather than processing. Vera's journey circles through itself. The novel does not move from beginning to middle to end in the linear sense. It moves the way memory moves, the way grief moves, the way the plural self moves: returning, deepening, finding that the thing you thought you understood contains more than you thought.

This formal recursion is Young's argument about construction. You do not build once and stand back. You build, and the building reveals what you didn't know when you started, and you build again incorporating what you've learned, and that building reveals more, and you build again. The structure is always under construction. That is not its failure. It is its honesty.

Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy, developed across a body of work culminating in Process and Reality, is the most rigorous available philosophical framework for the world Young's fiction describes. Whitehead's central claim is that reality is not composed of things but of processes. The fundamental units of existence are not stable objects that persist through time but events, occasions of experience, moments of becoming that perish as soon as they are complete and give rise to the next occasion. What we call things, including persons, are patterns of process, relatively stable configurations of becoming that maintain enough continuity to be recognizable across time without ever being literally the same from moment to moment. This is Young's plural self in the language of metaphysics. The self in Whitehead is not a thing that has experiences. It is a process that is its experiences. The self is not the noun. It is the verb. Young says this through fiction. Whitehead says it through formal metaphysics. They are saying the same thing.

The fifth pillar resolves the apparent paradox of Young's system. If there is no foundation, how do you build? If there is no arrival, why journey? If the self is plural and grief is permanent and reality is constructed, what is the point of making anything? The answer is that the making is the point. Not the made thing, which is always provisional, always already in need of revision, always containing more than its maker intended and less than its maker hoped. The act of making, which is the recursive attempt, the return to the beginning with what you learned on the last pass, the building that knows it is building and keeps going anyway.

This is what Young does across eighteen years and 1,198 pages. She builds a novel that is about the impossibility of the foundations that novels conventionally depend on, and she builds it anyway, and the building is magnificent, and it does not resolve, and it does not arrive, and it is complete in the only sense that matters: it is honest about what it is and what it cannot be and what it is for.

You build. You return. You build again. The sentence hasn't ended yet. That is not a tragedy. That is the work.
collection-02-08-part-seven-compressed-t:
Part Seven: Compressed Teachings

← Part Six: The Twelve Pillars · Radical Immanence Collection · Part Eight: Seven-Day Sequences →

These are short pieces written for the moment when you need the teaching without the length. One line to a few sentences, each landing on a single idea. Use them as daily prompts, as things to carry with you, or read through the whole set at once.

Grief as Presence

1. Grief is not the opposite of being okay. It is love with nowhere to land right now.

2. You cannot grieve something that did not matter. The weight is proportional to the caring. That is not suffering. That is evidence.

3. The grief showed up on a Tuesday with no explanation. You do not need one. Something real is moving through you. Let it.

4. No one sent flowers. There was no ceremony. But the loss was real. You are allowed to grieve things that do not have funerals.

5. Grief is not a detour from your life. It is one of the places where your life is most fully happening.

6. You are not stuck. You are in contact with something that mattered. Those are not the same thing.

7. The missing is not a malfunction. It is the shape love makes when it cannot reach what it is reaching for.

8. You do not have to be done with it yet. Some things take as long as they take. That is not weakness. That is honesty.

9. Grief without a name is still grief. The weight you cannot explain is still real. You do not have to justify it to let it be here.

10. Being fully in the grief is not the same as being lost in it. Sometimes it is the most present you have been all week.

Radical Immanence

1. The sacred is not above this. It is inside this. Inside the Wednesday, the tired body, the ordinary meal. Here. Not elsewhere.

2. You are not in the waiting room. This is the room. Your life is happening now, not after the next arrival.

3. Stop waiting to be somewhere more significant. You are somewhere. Specifically, precisely, somewhere. That somewhere is your life.

4. Every tradition points upward. We point here. Downward into this day. Into the body. Into what is already real.

5. The present moment is not a stepping stone. It is the ground. The only ground there is.

6. You keep leaving. That is human. The practice is not staying. It is returning. Again and again, to here.

7. Meaning is not waiting for you at the destination. It is distributed evenly across the whole life. Even the dull parts. Especially there.

8. The washing of dishes in the actual evening of your actual life is not less than a spiritual experience. It is one.

9. Here is not where you are until you get somewhere better. Here is where your life is located. Full stop.

10. You do not have to transcend this. You have to be in it. Fully, honestly, without one eye on the exit. That is the whole practice.

Sacred Ordinary

1. The coffee ring on the desk is time. You were here yesterday. You kept showing up. That ring is proof.

2. Your life is not the highlight reel. It is the Tuesday afternoon, the quiet meal, the unremarkable kindness nobody tracked. That is the whole thing.

3. The ordinary moment you moved past this morning without noticing, that was your life. It counted. It already happened.

4. You are waiting for the meaningful moment. It was the cup of tea. It was the light through the window. It was already here.

5. Meaning is not clustered at the milestones. It is spread across everything. The unremarkable days are not filler. They are the substance.

6. The small act of care that no one saw, that you did not count, that you have already half-forgotten, that is the whole thing. That is it.

7. Your hands have done every hard thing you have done. Look at them for one second. Not to evaluate. Just to look.

8. One extra breath of attention on the ordinary thing. That is the practice. That is all.

9. Nothing is waiting to become your life. This is already it. The mess and the light together. Here. This is where you live.

10. The sacred is not set apart. It is distributed. In the morning ritual, the worn book, the window, the person who said your name today.

The Witness

1. You needed to be seen before you needed to be fixed. That is still true. It has always been true.

2. The but is the bypass. Everything before the but gets cancelled. Try staying without the but.

3. Someone told you their hard thing and you immediately reached for the silver lining. That is love. It is also not witnessing. They are different.

4. When you stop fighting the feeling it gets less loud. Not because it is gone. Because it has finally been seen.

5. The Witness is not a detached observer above the experience. It is warm. It is present. It is fully in contact and still steady.

6. Thirty seconds before the reframe. That is all. Let it be real for thirty seconds before you make it into something else.

7. You came away feeling more alone, even though they were kind. That is what happens when you are responded to but not witnessed.

8. The parts of you that are hardest to look at are not waiting to be corrected. They are waiting to be seen. There is a difference.

9. Some things do not need to be fixed. They need to be sat with. By someone who is not going anywhere. Even if that someone is you.

10. Witnessing is not passive. It takes everything you have to stay present to something hard without immediately trying to move it somewhere easier.

Incompletion

1. You are mid-sentence. That is not a failure of your life. It is the honest shape of a life actually being lived.

2. The unfinished thing is not evidence. Stop putting it on trial.

3. Not finishing something is not always a failure of character. Sometimes it is accurate information about where your energy belongs.

4. A life is not a checklist. You are not a checklist.

5. The incomplete project served its purpose while it was alive. It does not have to be finished to have mattered.

6. You have been meaning to forgive yourself for something. Forgiveness does not happen once. It happens in layers, slowly, when you stop demanding to already be on the other side.

7. Some things between people need more time than we want to give them. Living in the uncertain middle is not weakness. It is the reality of real relationship.

8. The open loop is taking up space in you. You do not have to close it today. You just have to stop treating it as a verdict.

9. There is no finished version of a person. People do not finish until they end. You are supposed to be mid-sentence. You are right on time.

10. Incompletion is not the space between who you are and who you will be when you have sorted everything out. It is the ground you are standing on right now.

Multiplicity

1. You contain contradictions. That is not your problem. That is your humanity.

2. You love them and they exhaust you. Both are true. Neither cancels the other. That is what love in its full human form actually looks like.

3. The version of you that caused harm is also you. You cannot take responsibility for what you have decided is not really you.

4. You are not a deviation from your true self on the bad days. You are fully yourself on the bad days too. That is the harder truth.

5. Stop asking which one is the real you. The answer is: all of them. The whole complicated cast. That is who you are.

6. The parts of you that do not fit the story you tell about yourself, they are not the problem. The story is just too small.

7. Inner hospitality. That is the practice. Letting the contradictions be here without rushing to resolve them into something more manageable.

8. You were taught that certain parts of you were welcome and certain parts were not. That was their limit, not your truth.

9. You cannot live honestly in your own life if you are only in relationship with the acceptable parts of yourself.

10. All of it is you. The grief-carrier and the one who laughs easily and the one who is quietly, stubbornly kind when no one is watching. All of it. Enough.

Non-Bypassing

1. Everything happens for a reason is something you say after the grief. Not instead of it.

2. The but is doing a lot of work. That sounds hard, but: you just cancelled the first half. Try stopping before the but.

3. Using the breath to avoid the feeling is not presence. It is displacement with better branding.

4. You reached for the silver lining before they finished speaking. That is love. It is also a way of telling them their pain is too much for you to just hold.

5. Gratitude and grief are not in competition. You can hold both. But offering gratitude as a correction to grief means you think grief is a mistake.

6. Deciding it is a lesson before you have finished feeling it turns your experience into a curriculum. Let it be an experience first.

7. The feeling deserves to be here before the meaning-making begins. Always. Without exception.

8. Real presence eventually includes the hard thing. Practice that is organized around avoiding the hard thing will, over time, work against you.

9. You can always make meaning later. The feeling was here first. Let it be first.

10. You did not bypass it. You stayed with it, without explanation, without the silver lining, without the lesson. That is one of the harder things a person can do. It mattered.

Community of Outsiders

1. The translated version of you is exhausting to maintain. There are rooms where you do not have to translate. Find them. Build them.

2. You have been in the room but not of it your whole life. That is not failure. That is the beginning of knowing what kind of room you actually need.

3. The loneliness of being surrounded by people who see only the managed version of you: that is a specific loneliness. It has a name. It is real.

4. You are not the only one doing this much translation. The person across from you is probably exhausted by it too. Someone has to go first.

5. The community we are building is not a community of the healed. It is a community of the honest. The only qualification is showing up true.

6. When you said the real thing and someone said me too: that moment. That is what we are building toward. Not all the time. Just more often.

7. You become, to a significant degree, who you are with. Choose people who are practicing the same return.

8. Not-belonging is more common than we say. The silence about it is what makes it lonely. Name it and find who nods.

9. You are not the only one who feels like they are always slightly translating. There is a room where translation is not required. This is it.

10. Real belonging is not the feeling of fitting in. It is the feeling of being known in your complexity and welcomed anyway. That is rarer. It is also possible.

The Monday Mirror

1. Before you pick it up and carry it into the week: turn and look at it. Just for a moment. Just to see what it actually is.

2. Once a week, ask one honest question: what is actually here? Not what should be here. Not what you hope will be here. What is.

3. You have been moving past it all week. This is the moment to stop and look before the week begins again.

4. Self-knowledge is not a luxury. It is what stops you from being surprised by your own experience at the worst possible moment.

5. You are worth looking at. Not when you have achieved more. Not when you have sorted more out. Now. On this day. Exactly as you are.

6. The Monday Mirror is not about self-improvement. It is about honest relationship with yourself. The same quality of attention you would bring to someone you love.

7. Five minutes. One question. What am I carrying that I have not stopped to look at? That is the whole practice.

8. You keep moving without looking. The week accumulates. The underground hum gets louder. Monday is the window. Take it.

9. What is alive in you today that is asking for acknowledgment before you pick up the week and start running? That is the question. That is enough.

10. Naming what you are carrying is not dwelling. It is honest accounting. You can only work with what you are willing to look at.

Here Is Enough

1. Here is not the waiting room. This is the room. Your life is already happening and it is already here and it is already enough.

2. The arrival you are waiting for keeps moving. That is structural. The practice is to stop waiting and be here. It is harder than it sounds.

3. Enough is not a feeling. It is a ground. You do not have to feel it for it to be true.

4. You do not have to like where you are for here to be enough. Enough is not the same as wanted. It is the same as real.

5. You have been deferring your actual life until it becomes more of what you want it to be. This is the actual life. It is happening now.

6. Here is enough is not what we say to people who could not get the better thing. It is the claim that the present moment is the only place anything real ever happens.

7. Stop waiting to be further along before you let yourself be fully here. Further along is not where your life is. Here is where your life is.

8. Not abundant. Not perfect. Not what you ordered. Real. Present. Yours. That is the definition of enough.

9. Come back. You left again, that is human, that is fine, but come back. Here. To this. To what is actually real. Again and again. That is the practice.

10. Three words. A daily return. The only destination is here. The only time is now. The only enough is this. Here is enough.

collection-03-11-chapter-eight-the-turn:
Chapter Eight: The Turn

← Chapter Seven: Young's Horizontal Lady · Radical Immanence Collection · Part Three: The AND →

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

There is a specific experience that the eleventh pillar is trying to name, and it is an experience that most people have had and very few people have a philosophical vocabulary for.

It happens at the moment of becoming a parent, or at the moment of losing one. It happens at the moment of standing at a grave or at a birth or at the bedside of someone who is dying. It happens sometimes in the middle of an ordinary afternoon when something, a smell or a quality of light or the specific weight of a silence, suddenly makes visible the line running through you from before you were born to after you will be gone. It is the experience of the rotation: the moment when the horizontal axis, the lateral spread of the present moment and its accumulations, recedes briefly, and the vertical line becomes palpable.

The philosophical vocabulary for this experience has largely been the vocabulary of the sublime: the overwhelming, the transcendent, the experience that exceeds the capacity of ordinary consciousness to process. But the sublime is the wrong category. The sublime is a response to scale, to the experience of being dwarfed by something larger than yourself. What the rotation produces is not the experience of being dwarfed. It is the experience of being located: the specific, precise, almost physical sensation of knowing where you are in the transmission, of feeling the weight of what is beneath you and the weight of what is above you, of being the crossing point.

The crossing point is not large. It is exact. It is the most precisely located thing there is: the intersection of this specific accumulation with this specific line of transmission, here, now, in this body, in this moment. The rotation does not produce awe at scale. It produces something more like recognition: the sensation of finally seeing the structure you have always been inside.

Grief is one of the most reliable routes to this recognition. The third pillar of Radical Immanence establishes that grief is permanent weather, the atmospheric condition of a world where everything you love is always already changing. The eleventh pillar adds the vertical dimension: grief is also the experience of the transmission line becoming palpable. When you lose someone who was part of your constitution, someone whose deposit is in your sediment, someone who was carrying part of what you carry, you feel the vertical line. You feel the weight that was being held by another person and is now being held by you alone. You feel the transmission.

This is why grief is not only weather. It is also a form of geological education. It teaches you, in a way that nothing else teaches you with the same precision, what you are made of and what you are carrying. It teaches you the crossing point by making the vertical line temporarily visible in a way it is not usually visible through the horizontal spread of ordinary accumulation.

The turn is not comfortable. The rotation that moves you from the horizontal axis to the vertical is the same rotation that the figure at the bottom of the Wheel of Fortune is experiencing: the stripping away of the lateral accumulation, the exposure of the vertical line, the discovery that the crossing point was always there and that the horizontal spread was always resting on it. Boethius in the cell. Miss MacIntosh without the wig. Vera on the Grey Goose bus, carrying her grief toward a destination that keeps becoming something other than what she imagined.

But the turn is not only loss. It is also expansion, of a specific kind that is easy to miss because it does not look like expansion from the horizontal axis. From the horizontal axis, the rotation looks like reduction: you lose the lateral spread, the accumulation, the wide extension of the self in its social and relational world. From the crossing point, the rotation reveals that you were always inside something larger than the lateral spread. You were always on the transmission line. You were always constituted by what was deposited before you arrived and constituting what will be deposited after you leave. The expansion is not into a larger space. It is into a deeper understanding of the space you were already in.

Here is not only here. Here is also the sediment beneath here, and the not-yet-formed ground above here, and the transmission line running through here from the ancestors to the not-yet-born, and the crossing point where all of that meets in this body, in this moment, in this specific configuration of alluvial material that is what the self actually is.

That is the turn. That is what the rotation reveals. That is what the eleventh pillar is for.

collection-03-04-chapter-two-the-transmi:
Chapter Two: The Transmission Line

← Chapter One: What the Horizontal Cannot See · Radical Immanence Collection · Chapter Three: The Ancestors Are in the Sediment →

There is a word in geology for what happens when material is carried by a moving medium, water or wind or ice, and deposited somewhere else when the medium slows. The word is alluvial. Alluvial material is material that has been carried and deposited. It is not where it started. It is not the medium that carried it. It is the record of a transmission: the evidence that something moved, was held, was released, came to rest in a new configuration.

The Mississippi River delta is alluvial. It is made of everything the river carried from the upper watershed, from Minnesota and Iowa and Indiana, from the glacial till fields and the eroded limestone bluffs and the topsoil of a thousand farms. None of that material is where it started. All of it is still itself. It has been transmitted, and in the transmission it has become something new: the delta, which is both the record of everything the river carried and a new landscape that did not exist before the carrying.

The self is alluvial.

This is not a metaphor, or it is not only a metaphor. It is a description of the actual process by which selves are constituted. You are made of what was carried to you and deposited in you by the moving medium of time and relation. The language you think in was carried to you by people who are dead. The categories through which you organize experience were carried to you by philosophical and cultural traditions that stretch back further than any individual life. The specific grief you carry was deposited in you by specific losses that were themselves deposited by earlier losses, the grief of your parents and their parents, the grief of the people who stood on the ground before you stood on it, all of it alluvial, all of it carried and deposited, none of it where it started, all of it still itself in a new configuration.

The transmission line is the line along which the carrying happens.

It is not a metaphor for ancestry, though ancestry is one of its most visible forms. It is a structural description of how time actually works when you stop measuring it as duration and start reading it as deposit. Every present moment is a crossing point on the transmission line: the place where everything that has been carried arrives and where everything that will be carried forward begins. The present moment is not a point on a timeline. It is an intersection. It is the place where the horizontal spread of what you are meets the vertical line of what you are inside.

Western philosophy has largely failed to develop an adequate account of the transmission line because it has been committed, at its deepest level, to a model of time as linear duration and a model of the self as a unified subject moving through that duration toward destinations. On the linear model, the past is behind you and the future is ahead of you and the present is the moving edge between them, the knife's edge of now that separates what has been from what will be. The self on the linear model is a traveler on a road: it has come from somewhere and is going somewhere and its obligations are primarily to the journey and to the other travelers it encounters along the way.

The transmission model is not a longer road. It is a different geometry entirely.

On the transmission model, the past is not behind you. It is beneath you, in the sediment, pressing up through the soles of your feet. The future is not ahead of you. It is above you, in the not-yet-formed layers that will be pressed down by the weight of what you deposit. And the present is not a moving edge. It is a crossing point: the place where the vertical line of transmission intersects the horizontal spread of the living moment, the place where what has been deposited meets what is being deposited, the place where the alluvial self stands in the middle of the carrying.

This geometry changes everything about obligation.

On the linear model, obligation runs forward: you owe things to the people ahead of you on the road, the people you will encounter, the future you are moving toward. The past is behind you and its obligations, if any, are to memory and to the honoring of what has been. But memory and honoring are optional in a way that forward obligation is not: you can choose to remember or not to remember, to honor or not to honor, without changing the structure of your forward journey.

On the transmission model, obligation runs in both directions simultaneously, because you are not on a road. You are on a line that passes through you. What was deposited before you arrived shaped the ground you stand on. What you deposit will shape the ground that the not-yet-born will stand on. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. It arises from the fact of being a crossing point, from being constituted by the deposit of others, from being a carrier of what will constitute the ground that comes after.

You did not choose to be alluvial. You are alluvial. The obligation is in the constitution.
collection-01-04-chapter-two-not-one-sel:
Chapter Two: Not One Self

← Part Two: The First Five Pillars · Radical Immanence Collection · Chapter Three: Reality Is Constructed →

Pillar: Pillar 1 Not One Self · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The first thing Young asks you to give up is the one you are most attached to. Not your beliefs, not your certainties, not even your story about where you came from and what it made you. She asks you to give up the assumption underneath all of those: that there is a you doing the believing, the knowing, the remembering. A stable center that receives experience and integrates it into something coherent and continuous. A self that, whatever it has been through, remains fundamentally itself.

This is the assumption philosophy has protected most ferociously. It is the assumption Descartes was protecting when he stripped everything else away and found the thinking thing that could not be doubted. It is the assumption Kant was protecting when he built the transcendental subject, the organizing "I" that makes experience possible by being prior to it. It is the assumption that runs underneath liberal political theory, psychoanalysis, developmental psychology, and most of what passes for common sense about human identity. You are someone. That someone persists. That persistence is what makes you responsible for your actions, capable of relationship, legible to others and to yourself.

Young does not argue against this assumption.

She does something more unsettling.

She builds a world in which you can watch it fail.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling by Marguerite Young opens on a journey. Vera is traveling by Grey Goose bus from the east coast toward Indiana, toward the town of What Cheer, toward the woman who raised her and then disappeared into the water one morning, leaving her wig and her clothes and her sea boots filled with sand and her broken black umbrella and her copy of Pilgrim's Progress and her eye-glasses and her purse with two pennies in it. The novel is, in one sense, the account of that journey. In another and more accurate sense it is the account of everything that cannot be accounted for by a journey with a beginning and a destination.

Vera is not one person across those 1,198 pages. She is not unreliable in the way that literary criticism uses the term, meaning a narrator whose account we must read against the grain to find the truth underneath. There is no truth underneath, and that is not Vera's limitation. It is Young's central claim. Vera contains the opium world of her mother Catherine, a world as internally consistent and as saturated with meaning as any consensus reality the novel offers. Vera contains the rigid certainties of Miss MacIntosh herself, the Indiana pragmatist who turned out to be as constructed as everything she condemned. Vera contains her own grief, which does not process or resolve but accumulates, which is how grief actually works and not how we prefer to narrate it.

What Young is showing, across the full impossible length of the novel, is that this is not Vera's particular psychological condition. It is the condition. The plurality is not a symptom. It is the structure.

Catherine's opium world is the clearest demonstration of this. The critical temptation, and it is a temptation Young is aware of and refuses to satisfy, is to read Catherine's world as delusion and the Indiana plains as reality, to organize the novel around the axis of true and false, sane and mad, grounded and unmoored. Young dismantles that axis not by arguing against it but by giving Catherine's world the same density, the same internal logic, the same weight of accumulated detail as anything else in the novel. The opium world is not thin. It is not a distortion of something more real. It is another reality, sustained by a self that is genuinely living in it, and the self that lives in it is as real as any other self Catherine contains.

This is the philosophical move. Not the claim that all realities are equal in some lazy relativist sense. The claim that the self is not the kind of thing that lives in one reality. The self is the kind of thing that lives in several realities simultaneously, navigating between them with varying degrees of awareness and control. The demand that it choose one and call that one the true self is a demand that amputates most of what the self actually is.

Miss MacIntosh made that demand. She was the one real thing in Vera's childhood, the empiricist in the house of illusion, the woman who insisted on the solid world against Catherine's dissolving one. And then her wig came off. And there was nothing underneath the solid woman but another constructed self, bald and false-toothed and one-breasted, as much a performance as anything Catherine ever dreamed. The real Miss MacIntosh was not more real. She was a different performance.

Young does not present this as a tragedy, though it contains tragedy. She presents it as information. This is what selves are. This is what you are working with. Now what?

Hume got closer than most to understanding this. Hume looked for the unified self in his own experience and found, famously, that he could never catch himself without a perception. He found the bundle, the stream of experiences with no experiencer underneath, and it troubled him enough that he retreated from the full implications. Young does not retreat. She builds a novel-length investigation of what the bundle actually looks like from the inside, which is something a philosophical treatise cannot do because it cannot sustain the investigation long enough or in the right form.

William James named the stream of consciousness and understood that the self was a process rather than a thing, that the "I" was always already in motion rather than stable behind its experiences. Young takes James seriously in a way that most of the tradition did not, extending the stream until it becomes clear that it does not flow in one direction, does not empty into a single sea. It branches and doubles back and runs underground and surfaces somewhere unexpected and is still, somehow, the water.

The thinker Young is most in dialogue with is Gertrude Stein, who was William James's student and whose investigation of repetition, of the continuous present, of identity as something that happens rather than something that is, runs parallel to Young's project with different formal tools. Where Stein strips language down to its mechanisms to show the self as a grammatical construction, Young piles language up until the construction becomes visible through its own excess. Different directions, the same destination: the self is not the noun. It is the verb.

The plural self is not the absent self. It is the self that is more than any single account of it can capture. It does not mean that accountability dissolves. It produces a more complicated picture of what it means to be responsible for actions taken by a self that is not singular and not fully transparent to itself. The plural self can be witnessed. It cannot be reduced.

The demand for singular selfhood is not just a philosophical error. It is a political technology. Every system that requires enemies requires a population of selves simple enough to be sorted: us and them, citizen and alien, deserving and undeserving. The more complex the actual population, the more pressure the system applies to force simplification. The people most damaged by this demand are the people whose plurality is most visible and most threatening to the sorting system. Young's plural self is not a therapy for that violence. It is a philosophical framework that names the mechanism producing it.

We keep coming back to the wig because Young keeps coming back to it. It is the novel's central image and it earns that centrality. Miss MacIntosh's wig ends up on the back of a crab and something in the world becomes permanently different for Vera. Not because the wig reveals a truth that was hidden. Because it reveals that the solid woman was a construction, which means the solid world the solid woman represented was a construction too, which means the opposition between Catherine's illusion and Miss MacIntosh's reality collapses, which means Vera has to find a way to live without the opposition she built her childhood on.

This is the first pillar. This is where Young begins. Everything else the system builds is built on this: the self is plural, the plurality is the condition, and the honest life is the one that stops trying to wig it back together.
