writing-life-11-chapter-ten-the-sacred-i:
Chapter Ten: The Sacred Is Here

← Chapter Nine: Language Shapes What’s Possible · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Eleven: The Crossing Point →

Pillar: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here · Across every book

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

The tenth pillar is the most delicate of all the pillars and the one that required the most time to name accurately.

"Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" is suffused with a quality that can only be called sacred: a sense that the ordinary world, all of it is charged with a significance that exceeds ordinary description. But the significance does not point beyond the world. It points deeper into it. Young offers a way of experiencing the world as sacred that requires no transcendence, no beyond, no god outside the becoming. The sacred is immanent or it is nothing. This is the tenth pillar, and it is, in some ways, the one that holds all the others together.

Immanence is the philosophical term for what is present within rather than transcendent beyond. It is the opposite of the move that most philosophical and religious systems make when they encounter the difficulty of existence: the move upward, outward, beyond, toward the foundation that does not shift, the ground that holds still, the truth that exists outside the flux and can therefore anchor it. Young refuses that move at every level of her system. There is no transcendent ground in "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling". Everything that exists, exists here, in the immanent world, in the middle of the becoming, in the room with the contradiction.

Radical is the modifier that specifies how far the immanence goes. A moderate immanence might acknowledge that most of what we know is available within experience while leaving open the possibility of some transcendent anchor. Young's immanence is not moderate. It goes all the way down. The immanence is the whole of it. What is here is what there is, and what is here is plural, constructed, grief-saturated, and alive in ways that the search for transcendence has always prevented us from fully seeing.

The novel states this on its first page: “there is perhaps no God but what we dreamed.” Miss MacIntosh says it more bluntly: “God loves the wind, the empty places. There is no God.” Steven Shaviro, reading the novel, finds a vision “in no way transcendent or otherworldly,” a celebration of something “available to us, at every moment, in ordinary life.”

This is not nihilism. The refusal of transcendence is not the refusal of meaning. It is the insistence that meaning is made here, in the immanent world, by plural selves building provisional structures with the full knowledge that the structures are provisional. That is a harder and more honest account of meaning than any transcendent guarantee could provide. Young understood this.

Robin Wall Kimmerer's work on reciprocity and the intelligence of the living world enters the conversation around the tenth pillar. Kimmerer's insistence that the world is not a collection of objects but a community of subjects, that attention to the non-human is not sentiment but epistemology, rhymes with Young's own practice of giving the Indiana landscape the same density and interiority she gives her human characters. Every participant in the novel's world, carries the same weight of accumulated time and grief as any human character.

The tenth pillar is where the system becomes, if the word is not too large, spiritual, but spiritual in a way that requires no god outside the becoming, no transcendent ground beneath the flux. The sacred is the ordinary world attended to with the full quality of attention the witness brings.

That is the tenth pillar. That is radical immanence. That is what the title names.

No pillar travels farther in Young’s work than this one. It follows from the nature-worship of “Worship” (1927), which still addresses God and finds him “In stars and flowers and shining eyes,” through the graduate essay in which God “would hardly be missed,” to “Noah’s Ark” (1943), where God is “creation’s flaw,” to the novel, and finally to the sacred as labor in "Harp Song for a Radical". Young used a vocabulary that never left her: the angel she insisted “is real,” her pull toward the Catholic Church, and resurrection, the word she never gave up.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

"Worship" (1927) is the starting point: "God, I don't pray to you in church," and "I see you only / In stars and flowers and shining eyes, / In dewdrops and in pearls." In "Twilight" the garden's quiet could "Be peopled by angels even." "Door-Way" puts death, the threshold of the beyond, on an ordinary street.

Complication: this God is still addressed as "Thine." It is theist immanence, God found in nature, which Young's later work would take apart.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

This is the pillar that moves most in Phase Two. The Patmore essay says that "God as God, if subtracted from that cosmos, would hardly be missed." The Night Thoughts essay ends by equating the mystic's eternity with the modern unconscious. The poems bring heaven down. "Wild Orchard" may be Young's clearest early image of immanence: "For man is rooted at the last, / He is rooted and held fast, / Confounded by the strangest sainthood / Blowing in wind, wild orchard." Holiness is rootedness in earth. In "Sky of Grasses," "Heaven has shrunk to the dim size / Comprehended by insects' eyes." In "Fall of Man" the angels fall "Among brier roses" and "The blue deep was a field of clover." In "Strange Prophecy" the skull becomes "a hive for honey bees." "Lenten Feast" warns that anyone who will not feast on the world's small beauties becomes bones that "Rattle in void eternity."

Complication: "Rosary in Discord" still prays to the Trinity, though the prayer opens out to "the multiform, / The crowded sea / And populous storm." "Lover" ends "dust will never / Be all of him." "The Visit" closes on "The balm in Gilead for me." The theist God of "Worship" is fading but not gone.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

Here Young goes furthest. "Noah's Ark" (1943): "God is the impotent old man, and withered," and "He is creation's flaw / And celibate, nor passenger of this uniting ark." "The Contravalid": "Of heaven, we do not need to go there to be there this night." "Elegy": "our God is not the God of Weight / But ourselves." Drafts: "we are God and little pepper moths," and "God could not compass His own death." "The White Rat" puts the pillar's question in Augustine's mouth inside a laboratory cage: "O, my God, art Thou without or within?" "The Trains" (1942): "there is an angel mental as man." "Marriage in Heaven" weds the soul to an earth that "has no home."

Complication: the pull toward transcendence is strongest here too. "Night Watches" (1942): "exiled is man... Whose Orient is origin not earth." A draft imagines life arriving as "the super-sensible cell, / All futurity from another planet fallen." Berkeley hopes God may "be real / And not postulated merely as our theory."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

The title angel is reduced: "There was no angel, nor even a way to deduce one from such a primitive landscape." Instead "there was a wild turkey, almost as handsome." The storekeeper puts on Rapp's spectacles and "By God, he almost saw an angel." Thomas Say "sought nothing supernatural but the Spirit of Nature." Owen locates worship in "inexpressible feelings of wonder."

Complication: Robert Dale, the rationalist's son, ends haunted by spirits, with "no harmony at all in the universe, no center but whirlwinds." Of the two visions merging, the narrator says, "Perhaps not." The supernatural returns in the children of unbelief.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

The first page: "there is perhaps no God but what we dreamed, and there is no train." Miss MacIntosh: "God loves the wind, the empty places. There is no God." As Shaviro puts it, what the novel celebrates is available "at every moment, in ordinary life."

Complication: the last page is full of Gabriel's horn, the golden cock, and the old white mule, though the horn will be "a silent horn for us." The vocabulary remains, and its meaning moves to earth.

What the novel adds is the earthly turn stated in a character’s voice rather than argued in verse. The poems of the war years reached God as “creation’s flaw” by reasoning. The novel opens by assuming it. The pillar is still partial here, since the vocabulary of the beyond remains on the last page.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

On Broch's dying Virgil: "We are the only God we know of." The essays find the marvelous in the ordinary: the Midwest's dead whale in a boxcar and sow at the wheel of a Ford, Marianne Moore's strawberry "that's had quite a struggle," Raggedy Ann with her nose forgotten. "Angels are the dreams of men." "As long as you're still dreaming, you're alive."

Complication: she was "very, very drawn to the Catholic Church," read the Bible daily, studied the mystics, defended "angels and unearthly creatures, spirits without bodies," told Neville "the angel is real," named "transmutation and transmigration, metempsychosis" and "resurrection" as her meaning, saw Poe's "astral body," and was visited nightly by Henry James. "The Artist as Wanderer" calls art "an act of faith."

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 10: The Sacred Is Here

The sacred moves into labor: the "divine spark" in the dead souls of America, "the proletaire of Galilee," railroad ties as crosses for "any railroad Christ." Weitling is "an agnostic who had remained under the spell of the icons of Catholicism," which also describes Young. Resurrection, the word she never gave up, now means organizing the working poor.
writing-life-01-introduction:
Introduction

Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter One: Not One Self →

Marguerite Young said she spent her entire career writing about one thing her entire life. She understood something philosophy has been circling for centuries without quite saying: the self is not something a person finds. It is something a person keeps surviving. The philosophy she was developing carries across Young’s childhood poems, gained a method in her graduate years, was argued outright in her verse, turned toward history and community in her prose, and was still changing in the unfinished book she left at her death. This study follows that philosophy. Through years of studying her work I called it Radical Immanence before I knew the history of the term. Where she fits historically with the term and the philosophy around it has been covered on Substack here. This book asks whether Young can fairly be credited with developing it through her writing.

Young was filed under the wrong category. Not maliciously, not carelessly, but wrongly in a way that has cost us something. We call her a novelist, an eccentric, a maximalist, a writer’s writer, a forgotten genius waiting to be rediscovered. All of that is true and none of it is the point. The point is that Young built a philosophical system, and she built it in poetry, fiction, and history because she was honest enough to know that the system could not survive in any other form. A treatise on the impossibility of stable selfhood written in stable expository prose would contradict itself before the second paragraph.

Philosophy, as it has been practiced in the Western tradition, depends on formal commitments that Young’s system cannot make without self-betrayal. It depends on the resolvable argument, the claim that can be stated, supported, and concluded. It depends on the stable authorial voice, the consistent “I” who stands behind the claim. And it depends on the assumption that reality yields to systematic description, that if the right method is applied rigorously enough, the truth will hold still long enough to be captured. Young refuses all three. Resolution is the lie her system is built to expose. A stable voice performing a theory of plural selfhood undermines the theory. And reality, for Young, is precisely the kind of thing that keeps becoming something else while it is being described.

Why the Tradition Missed Her

The Western philosophical tradition handles thinkers who do not fit its categories in three ways. It absorbs them, keeping the parts that translate into acceptable philosophical language and calling the rest style. It files them, assigning the work to a discipline that can contain it without being challenged by it: literature, mysticism, women’s writing, experimental fiction. Or it ignores them, which is easier than it sounds when Young’s central work is a 1,198 pages long novel that refuses to summarize. Young got all three.

She fits the profile of the missed thinker with uncomfortable precision. She was a woman. Her work was long in a way that read as excess rather than ambition, because excess and ambition are distributed differently by gender in every critical tradition we have. Its texture was emotional, full of grief and longing and interior weather, and emotional texture has historically moved work out of the philosophy section regardless of the rigor underneath. And it refused the payoff.

Philosophy advances through contestation, through claims that can be refuted and refined. Young’s novel does not say the self is plural. It enacts plurality in a way that makes the reader experience the argument rather than evaluate it. That is a more honest move for this particular argument, but it is not one the tradition knows how to answer. This is not Young’s failure. It is the tradition’s limitation.

There is also the question of timing. Young’s novel appeared in 1965, one year before Foucault’s Les Mots et les Choses was published in French and two years before Derrida’s Of Grammatology. The conversation best equipped to receive her, the poststructuralist dismantling of the unified subject and the attention to how form carries argument, was only beginning in Europe and had not yet reached American intellectual culture with any force. She was not ahead of her time in the romantic sense. She was genuinely prior to the moment that would have known what to do with her. By the time that moment arrived, she had been filed, and filed things do not get reconsidered easily. Again this is covered in depth on the Substack here.

The Name and the Test

Radical Immanence is a later name. Young never used it, and she never set out her ideas as a system. Steven Shaviro comes closest when he calls her vision “in no way transcendent or otherworldly,” a celebration of something “available to us, at every moment, in ordinary life.” To read Young’s novel alone is to see the philosophy at its fullest. To credit Young with developing it requires more: a philosophy that is developed, rather than merely present, should show a history, with early forms, later refinements, turns, and returns.

The evidence comes from the whole of Young’s record: interviews and remembered conversations, the published criticism, the essays, stories, and reviews in "Inviting the Muses", and her books "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling", "Angel in the Forest", "Harp Song for a Radical", and her "Collected Poems". Each source has been weighed on its own against the eleven pillars of Radical Immanence and then placed in order of composition and publication.

The work falls into seven phases

Phase One covers the childhood and early poems, from 1908 to 1934, where the philosophy appears as feeling.

Phase Two covers the Chicago years, the graduate essays, and Prismatic Ground, from 1935 to 1937, where it gains a method in William James, a founding act of witness beside Minna Weissenbach, and its first prose statements.

Phase Three covers the philosophical poems of 1938 to 1945, where Young argues the pillars most directly.

Phase Four covers her book "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters,” from 1945 to 1946, where the philosophy turns toward history and community.

Phase Five covers "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling", written over about eighteen years and published in 1965, where the philosophy is lived by characters and reaches its fullest form.

Phase Six covers the occasional prose, the interviews, and Young’s readings of her own work, where she both confirms the philosophy and speaks against parts of it.

Phase Seven covers "Harp Song for a Radical", written in her last decades and published in 1999, where the philosophy turns fully to labor, power, and memory.

Some cautions run through every phase

Writing dates and publication dates often differ. Most of the essays in "Inviting the Muses" are undated, and the interviews come mostly after 1965. The appendix of drafts in "The Collected Poems" holds work Young never chose to publish. "Harp Song for a Radical" was arranged by its editors after her death. Where dates are uncertain, work is placed by period rather than by year.

The following has eleven chapters that cover each pillar of Radical Immanence with analysis of the seven phases of Young’s work. Each phase takes the eleven pillars in turn, gives the evidence that supports each and, where the record holds it, the evidence that complicates it. Complications are given equal weight. A philosophy credited to a writer should be found in what she wrote, including the places where she argued against it. That, too, is faithful to her. A system built on the refusal of false wholeness should not be presented as more finished than it was.

Below is a summary of the context around each phase and what the phase adds to the whole.

Philosophers get named for their positions.

Young’s position is Radical Immanence.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Context

Marguerite Young was born in Indiana on August 26, 1908. The philosophy begins before any published work. In her family's telling, she was the reincarnation of her dead cousin Harry, whom her grandmother believed "had been born again in me," and in her own later account "the child becomes a vehicle for the grandmother." She said her first poem, written at five, was about loss, and she offered a poem written at six as proof that the whole of her work lay in her from childhood. Near eighty, she could still recite from memory "I Heard a Bird," written at nine, and dictated it for her collected poems.

Her first published poems appeared in college literary magazines from 1927 to 1930, and "Jonathan's House" won first prize in the Butler Literary Contest in 1929. From 1930 to 1934 she published in Poetry: "Recurring," "Ballad-Loving Woman," "Lot's Wife," and "A Girl's Song" in 1930, "Biography" in 1932, and "Minnows and a Monster" and "Woodlands Far Removed" in 1934. Several of these were later collected in Prismatic Ground (1937), but they were written and first published in this phase. The forms are conventional: sonnets, ballads, triolets, refrain songs. The subjects are local: old women sweeping leaves, a farmer with postcards, a peddler woman with a wagon, a widow in a stone house. Here the philosophy shows up as feeling, not argument.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase One gives the philosophy its emotional ground. Grief that does not end, the self both merged and alone, the fragile thing built anyway, and God found in the world are all present by the time Young was twenty-six. Her later claim that "everything is prophetic in writing" holds for these poems. What is missing is argument, politics, and a sacred that is free of theism. Those come later.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Context

Young took her MA in early modern English literature at the University of Chicago in 1936. These are the years in which she sat with Minna Weissenbach. By her graduate years she was reading William James, whose Psychology she studied "as if it were a Bible." Her academic essays come from her graduate study, though the record does not give their exact dates: "Coventry Patmore's Theory of Knowledge" and "The Theistic Mysticism of Young's Night Thoughts." Her poems appeared steadily: eight in Poetry in September 1935, others in Comment in 1935 and 1936, five more in Poetry in March 1937, and "Daniel" in The New Republic in August 1937. Prismatic Ground, her first book, came out in 1937.

The poems of this phase are denser and stranger than the early ones. Angels fall into clover, a man turns into an orchard, frogs watch a girl in the dark. This is the phase in which the sacred moves decisively into the world.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase Two gives the philosophy its method, its founding experience, and its first prose statements. James supplies the plural self and the wild data. Minna supplies the witness. The graduate essays supply three sentences that state Pillars 2, 9, and 10 almost outright. The poems move the sacred from God-in-nature to sainthood-as-rootedness and heaven-as-clover. The complications also take shape: witnessing that comes too late, testimony that fails, and the racial stereotypes that would run through Young's later work.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Context

These are the war years, and the years in which Young argued her philosophy most directly. She published in the leading literary journals: "Ventriloquist: The Coffee Hour" in Poetry (1940); "Death by Rarity" and "The Long War" in The Kenyon Review (1940); "The Funeral," "Snow in the Mountains," "Slow Motion," "The Clinic," and "At the Cinema" in New Directions (1941); "Guide to New Harmony, Indiana" in The Saturday Review (1941); "A Crystal Principle" and "Moderate Fable" in The Kenyon Review (1942); others in The Southern Review, Accent, and American Prefaces. Moderate Fable (1944), dedicated to the memory of Minna Weissenbach, was named poetry book of the year by the National Academy of Arts and Letters, according to her editors. The late poems appeared in 1945: "Of Deed, Love, Death" in The Kenyon Review, "Proem to Reality" in Partisan Review, and "The Contravalid" and "Elegy" in Accent. The unpublished drafts in the Beinecke papers come from the same years.

At the same time Young was writing "Angel in the Forest", first as lyric ballads. "Guide to New Harmony, Indiana" (1941) survives from that version. The poems argue with Berkeley, Descartes, Aquinas, Heraclitus, Calvin, Plato, and Pythagoras. The vocabulary turns technical: "negative magnitude," "null class," "the if-then relation," "schemata," "specious present." The war comes in as parachutists, airmen, submarines, and walrus herds.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase Three is the philosophy argued. Every pillar gets either a formal statement or an exact image within these eight years, and several get their clearest statement anywhere in Young's work: the flaw, the contravalid, the wound of absence, God as creation's flaw. The war turns witness and grief toward the state, the laboratory, and extinction. The phase also holds the strongest counterarguments: the past as nothing, the self's division as terror, and the soul as exile from elsewhere. In 1945 Young left the lyric, and the arguments passed into prose.

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Context

"Angel in the Forest" began as about sixty lyric ballads, became "a long pseudo-Miltonic blank verse poem," and became prose only when Young found verse "inadequate for the inclusion of facts and figures." She said she "stumbled into prose almost reluctantly." The book is a history of two utopias at New Harmony, Indiana, the Rappites and the Owenites, set beside the town in 1940. It was published in 1945 and praised by Mark Van Doren and Robert Penn Warren. What first drew Young to New Harmony, by her own account, was "a kind of group of Steinbeck characters living in tents at the outskirts," the stragglers "who sat at the gates of both utopias and never joined either one," and a band of wandering Ozark coal miners. In 1945 she was also, by her own account, a pacifist. "Complex Life and Complex Letters" (1946) followed, an argument about the nature of reality in the form of a literary manifesto.

The change of form is a change in the philosophy. The ideas argued in the poems move into history, community, and economics.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase Four turns the philosophy outward. Pillars 2, 4, 5, 8, and 9 gain a social and political dimension: who keeps the shared illusion, who witnesses and for whom, who builds and who is sacrificed, whose bones lie under whose graves, who controls the words. The tone is drier and more comic than the poems. The book holds both sides of every question, utopia and doubt, perfection and flaw, and the one sure thing it reaches is the miller's thumbprint.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Context

Young began the novel soon after "Angel in the Forest" and worked on it for about eighteen years. It was published in 1965, nearly twelve hundred pages long. Her accounts of its making bear on the philosophy. She said she "knew the last scene the day I started," that she was "controlled by intellectual ideas" and not automatic writing, and that she listened "until I heard a kind of inner music." The book "took on its cosmic magnitude" only when she rewrote Mr. Spitzer so that he does not know whether he is himself or his dead twin. She folded the unwritable flour-miller story into every manuscript. She built the book from monologues, "one character at a time," and refused the walk-on butler, since every minor figure must move "in an orbit of his own dream." In these years she also wrote to President Kennedy about atomic testing. The novel draws the strongest critical readings of her philosophy, including Petrolle's "magical metaphysic" and Shaviro's "pluralistic ontology."

The novel holds the philosophy at full strength. What does the novel add to the work that came before it? For each pillar the question is what changed over eighteen years of composition, which pillars first become fully lived here.

What the Novel Adds

Phase Five is the synthesis. The philosophy argued in the poems and set in history in "Angel in the Forest" is lived by characters across 1,198 pages. Measured against the earlier work, the novel adds four things. It turns the pillars from statement into character, since every minor figure moves “in an orbit of his own dream.” It makes the keeper of the shared fiction a beloved person, so that discovery and grief arrive together. It brings race to the center of witness and memory: the white detective, the lynching rope, and a narrator who names her own failure to see.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Context

This phase is defined less by dates than by kind. "Inviting the Muses" (1994) gathers essays, stories, and reviews written across decades, and the record does not date most of them. The interviews, with Studs Terkel, Susan Neville, LaVerne Harrell Clark, Charles Ruas, and others, come mostly after the novel appeared in 1965. Young taught for decades, at the New School, Fordham, and elsewhere, and told students to read James's Psychology as a writer's central text. In 1989 she wrote the introduction to her collected poems. In this phase Young explains her philosophy in her own voice, and also speaks against parts of it.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase Six is Young interpreting herself. She confirms the pillars in her own sentences and extends Pillars Seven and Nine to deafness and life without language. It is also the phase of her clearest dissents: the steady self, the wish for permanence, the voice from nowhere, the full vocabulary of angels and resurrection. Her habit of holding opposite positions at once is most visible here, in her own voice.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Context

After the novel, Young turned to Eugene V. Debs. In 1989 she described "the presently forthcoming volumes of the Debs trilogy," along with a biography of James Whitcomb Riley and novellas. She wrote that Dostoyevsky and Tolstoy influenced "all my mature work and particularly that of the present," and recalled that Debs spoke of "the Lazarus flowers of Socialism." Ruas reports that she saw the Vietnam protests as "a modern-day recapitulation" of Debs's issues, and that she wanted "tremendously big archetypal figures" because history "is directed by the individual." She called the work a "transcendental socialism." She was writing the Pullman strike chapter when she fell ill. Her drafts "became mixed together" during a building renovation, and she died on November 17, 1995. Charles Ruas prepared the text, and "Harp Song for a Radical" appeared in 1999. Its prose is hers, and its arrangement is partly the editors'.

What This Phase Contributes

Phase Seven gives the philosophy its political and historical body. The illusion becomes capitalism, the witness becomes the record-keeper of the working dead, the past becomes Sand Creek and Ludlow, the word becomes "red," and the sacred becomes the spark in the dead souls of labor. The crossing point gets its strongest image, and transmission finally succeeds. The complications are great-man history, narrowed sympathy for some women, and an incompletion that Young did not choose. The book's last words fit Debs and fit her too. The elegiac sense continues "perhaps long afterward. As will be seen."

Chapter Eleven: The Crossing Point

← Chapter Ten: The Sacred Is Here · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Conclusion →

Pillar: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point · Across every book

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh

Every pillar stands vertical. Every pillar holds a horizontal load. The architecture of the ten pillars is already, in its form, a crossing point: the vertical supports bearing the horizontal weight of what the system carries. What has not yet been named is the intersection itself. The place where the two axes meet. The place where you are already standing.

That place is the eleventh pillar. It is not added to the ten. It is found inside them, at the center of the architecture, where the weight crosses.

It has been there the whole time.

Every one of the ten pillars describes the self on a lateral axis. The plural self spreads across multiple registers simultaneously. The sedimentary time presses down in layers, accumulating horizontally beneath the present moment. The permanent grief moves through the atmospheric conditions of a life, spreading rather than resolving. Even the recursive construction, which might seem to involve a vertical dimension, is described as a return to the beginning on the same level, a circling back rather than a descent or an ascent.

The horizontal axis is the axis of accumulation. It is the axis on which you can see the full spread of what a self contains: the multiple registers of the plural self, the layered sediment of time, the wide atmospheric spread of grief. It is the axis that the ten pillars map with extraordinary precision.

What the horizontal axis cannot see, by definition, is the vertical.

The vertical axis is the axis of transmission. It is the line that runs through the crossing point from what was given to what will be required. It is the line that connects the ancestors in the sediment to the not-yet-born in the not-yet-formed ground. It is the line that makes obligation possible, not as a chosen commitment but as a structural fact: you are constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and you are constituting what will be deposited after you leave. The vertical axis is not something you can opt into or out of. It is the dimension you are already inside.

The ten pillars describe what you are. The eleventh pillar describes what you are inside of.

To be a carrier is not to be a vehicle. A vehicle is a neutral medium. The thing carried passes through it unchanged. What you carry, you change, and what changes you, you carry forward transformed. The transmission is not neutral. It is not a pipeline. It is a process of sedimentation, and you are both the sediment and the thing being deposited, both the weight pressing down and the layer being formed.

There is a word in geology for what happens when material is carried by a moving medium, water or wind or ice, and deposited somewhere else when the medium slows. The word is alluvial. Alluvial material is material that has been carried and deposited. It is not where it started. It is not the medium that carried it. It is the record of a transmission: the evidence that something moved, was held, was released, came to rest in a new configuration.

The self is alluvial.

This is not a metaphor, or it is not only a metaphor. It is a description of the actual process by which selves are constituted. You are made of what was carried to you and deposited in you by the moving medium of time and relation. The language you think in was carried to you by people who are dead. The categories through which you organize experience were carried to you by philosophical and cultural traditions that stretch back further than any individual life. The specific grief you carry was deposited in you by specific losses that were themselves deposited by earlier losses, the grief of your parents and their parents, the grief of the people who stood on the ground before you stood on it, all of it alluvial, all of it carried and deposited, none of it where it started, all of it still itself in a new configuration.

The transmission model is not a longer road. It is a different geometry entirely.

On the transmission model, the past is not behind you. It is beneath you, in the sediment, pressing up through the soles of your feet. The future is not ahead of you. It is above you, in the not-yet-formed layers that will be pressed down by the weight of what you deposit. And the present is not a moving edge. It is a crossing point: the place where the vertical line of transmission intersects the horizontal spread of the living moment, the place where what has been deposited meets what is being deposited, the place where the alluvial self stands in the middle of the carrying.

There is a specific experience that the eleventh pillar is trying to name, and it is an experience that most people have had and very few people have a philosophical vocabulary for.

It happens at the moment of becoming a parent, or at the moment of losing one. It happens at the moment of standing at a grave or at a birth or at the bedside of someone who is dying. It happens sometimes in the middle of an ordinary afternoon when something, a smell or a quality of light or the weight of a silence, suddenly makes visible the line running through you from before you were born to after you will be gone. It is the experience of the rotation: the moment when the horizontal axis, the lateral spread of the present moment and its accumulations, recedes briefly, and the vertical line becomes palpable.

The philosophical vocabulary for this experience has largely been the vocabulary of the sublime: the overwhelming, the transcendent, the experience that exceeds the capacity of ordinary consciousness to process. But the sublime is the wrong category. The sublime is a response to scale, to the experience of being dwarfed by something larger than yourself. What the rotation produces is not the experience of being dwarfed. It is the experience of being located: the specific, precise, almost physical sensation of knowing where you are in the transmission, of feeling the weight of what is beneath you and the weight of what is above you, of being the crossing point.

The crossing point is not large. It is exact. It is the most precisely located thing there is: the intersection of this specific accumulation with this specific line of transmission, here, now, in this body, in this moment. The rotation does not produce awe at scale. It produces something more like recognition: the sensation of finally seeing the structure you have always been inside.

Grief is one of the most reliable routes to this recognition. The third pillar of Radical Immanence establishes that grief is permanent weather, the atmospheric condition of a world where everything you love is always already changing. The eleventh pillar adds the vertical dimension: grief is also the experience of the transmission line becoming palpable. When you lose someone who was part of your constitution, someone whose deposit is in your sediment, someone who was carrying part of what you carry, you feel the vertical line. You feel the weight that was being held by another person and is now being held by you alone. You feel the transmission.

This is why grief is not only weather. It is also a form of geological education. It teaches you, in a way that nothing else teaches you with the same precision, what you are made of and what you are carrying. It teaches you the crossing point by making the vertical line temporarily visible in a way it is not usually visible through the horizontal spread of ordinary accumulation.

The turn is not comfortable. The rotation that moves you from the horizontal axis to the vertical is the same rotation that the figure at the bottom of the Wheel of Fortune is experiencing: the stripping away of the lateral accumulation, the exposure of the vertical line, the discovery that the crossing point was always there and that the horizontal spread was always resting on it.

But the turn is not only loss. It is also expansion, of a specific kind that is easy to miss because it does not look like expansion from the horizontal axis. From the horizontal axis, the rotation looks like reduction: you lose the lateral spread, the accumulation, the wide extension of the self in its social and relational world. From the crossing point, the rotation reveals that you were always inside something larger than the lateral spread. You were always on the transmission line. You were always constituted by what was deposited before you arrived and constituting what will be deposited after you leave. The expansion is not into a larger space. It is into a deeper understanding of the space you were already in.

Here is not only here. Here is also the sediment beneath here, and the not-yet-formed ground above here, and the transmission line running through here from the ancestors to the not-yet-born, and the crossing point where all of that meets in this body, in this moment, in this specific configuration of alluvial material that is what the self actually is.

Young knew about the vertical. Young's sentences are crossing points. They are the places where the horizontal spread of the plural self meets the vertical line of transmission, where the accumulation of the present moment is intersected by the weight of what came before and the weight of what will come after. The sentences that circle back and refuse to finish are sentences that are trying to hold both axes at once, to stay in the horizontal spread of the present moment while feeling the pull of the vertical line.

The crossing point does not turn. The wheel turns around it. The discovery is not that fortune is unstable. The discovery is that the crossing point is stable. Not stable in the sense of permanent or unchanging, but stable in the sense of being the axis rather than the rim: the thing that holds while everything else rotates. The wheel is not a description of the instability of fortune. It is a description of the rotation between two axes.

Before writing, before organized religion, before the wheel and the plow and the organized political state, human beings were making a specific mark on the surfaces available to them. It appears in the cave paintings of the Upper Paleolithic. It appears in the earliest known writing systems. It appears in the Neolithic petroglyphs of every inhabited continent. It appears in the cosmological systems of cultures that had no contact with each other and no shared tradition of any kind.

It is the simplest possible mark that contains two dimensions. It is two lines crossing.

Western Christianity made the cross into a specific theological symbol, and that specificity has made it difficult for secular philosophy to think clearly about what the cross was before it was a theological symbol, and what it continues to be underneath the theology. But the cross is older than Christianity. It is older than any of the religious traditions that have claimed it. It is the mark that human beings make when they are trying to represent the structure they are inside: two axes, their intersection, the crossing point.

The cross is a symbol of the crossing point: the structure of existence that becomes visible when you stop moving along one axis long enough to feel the other. Every religious tradition that has made the cross central has been responding to this recognition, though most have translated it into the language of transcendence: the vertical arm points upward to God, to heaven, to the beyond. The eleventh pillar reads the vertical arm differently. It points downward as much as upward. It points into the sediment as much as into the sky. It is the transmission line, not the transcendence line, and the distinction illuminates the philosophical difference.

The fourth pillar of Radical Immanence establishes the witness as the central ethical stance of the system: the one who stays in the room with the contradiction and does not flinch and does not conclude. The witness maintains the quality of attention that the thing in front of them deserves, the attention that does not look away when the looking becomes painful and does not rush toward resolution when the contradiction becomes uncomfortable.

The eleventh pillar extends this into the vertical dimension.

The intergenerational witness is the one who stays in the room with the transmission and does not flinch and does not conclude. The room is larger than any single life can contain. The thing in front of the intergenerational witness is not only the present contradiction but the full vertical span of what was given and what will be required, the full weight of the sediment beneath and the not-yet-formed ground above.

What does it mean to witness the ancestors? Not to honor them in the sense of performing reverence for what they did. Not to judge them in the sense of applying present moral standards to past actions. To witness them: to read the sediment they deposited with the full attention it deserves, to not flatten what they carried into a more useful shape, to acknowledge the weight of what was given without pretending it was lighter or heavier than it was.

The honest witnessing of ancestors is one of the most politically demanding acts available. It requires acknowledging what was deposited in the sediment that the present stands on, including the deposits of violence and extraction and exclusion that the present political arrangement has been built on top of and has largely preferred not to read. The sediment is not only the deposit of wisdom and beauty and genuine human achievement. It is also the deposit of the long con: the centuries of systematic exclusion, the theft of land and labor, the construction of hierarchies that were natural in the sense of being deposited so deep in the sediment that they feel like bedrock rather than alluvium.

The intergenerational witness reads the sediment honestly. It does not require that the reading produce guilt as a permanent condition. It requires that the reading produce acknowledgment: the honest recognition that the present is built on the accumulated past, that the past is not behind us but beneath us, and that building justly requires attending to what is in the substrate rather than pretending the ground is neutral.

The hardest philosophical problem the eleventh pillar creates is also the most important one: how do you ground intergenerational obligation without transcendence?

The eleventh pillar cannot use any of these grounds. It is committed to radical immanence: the sacred without the beyond, the ethical without the transcendent anchor, the obligation that is real without being grounded in anything outside the world it operates in.

The ground the eleventh pillar offers is structural rather than moral. The obligation to future generations does not arise from a moral principle that transcends the present moment. It arises from the fact of being a crossing point: from being constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, from being a carrier of what will constitute the ground that comes after. The obligation is not chosen. It is constitutional. It is in the structure of what you are.

The crossing point is not outside the obligation. The crossing point is constituted by the transmission that generates the obligation. You cannot step outside the obligation any more than you can step outside the sediment you are standing on. The obligation is not something that applies to you from outside. It is something you are made of.

This does not mean the obligation is unlimited. The crossing point is finite. The life that stands at the crossing point is sixty, seventy, eighty or ninety years against the age of what surrounds it. The obligation is not to carry everything. It is to carry honestly: to acknowledge the weight, to not flatten it into a more useful shape, to pass it forward with the full recognition of what it is and where it came from.

The crossing point does not resolve the tension between the finite self and the infinite transmission. It holds the tension. That is what crossing points do. They hold the intersection of what cannot be reconciled into a single axis, the horizontal and the vertical, the finite and the geological, the present moment and coming generations. The obligation is to hold that intersection honestly, without pretending it is lighter than it is, without pretending the ground is neutral, without pretending you are not already inside the transmission.

Here is enough. The tenth pillar of Radical Immanence establishes this: the sacred without the beyond, the ordinary world charged with a significance that points not outward to a transcendent ground but deeper into the immanent one. Here is enough because here holds all of it, the plural self and the constructed real and the permanent grief and the witness and the recursive construction and the incompletion and the marginal and the sedimentary time and the honest language and the immanent sacred.

Here is also enormous. The eleventh pillar adds this: here is not only the lateral spread of the present moment, the horizontal accumulation of the ten pillars. Here is also the vertical line of the transmission, the crossing point where the ancestors in the sediment meet the not-yet-born in the not-yet-formed ground. Here is the intersection of everything that was given and everything that will be required. Here is the crossing point.

Here is enough. Here is also enormous. Here is the crossing point.

That is the eleventh pillar. That is what Young's sentence was always reaching toward. That is what the wheel was always turning around. That is what the cross was always marking.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"Minnows and a Monster" (1934) is the emblem. The speaker casts "delicate meshes" for minnows on a stream and catches "this enigma gleaming," which draws "the boatman under / The unfurled dark! I know not; / I sink with him in wonder." A small, located act opens onto something vast. Young read this poem as her own fate in 1989: the fisherman who "went out with a net to catch minnows and caught a whale."

Complication: the poem ends in wonder, which is close to the awe the pillar sets aside, rather than recognition.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The evidence is thin. "Awakening" (1937) has a body "Bearing the mark of many whips" that "Was changed in a single night." The nightly reading to Minna is the closest biographical case: one exact act, repeated, becoming a passage into another world.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"Slow Motion" (1941) holds the instant "with a fabulous precision." "The Funeral" (1941) gives recognition rather than awe: the farmer tethers his horse "as he had always done," "it all seemed simple, ample, and profound," and then "earth was turning on another course. / I felt its turn." "The Contravalid" names "One heartbeat separating each life and total death." "That Cloud" names the "hard jewel of consciousness," and a draft finds "a public destiny / Even in the most delicate event." Transmission appears in "Death Bed of Beauty": Beauty dies, and her sister's children are "Beauty's, her children, / Her unburied eyes." "Wild Yam Fruit" gives the located sign without its line: "Having no vine I saw, it fell like snow."

Complication: the scale is cosmic: Uranus, Saturn, Sirius, Aldebaran, and "Earth is the loneliest voyager."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The book ends on the miller's parable. No two millers make the same flour "even though they be father and son." The flour "bears the impression of the miller's thumb and the miller's soul," a difference "so slight that nobody can name it, nobody can catch hold of it. That is life." The located sign of a body and its failed passage down a line become the book's last philosophical statement.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Esther says: "I do not know the night in which I conceived as I do not know the night in which I was conceived." The most exact moment of transmission is unlocatable. Miss MacIntosh asks: "If you have seen me every day and do not know me now, how will you know me in the future?" That is recognition of what was always there. When she removes her wig, life delivers "a cold surprise."

Complication: Mr. Spitzer's single note becomes "two notes or one and its echo." Shaviro calls the book "an inverted circle whose circumference is everywhere, and whose center is nowhere."

In the novel it is present. Its strongest image waits for Young’s last book.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The flour miller is "the thing I never could write," "the idea of identity and passage of the soul." The violinist plays one true note after twenty years: "you hit reality once and die." To Terkel: "you frighten me by being so absolutely right." Her method was exact: one small street error in all of Boston, two weeks on a sentence. In 1989: art "exists not in objective time alone but in the subjectivity of time," and she was "still in the process of awakening."

Complication: she wanted "a universal or cosmic statement," a book "endlessly expanding like a universe."

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Dostoyevsky kneels hooded in the snow, thinking "I might perhaps have five minutes more to live," at "the evermoving boundary line between sleeping and dreaming." Young ties the moment to Debs "recording the deaths." Transmission works here, unlike with the miller's son: the dream "never really dies as some other dreamer must take over the dream." Debs learns French poetry from his father at three, and his names come from Sue and Hugo.

Chapter Nine: Language Shapes What’s Possible

← Chapter Eight: The Past Doesn’t Go Away · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Ten: The Sacred Is Here →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The ninth pillar addresses the medium through which all of the other pillars are expressed and contested.

If the self is plural, if reality is constructed, if knowledge is situated, if community is held through difference, if time is sedimentary, then language is not the neutral medium through which these truths are communicated. It is the medium in which they are constructed, contested, and either honored or betrayed. The ninth pillar: language is not the vehicle of truth but the medium of its construction, and must be held accordingly.

Gertrude Stein's investigation of language, conducted across her poetry, her prose experiments, and her theoretical essays, is an investigation of the relationship between grammatical structure and the structure of experience. Stein understood that the grammar of a language is not a neutral tool for expressing pre-existing thoughts. It is a set of commitments about what kinds of things exist, how they relate to each other, and what counts as a complete thought. The noun, in standard English grammar, is the primary unit of existence. Things are nouns. People are nouns. The verb is what happens to or between nouns. This grammatical structure encodes a metaphysical commitment: the world is made of stable things that persist through time, and change and action are secondary to the stable things that undergo them.

Stein's experiments with grammar are experiments in building a language that can hold a different metaphysical commitment: the commitment to a world made of processes rather than things, of becoming rather than being, of the verb rather than the noun. Young inherits this project and extends it. The long sentences of "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling", the sentences that circle back and refuse to finish and accumulate subordinate clauses like geological layers, are sentences that resist the grammatical commitment to stable nouns and clean predications. They are sentences built for a world where the self is a verb and reality is a construction and grief is permanent weather rather than a temporary condition.

Young found the principle early and kept refining it. In her graduate essay on Coventry Patmore she observed that in his world “even the nouns act like verbs.” Her drafts of the 1940s name “the error of language” that “conceives / The whole as whole hypostasizing.” Late in life she said it in three words: “Style is thinking.” The short sentence catches “maybe a tenth of what you think,” and the long sentence is a dragnet for thoughts that, in James’s phrase, we never catch “on the wing.”

The language through which political life is conducted is not a neutral medium. It is a set of commitments about who exists, what counts as a person, what kinds of experience are real and what kinds are marginal. The people whose existence is not captured by the stable nouns of political grammar are not simply underrepresented. They are grammatically erased. The plural self cannot be a noun in the grammar of liberal political theory, which requires the unified rational agent as its primary unit. The person whose identity is multiple, whose interests are not unified, whose experience crosses the categories that the grammar of political discourse has built, is not a person that the grammar can process.

Young's language, with its resistance to the stable noun and its commitment to the ongoing process, is a political act in this sense. It is the construction of a grammar that can hold the plural self, that can give voice to the experience that standard political grammar erases, that can make visible the people who are invisible to the language of the long con.

Adrienne Rich's essay "Notes Toward a Politics of Location" brings the ninth pillar into direct conversation with feminist practice. Rich argues that political speech is always located, always spoken from a particular body in a particular place with a particular history, and that the pretense of speaking from nowhere is not a form of universality but a form of domination. The voice that claims to speak for everyone is always the voice of someone in particular. Rich's politics of location requires that speakers name their location, acknowledge the partiality of their perspective, and build their political speech from the honest acknowledgment of where they are standing rather than from the pretense of standing nowhere.

This is the ninth pillar's political expression. Language that names its own location is language that can be held accountable. Language that pretends to speak from nowhere is language that cannot be questioned, because there is no particular location to question. Young said the same in her own terms. “It was my fate to be born in Indiana,” she said, and she told her students to “start where you are.”

The political half of this pillar arrived late. It first appears in Young’s own pages in "Angel in the Forest", where the opponents of a common good “substitute words for things.” In the novel it becomes Miss MacIntosh’s “jargon of old saws” set against a counter-language of touch, and in "Harp Song for a Radical" it becomes the politics of naming, as when the word “red” calls up “the red man who had been slaughtered.” This also records a tension with this chapter’s reading of Rich: Young sometimes called herself “a mirror” and “neither a woman or a man,” which comes close to the voice from nowhere.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

Language is the farmer's way out in "The Seeker," since grammar is what the farm took from him and what he tries to win back alone. "Song of Two" lets spoken words "Dip softly, softly through my days." The song is something "welded together." There is no theory yet.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

The Patmore essay supplies the most striking match in the whole record: in Patmore's world "even the nouns act like verbs." The poems weigh language's power and its limits. "Experience in Song": "But pollen of a syllable / Receives celestial ground." In "Anthology Piece," a girl's "moon-struck syllables" "Draw as the moon the angry waters," though "None will ever speak her name." "Elegy for the Body" asks "What metaphor / Of bird or flower / Can make her heart / To beat again," and answers that "imageless / Is quietness."

Complication: the politics of language is absent.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

The drafts state the critique of nouns: "the error of language conceives / The whole as whole hypostasizing." "That Apple Was Mental" names "A noun which has no corresponding entity in space." In "That Cloud," "the personal pronoun attains a status in infinity," and April "has its being only in a name." "Who is limited?" places the limit in definition itself: our hearts denied our contiguity with the universe, "having defined / Limitations." Against nouns stand process: "all things are process," and "Ourselves that process." "Speculative Evening" uses James's own term, "specious present."

Complication: the politics are present only through logic. Logicians omit spinsters, a definition is "but a thistle stalk," and "all their words were adjusted long ago" in "At the Cinema."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

The political side of the pillar appears for the first time in Young's own pages. The 1940 philosopher says the opponents of a common good "substitute words for things. They purchase space in newspapers." The Rappites' "exclusive use of the German language" is "another barrier between themselves and their neighbors." Owen wants "a Bible of his own, in plain, simple language, without mystery, wigs, or parrots," and offers Mrs. Malaprop as proof that minds are written on.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

Vera's childhood is drilled in "hackneyed proverbs and moral aphorisms," a "jargon of old saws," the inherited grammar of good sense. Young said of Miss MacIntosh, "it's just her verbalism that makes her seem sensible." The ending offers a counter-language. Vera spells her name on her lover's hand, and he answers, "There be words of ours... not in the alphabet of the stars. Flowers spell them out on the earth, and grasses talk." Esther's misspelled sign still says what it needs to.

What the novel adds is inherited language as a character’s whole mind, and a counter-language set against it. "Angel in the Forest" named the politics of words. The novel shows a child raised inside a grammar of good sense and an ending that speaks in touch, flowers, and misspelling.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

"Style is thinking." The short sentence catches "maybe a tenth of what you think." The long dragnet sentence tries to catch thoughts that, in James's words, we never catch "on the wing." In 1989 she described it as including "without undue censorship." In Woolf she finds "a journey, but there is hardly a journeyer." "The World of Silence" asks how a man with no language can describe "his guilt complex if he has not even one small word," notes that sign language exists "all in the present tense," and suspects that for the deaf "time may be an illusion, a human construct." "It was my fate to be born in Indiana," and students should "start where you are."

Complication: she called herself "neither a woman or a man," wrote in "Feminine Sensibility" that sexual differences "dissolve, bearing no relation to art," and called herself "a mirror," close to a voice from nowhere. Only late did she name "a rage against women" in her reviewers. Also in an interview Young said she wanted to be a detective or a journalist but she realized the opportunities for women were limited at the time.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 9: Language Shapes What’s Possible

Debs speaks in "the time-worn, often antique coins of speech" to reach "all the orphans in this orphaned world." Marx might have fared better in America "if it had not been called dialectical materialism," or if the "most unread red book in America had not been called red," since the word called up "the red man who had been slaughtered." Weitling's universal language is a "Simple Simon language" that "never did get off its feet." Young told Ruas that these Americans "all spoke in metaphors."
