Bibliography

← Conclusion · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Primary Texts

Young, Marguerite. Prismatic Ground. 1937. Her first book of poems; the evidence for Phase Two.

Young, Marguerite. Moderate Fable. 1944. Poems, dedicated to the memory of Minna Weissenbach; the evidence for Phase Three.

Young, Marguerite. "Angel in the Forest". 1945. A history of the Rappite and Owenite utopias at New Harmony, Indiana; the evidence for Phase Four.

Young, Marguerite. "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling". New York: Scribner’s, 1965. 1,198 pp. Read throughout Part One as the fullest form of the philosophy, and in Part Two as its fifth phase. The novel’s formal properties, including sentence length, recursive structure, and refusal of linear resolution, are treated as philosophical arguments in their own right.

Young, Marguerite. "Inviting the Muses". 1994. Essays, stories, and reviews, mostly undated; evidence for Phase Six.

Young, Marguerite. "Harp Song for a Radical". 1999. The unfinished Debs history, prepared by Charles Ruas after her death; the evidence for Phase Seven.

Young, Marguerite. "The Collected Poems", with Young’s introduction of 1989 and an appendix of unpublished drafts; evidence for Phases One through Three.

Critical and Biographical Sources

Critics, biographers, and interviewers: Steven Shaviro, Petrolle, Fuchs, Strehle, Oboler, Duncan, Friederich, Moore, Dowling, Studs Terkel, Susan Neville, LaVerne Harrell Clark, and Charles Ruas.

Secondary Philosophical and Theoretical Sources

Arendt, Hannah. The Human Condition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1958.

Cited in relation to the seventh pillar, the ontology of the marginal, and the concept of the space of appearance as the political space in which plural beings appear to each other in their difference rather than their sameness. Also cited in the map of philosophical conversations convened by the ten pillars, under both the plural self and the witness.

Arendt, Hannah. The Origins of Totalitarianism. New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1951.

Cited alongside The Human Condition in the discussion of the seventh pillar. Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism as the destruction of plurality, rather than primarily the use of violence, is applied to Young's treatment of the demand for the "real" Miss MacIntosh beneath the wig as a totalitarian demand in Arendt's sense.

Mikhail Bakhtin

Bakhtin, Mikhail. The Dialogic Imagination: Four Essays. Translated by Caryl Emerson and Michael Holquist. Austin: University of Texas Press, 1981.

Cited in the discussion of the seventh pillar for the theory of the dialogic, in which meaning is produced in the encounter between voices rather than by a single voice speaking a single truth. The text extends Bakhtin's principle to argue that the voices in "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" by Marguerite Young are not only the voices of different characters but the voices of different selves within Vera herself. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under the ontology of the marginal.

Walter Benjamin

Benjamin, Walter. The Arcades Project. Translated by Howard Eiland and Kevin McLaughlin. Cambridge: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 1999.

Cited in the discussion of the sixth pillar, the ethics of incompletion, as a supreme example of the unfinished work whose incompleteness is not incidental but integral to its argument. The Arcades Project's fragmentary form is presented as enacting the same principle Young's system names: that the honest engagement with a world that does not resolve produces work that does not resolve.

Benjamin, Walter. "Theses on the Philosophy of History." In Illuminations: Essays and Reflections, edited by Hannah Arendt, translated by Harry Zohn. New York: Schocken Books, 1968.

Cited extensively in the discussion of the eighth pillar, sedimentary time, for the image of the angel of history facing the accumulated wreckage of the past while being blown forward into the future by the storm of progress. Benjamin's critique of the progressive view of history is directly connected to Young's permanent grief extended to the scale of history. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under both grief as permanent weather and sedimentary time.

René Descartes

Descartes, René. Meditations on First Philosophy. 1641.

Cited as a representative of the philosophical tradition Young refuses, specifically the tradition that protects the assumption of the unified self. The evil demon thought experiment is referenced in the discussion of the second pillar, illusion as primary, as the nightmare that Young reframes: not the demon but the dream of escaping the demon.

Michel Foucault

Foucault, Michel. The Order of Things: An Archaeology of the Human Sciences. English translation. New York: Pantheon Books, 1970. (Originally published in French as Les Mots et les choses, 1966.)

Cited in the discussion of why the tradition missed Young, as part of the poststructuralist conversation that would have been most equipped to receive her work but arrived in American intellectual culture too late to create a context for "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" by Marguerite Young.

Jacques Derrida

Derrida, Jacques. Of Grammatology. Translated by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1976. (Originally published in French, 1967.)

Cited alongside Foucault in the discussion of timing and the tradition's failure to receive Young. The poststructuralist dismantling of the unified subject and the critique of presence are identified as the philosophical conversation that would have known what to do with her work.

David Hume

Hume, David. A Treatise of Human Nature. 1739-1740.

Cited in the discussion of the first pillar, the plural self, for Hume's famous introspective discovery that he could never catch himself without a perception, finding the bundle of experiences with no experiencer underneath. The text notes that Hume retreated from the full implications of this discovery, while Young does not.

William James

James, William. Works on the stream of consciousness and the self as process, including The Principles of Psychology. New York: Henry Holt, 1890.

Cited in the discussion of the first pillar for James's naming of the stream of consciousness and his understanding that the self was a process rather than a thing. The text argues that Young takes James more seriously than most of the tradition did, extending the stream until it becomes clear that it does not flow in one direction. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under the plural self.

Immanuel Kant

Kant, Immanuel. Critique of Pure Reason. 1781.

Cited as a representative of the philosophical tradition that protects the assumption of the unified self, specifically through the transcendental subject, the organizing "I" that makes experience possible by being prior to it.

Robin Wall Kimmerer

Kimmerer, Robin Wall. Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants. Minneapolis: Milkweed Editions, 2013.

Cited in the discussion of the tenth pillar, immanent transcendence, for the insistence that the world is not a collection of objects but a community of subjects, and that attention to the non-human is not sentiment but epistemology. Kimmerer's work is connected to Young's practice of giving the Indiana landscape the same density and interiority as her human characters. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under immanent transcendence.

Plato

Plato. The Republic. c. 375 BCE.

Cited as the origin story of the Western philosophical tradition's foundational opposition between the real and the illusory, specifically the allegory of the cave. Young's second pillar is presented as a direct answer to Plato: there is no sunlit world outside the cave, only a larger cave more elaborately lit.

Adrienne Rich

Rich, Adrienne. "Notes Toward a Politics of Location." In Blood, Bread, and Poetry: Selected Prose 1979-1985. New York: Norton, 1986.

Cited in the discussion of the ninth pillar, language as construction, for the argument that political speech is always located, always spoken from a particular body in a particular place with a particular history, and that the pretense of speaking from nowhere is a form of domination rather than universality. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under language as construction.

Gertrude Stein

Stein, Gertrude. Works including poetry, prose experiments, and theoretical essays. Key texts include Tender Buttons (1914), The Making of Americans (1925), and Lectures in America (1935).

Cited in the discussion of the first pillar as the thinker Young is most directly in dialogue with, identified as William James's student. Stein's investigation of repetition, the continuous present, and identity as something that happens rather than something that is, is described as running parallel to Young's project with different formal tools. Where Stein strips language down to show the self as a grammatical construction, Young piles language up until the construction becomes visible through its own excess. Cited again in the discussion of the ninth pillar for the investigation of the relationship between grammatical structure and the structure of experience, and in the map of philosophical conversations under both the plural self and language as construction.

Simone Weil

Weil, Simone. Works on attention and ethics, including Waiting for God. Translated by Emma Craufurd. New York: Putnam, 1951, and "Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God." In Waiting for God.

Cited in the discussion of the fourth pillar, the witness, for the ethics of attention: the argument that the foundation of ethics is not duty or utility or virtue but attention, the capacity to truly see the person in front of you without the distortions of projection or self-interest. Weil's attention is described as an act of love understood as a practice rather than a feeling. Young's witnessing is described as Weil's attention made systemic. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under the witness.

Alfred North Whitehead

Whitehead, Alfred North. Process and Reality: An Essay in Cosmology. New York: Macmillan, 1929.

Cited in the discussion of the fifth pillar, recursive construction, as the most rigorous available philosophical framework for the world Young's fiction describes. Whitehead's central claim that reality is composed of processes rather than things, that the fundamental units of existence are events and occasions of experience rather than stable objects, is presented as Young's plural self in the language of metaphysics. The self in Whitehead is described as a process that is its experiences, the verb rather than the noun. Cited again in the map of philosophical conversations under both recursive construction and immanent transcendence, in relation to process theology.

Note on Missing Publication Details

Several sources are referenced in the text in ways that identify the thinker and argument but do not specify individual titles, including the traditions of indigenous philosophy, coalition politics, and process theology, as well as the constitutional tradition of democratic revision and the feminist tradition of ongoing political construction. These are cited as traditions rather than individual texts, reflecting the text's approach of situating Young within broad intellectual communities rather than limiting her to specific academic conversations.
writing-life-03-chapter-two-reality-is-c:
Chapter Two: Reality Is Constructed

← Chapter One: Not One Self · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Three: Grief Doesn’t End →

Pillar: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

The second pillar is the one most likely to be misunderstood, so it is worth unpacking. Young does not argue that illusion is preferable to reality, that we should choose fantasy over fact, or that the interior life is more valuable than the exterior world. She argues something more fundamental and more disturbing: that the distinction itself is false. That illusion is not the opposite of reality but its medium. That human beings do not live in the world and then sometimes retreat into illusion. They live in illusion the way fish live in water, and what we call reality is one particular illusion that has achieved consensus.

Western thought has organized itself around the real and the illusory as a foundational opposition. Plato's cave is the origin story: the shadows on the wall are an illusion, the sunlit world outside is reality, and the philosopher's task is to drag people from the former toward the latter. Young answers this differently. The evil demon is not the nightmare. The dream of escaping the demon is the nightmare, because the escape route leads nowhere. There is no sunlit world outside the cave. There is only a larger cave, more elaborately lit, whose inhabitants have agreed to call their shadows real.

Young accomplishes this by giving illusions the same novelistic density she gives everything else, the same accumulation of specific detail, the same insistence that this place is real because a self is genuinely living in it.

In Chicago in the mid 1930s, Young spent about two years reading aloud, night after night, to Minna Weissenbach as the woman passed into opium dreams. As Dowling tells it, Young came to see herself as providing “the verbal passport” to another world. She dedicated Moderate Fable to Minna’s memory, and she later said that her poem “Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne,” with its brain kept in fluid and furnished with a false world, “contains the future opium lady.” The density Young gives the world is the density of a world she once sat beside and listened to.

The philosophical point is not that this way is right and that way is wrong. It is that the framework that would let us adjudicate between them, the framework that sorts experience into real and illusory, is itself an illusion. The solid world is sustained by the same mechanism as the opium world: a self that has organized its experience around a set of commitments and called those commitments reality. The solid world was always a performance of solidity.

The self does not receive reality passively. It constructs reality actively, from the materials available to it, shaped by desire and grief and history and the particular plurality it contains. What we call consensus reality is the construction that enough selves have agreed on to treat as given. It is not less constructed for being agreed upon. It is just more crowded.

Young had put the claim in one sentence long before the novel. In a graduate essay on Edward Young’s Night Thoughts she wrote that “Sanity may consist only in sharing the hallucinations of our neighbors.” In “Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne” (1944) the claim becomes verse: “there is no substratum of dead fact,” and “We eat and drink ideas, we are clothed with them / As water clothes the waterfall.”

If illusion is primary, if the real is always already a construction, then the question of who gets to construct it is a political question of the first order. Every dominant political system depends on the naturalization of its own construction: the idea that the way things are is the way things are, not the way things have been arranged by people with interests in keeping them arranged that way. Young's insistence that all reality is constructed does not produce the conclusion that all constructions are equal. It produces the opposite conclusion: that the question of which constructions dominate, and at whose expense, is the central political question, and that the first act of political resistance is the refusal to mistake the dominant construction for nature.

Young drew this conclusion herself. Understanding illusion, she said, keeps a person from “blindly following a leader.” A year after the war, in “Complex Life and Complex Letters,” she attacked critics who praised the dull as “good, old American,” and observed that “Goering and Goebbels were sensible.” Common sense as a faith lived by, had shown what it could be made to serve.

Young's formal choices in her writing are themselves an argument about illusion. Young refuses the formal signals that literary fiction conventionally uses to mark the boundary between interior and exterior, between dream and waking, between illusion and reality. This is not a stylistic quirk. It is a philosophical position expressed through craft. The form would be saying what the argument denies if it treated one character’s world as thinner than the another character. Young is too rigorous for that inconsistency.

The result is a reading experience that is genuinely disorienting and genuinely clarifying by the time you understand what Young is doing. The disorientation is not a failure of communication. It is the communication. You are being asked to experience the collapse of the real and the illusory, not to be told about it.

That is the second pillar. Reality is not what we thought it was. It is not less real for that. It is more real, because what we thought it was was always already a simplification, and the world Young is pointing toward is the actual one: plural, constructed, contested, and alive in ways that the simplified version never was.

It begins gently, in early poems where a farmer keeps his world alive on a teacher’s old postcards and the construction is allowed to stand as what keeps him going. It becomes epistemology in the graduate essays and the Berkeley poem, turns social and political in "Angel in the Forest", where Father Rapp is a “manufacturer of whisky and illusion,” and ends as the economic illusion of capitalism in "Harp Song for a Radical". Throughout, Young held that experience, dream included, is real, and she was a stubborn realist about facts: “I don’t make up anything.” The construction she attacks is the common-sense world, not experience itself.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

The pillar is present only lightly, and in a tender form. "The Seeker" (1928) is about a farmer who keeps a whole world alive through a teacher's old postcards and a son in Paris whose letters "have been lost somewhere at sea." The world he lives in is held together by the story he tells, and the poem does not expose him. It lets the construction stand as what keeps him going. "Street Fires" (1927) gives the first image of common sense against beauty. The old women of Hawthorne Lane sweep their lawns until "Not one gleam on their lawns they keep," and "That Beauty may die, they light their fires." The "Sonnet" (1928) honors a woman who bought "Thin painted china when she needed bread" while others "laughed at loving this so old." In both poems a shared sense of what is proper is set against a private sense of what matters. That is the seed of Miss MacIntosh's "Common sense is the finest sense."

Complication: no argument is made yet, and the constructions shown are mostly kindly.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

The Night Thoughts essay gives the pillar in one sentence: "Sanity may consist only in sharing the hallucinations of our neighbors." The Patmore essay places Patmore between idealism and realism, draws on James's "wild data" and Arthur Lovejoy's question of where the image of a distant star is located, and concludes that "the wild data continue to behave in a wild manner."

The poems keep testing the ground. The sleepwalker of "Dubious Ground" is "always aware / Of the dubious texture of the ground." "Drowning Song" instructs: "Be lucid of that element... For thus you turn from fact to dream." The cow of "Country Scene" meditates "above the illusion of grass, / In implausible meadows." "The Dark Wood" makes the same wood two worlds. At night Ellen is trapped by watching frogs. At dawn, "Limpid with bird song," it is "The innocent wood."

The question of who benefits appears for the first time in "Paradise Is Still Lost." Heaven is a police order run by "God the great G-man," whose stool pigeon is a tuberculous boy: "They will get him yet."

Complication: the Patmore essay's "wild data" already points to Young's later position. Reality is not only agreement. It is wilder and larger than any agreed version.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

"Bishop Berkeley of Cloyne" (1944) is the center: "The outer realm of fact was always false," "there is no substratum of dead fact," and "We eat and drink ideas, we are clothed with them / As water clothes the waterfall." The poem also imagines a brain kept in fluid and furnished with a false world. Young later said it "contains the future opium lady" of the novel. "A High Subjectivity" says "The idea of the universe is inconclusive." "The Responsibility of Parentage" takes a Jamesian, practical turn: "the unreality of experience makes no ascertainable / difference / To the strings of the harp." In "Winter Scene" (1942) earth is "celebrant for the failure of a theory." "Proem to Reality" (1945): "There is no reference but to shifting fixity," and "There is no whole."

The political edge sharpens with the war, from the state's execution room in "The Clinic" (1941) to "Didactic Poem Against War," which says "this century has willed / Men like walrus herds shall all be killed," and "our own nature has willed this most sorrowful theory." A draft calls matter "that courtesan," and says "Elevation... is not salvation."

Complication: the argument is never allowed to win. Berkeley asks, "Yet how will away the absent hills?" "Null Class" demands, "Who shall prove the farmer in the field / And that lean horse whose ear twitches." The unpublished "Wild Yam Fruit" is a plain poem of things seen: hulls, persimmons, oak leaves.

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

Rapp is a "manufacturer of whisky and illusion." The New Harmony of 1940 is "nothing certain, but illusion in every facet." Owen's creed is that people are "the creatures of circumstance." In Young's account Rapp keeps order by seeming to see everything, "as many eyes as the eyes in the feathers of a peacock's tail," and "As vice-regent of the Deity, Father Rapp left nothing to the Deity." The keeper of the shared fiction is the one who benefits from it.

"Complex Life and Complex Letters" (1946) carries this into culture. It attacks critics who praise the dull as "good, old American," and notes that "Goering and Goebbels were sensible." A year after the war, common sense is named as a political danger.

Complication: illusions have material results: the whisky sold, the graves dug, the Ozark dead "who had perished on the asphalt road." The Owenites, "by omitting all which did not come within the domain of reason," found "they had omitted reason itself." The construction is real in its effects.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

Petrolle reads the book as a contrast. Catherine knowingly makes her own fictions, while Miss MacIntosh accepts the culture's ready-made ones, down to her belief that her baldness is ugly. Oboler finds culture as the "organization of illusion, of memory," and common sense as the deepest American illusion. Miss MacIntosh is the keeper of that sense: "Common sense is the finest sense." When Vera sees her bald, she cries out the pillar herself: "Nothing that you think is happening is happening! Nothing that you think is true is true. Nothing that you see is real!" Petrolle cites Mr. Spitzer: "Nothing lived except through imagination."

Complication: some shared constructions are kind. The stone-deaf man says they will marry "for legality helped," and the book treats this tenderly. Shaviro's reading holds that "even the unreal things were real," which keeps Young's realism about experience.

Part One sets Catherine’s world against Miss MacIntosh’s (Chapter Two). What the novel adds is a keeper of the shared fiction who is loved. In the graduate essays and the Berkeley poem the pillar was a question of knowledge, and in "Angel in the Forest" the keeper was Father Rapp, a figure of power. Here the keeper of common sense is the person Vera loves most, so the collapse of the solid world arrives as grief as well as discovery.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

She told Clark there is no reality except, realistically, its unreality, and told Neville that "everything is fiction," even God. She said that understanding illusion keeps a person from "blindly following a leader." "Horse Utopia" reports a rancher's paradise that restores men's "ancient dignities" and ends on a ducking stool for rebellious women.

Complication: she was a stubborn realist about facts: "I don't make up anything. I always know if it didn't happen." She checked her inventions against a psychiatrist, a hairdresser, and medical literature.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 2: Reality Is Constructed

The pillar becomes economic. Marx sees a society "based upon the appearances of the ghosts of illusion as if they were real," and hopes for "the death of the illusion of capitalism." Capitalism is "an institution as sacred as if it had been handed down by God to man." A reservation is "a land of promise of which the promises were all illusion even as were the promissory notes." The czar's mock execution of Dostoyevsky is a "theatrical pseudo-masterpiece": power writes better fictions than the utopians. Ruas records Young's definition of maturity: "When you have examined all the illusions of life, and know that there isn't any reality, but you nevertheless go on, then you are a mature human being."

This answers the question that runs from "Paradise Is Still Lost" through "Complex Life and Complex Letters": the owners of rails, mines, and land, and the state that stages their fictions, benefit from the shared construction.

writing-life-02-chapter-one-not-one-self:
Chapter One: Not One Self

← Introduction · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Two: Reality Is Constructed →

Pillar: Pillar 1 Not One Self · Across every book

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The first thing Young asks you to give up is the one you are most attached to. Not your beliefs, not your certainties, not even your story about where you came from and what it made you. She asks you to give up the assumption underneath all of those: that there is a you doing the believing, the knowing, the remembering. A stable center that receives experience and integrates it into something coherent and continuous. A self that, whatever it has been through, remains fundamentally itself.

This is the assumption philosophy has protected most ferociously. It is the assumption Descartes was protecting when he stripped everything else away and found the thinking thing that could not be doubted. It is the assumption Kant was protecting when he built the transcendental subject, the organizing "I" that makes experience possible by being prior to it. It is the assumption that runs underneath liberal political theory, psychoanalysis, developmental psychology, and most of what passes for common sense about human identity. You are someone. That someone persists. That persistence is what makes you responsible for your actions, capable of relationship, legible to others and to yourself.

Young does not argue against this assumption.

She does something more unsettling.

In "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" she builds a world in which you can watch it fail.

Young’s central claim is there is no truth underneath. Young is showing that plurality is not a symptom. It is the condition. It is the structure. Young shows another reality, sustained by a self that is genuinely living in it, and the self that lives in it is as real as any other self.

This is the philosophical move. Not the claim that all realities are equal in some lazy relativist sense. The claim that the self is not the kind of thing that lives in one reality. The self is the kind of thing that lives in several realities simultaneously, navigating between them with varying degrees of awareness and control. The demand that it choose one and call that one the true self is a demand that amputates most of what the self actually is.

Characters are performing and Young does not present this as a tragedy, though it contains tragedy. She presents it as information. This is what selves are. This is what you are working with. Now what?

Hume got closer than most to understanding this. Hume looked for the unified self in his own experience and found, famously, that he could never catch himself without a perception. He found the bundle, the stream of experiences with no experiencer underneath, and it troubled him enough that he retreated from the full implications. Young does not retreat. She built an investigation of what the bundle actually looks like from the inside, which is something a philosophical treatise cannot do because it cannot sustain the investigation long enough or in the right form.

William James named the stream of consciousness and understood that the self was a process rather than a thing, that the "I" was always already in motion rather than stable behind its experiences. Young takes James seriously in a way that most of the tradition did not, extending the stream until it becomes clear that it does not flow in one direction, does not empty into a single sea. It branches and doubles back and runs underground and surfaces somewhere unexpected and is still, somehow, the water.

The debt to James is a matter of record, not only of affinity. In her graduate years Young studied his Psychology “as if it were a Bible,” and decades later she still told her students to read it as a writer’s central text. She took from him the many selves living “under one roof or dome or hat” and “the person you did not become.” By 1935 a poem of hers could say of a woman, “Oh, she was plural; / She multiplied,” and a poem of the war years could say that “within my skull the you becometh I.” Her writing did not discover the plural self. My MacIntosh, My Darling gave a position she had been writing toward for twenty years, a world large enough to hold it.

The thinker Young is most in dialogue with is Gertrude Stein, who was William James's student and whose investigation of repetition, of the continuous present, of identity as something that happens rather than something that is, runs parallel to Young's project with different formal tools. Where Stein strips language down to its mechanisms to show the self as a grammatical construction, Young piles language up until the construction becomes visible through its own excess. Different directions, the same destination: the self is not a noun. It is a verb.

The plural self is not the absent self. It is the self that is more than any single account of it can capture. It does not mean that accountability dissolves. It produces a more complicated picture of what it means to be responsible for actions taken by a self that is not singular and not fully transparent to itself. The plural self can be witnessed. It cannot be reduced.

The demand for singular selfhood is not just a philosophical error. It is a political technology. Every system that requires enemies requires a population of selves simple enough to be sorted: us and them, citizen and alien, deserving and undeserving. The more complex the actual population, the more pressure the system applies to force simplification. The people most damaged by this demand are the people whose plurality is most visible and most threatening to the sorting system. Young's plural self is not a therapy for that violence. It is a philosophical framework that names the mechanism producing it.

This is the first pillar. Everything else the system builds is built on this: the self is plural, the plurality is the condition, and the honest life is the one that stops trying to put it back together.

"Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" is where this pillar stands at full height, but it is not where it began. Young was writing toward the plural self long before Vera boarded the Grey Goose bus. It shows up first as feeling, in a family story that made the child a vessel for her dead cousin Harry and in the dropped mirror of “Transition” (1930), where “all things multiply.” It takes on method when she reads William James in Chicago, and it is argued outright in the poems of the war years. In her interviews she sometimes speaks of the self in terms the novel would not allow, saying in 1965 that she “became more myself all the time.”

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

The plural self starts in Young's own origin, a child believed to carry a dead boy's life. "Transition" (1930) gives it its first image. A dropped mirror breaks, "all things multiply," one bluebird becomes a thousand, and the speaker is "lost forever now." "Biography" (1932) is about "young Harry playing chess / With Lucifer," a boy losing everything because his mind is on everything "but not the game." Whether Young meant the name to recall her cousin, the poem does not say. "Eclipse" makes the soul kin to an animal: "The lizard and my spotted soul / Kept their counsel well, / Remembering the sun."

The complication is just as old. "Little Fawn," undated and dictated late, so that its place in this phase is a guess, keeps asking "Can't you stay by yourself, little fawn?" because the mother's "tracks are lost in the snow." The lesson is "Better learn now to stay by yourself." From the beginning, the merged self (Harry, the mirror) sits beside the lonely self that must learn to stand alone. That is the same pairing as the novel's "the individual is the one illusion" and its narrator who has "walked alone."

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

James supplies the theory: the many selves "under one roof or dome or hat," and "the person you did not become." The poems supply the images. "Elegy for the Body" (1935): "Oh, she was plural; / She multiplied; / All sparrows fell / If once she died." In "Like Secret Roots" (1935) the beloved enters the speaker's mind until "I must be both sky and field." In "Whorl," "No one can tell which is the tree / Of bloom reflected, which is she." "Wild Orchard" turns a man into a tree: "Man, the errant vegetable," with "Slow rain not blood" in his veins.

Complication: "Heart Who Stays" (1935) keeps something fixed: "the Head remembers the Heart who stays, / Remembers the Heart, who cannot go." A core remains, which anticipates the steady self Young claimed in 1965.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

"That Cloud" states the pillar as an argument: "Difference of persons but a specious truth / When within my skull the you becometh I," and "in this confusion is our only existence possible." "Ventriloquist: The Coffee Hour" (1940) nests voice inside voice: "I am the tree, and he is the tree's shade," and the ventriloquist is himself "a wooden boy against the imponderable / Knee of what unseen man." In "Snow in the Mountains" (1941) the lovers are "twin souls / Of real and unreal, both real and our shadow face."

Complication: the war years make division frightening. "That Apple Was Mental" calls it "not ego but terror, ourselves dispersed." "Of Deed, Love, Death" (1945) imagines the soul splitting "like an annalid," and ends: "True terror is each soul to seem / The shrivelled body hanging from a floating tree." Separateness also returns. A draft prefers this earth to a counter-earth where "would I / Be but a repetition of a more perfect self." "Address to the Birds" knows that "between us the gulf forever roars." The giraffe lives as "only one, among the buds of stars."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

The Rappite angel is built from mixed parts: "the breast of woman, the head and feet of man," "grass and fire and homely as an old shoe." Rappite doctrine holds that "Adam, before he fell, was possessed of both sexual elements." The plural self becomes theology.

Complication: the book ends on the miller's irreducible difference. The flour bears "the impression of the miller's thumb and the miller's soul," and "There will always be as many flours as there are millers." The difference is "so slight that nobody can name it." Owen gives a third view, that men are "all cut off the same bolt" and the mind is "a blank page." The book sets sameness, difference, and mixture side by side without choosing.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

The novel opens with the pillar as doctrine: "Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. Every face is the other face. The individual is the one illusion." Mr. Spitzer cannot tell himself from his twin, and Young saw them as "the two parts of the same man," a "duality which might be in all of us." Miss MacIntosh is "a bald prince, disguised," "neither male nor female." Vera projects herself into each stranger until "she is all of them." Catherine Cartwheel's first person dissolves into the divan, the mirror, and Brooklyn Bridge. The ending merges Vera with Esther: "Esther Longtree would be me." Fuchs reads the book as a critique of fiction that "fetishizes" a single self.

Complication: the opening treats unity as a question asked of "some omniscient eye," while the narrator has "walked alone." The oneness is believed in, not felt.

Against the earlier work, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" adds two things. The plural self becomes doctrine spoken on the first page rather than an image in a lyric, and it becomes something the narrator undergoes. The poems argued that “the you becometh I.” In the novel Vera becomes each stranger she meets, and the book closes on her merger with Esther.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

Young called herself "a pluralistic person" who preferred "the many as opposed to the one." In the story "The Dead Women" the narrator feels like "two women, herself and someone else." Her changing accounts of her own origins enact the pillar.

Complication: this is where the pillar is most directly qualified. In 1965 she said she "became more myself all the time," and that "we don't change any more than we change the color of our eyes about the deepest things of our lives." She called herself "doomed to be a writer" and said she "never altered" her style. The steady core is her own claim.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 1: Not One Self

The doubles return as history. Hope and despair are "two of the most famous twins of the nineteenth century." Theodore Debs is "almost his other self." Heine and Börne should be "a two-headed subject followed not by a plural but a singular verb." Lincoln is "many-sided," with "a sense of the many and not the one truth," against Wendell Phillips, "a nonrelativistic worshiper of the absolute."

Complication: great-man history keeps the single heroic figure at the center. The book resolves this through the dream, which "transcends the individual."
writing-life-09-chapter-eight-the-past-d:
Chapter Eight: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

← Chapter Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Nine: Language Shapes What’s Possible →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh

The eighth pillar addresses the relationship between the past and the present, between what has been lost and what continues to carry it.

The third pillar establishes that grief is permanent weather, that the losses built into the foundation of individual and collective life do not resolve. The eighth pillar extends this into a full account of time: time is not linear but sedimentary. The past does not recede. It accumulates.

Walter Benjamin's "Theses on the Philosophy of History," written in 1940 shortly before his death, offers the most compressed and powerful account of sedimentary time available in the philosophical tradition. Benjamin's image of the angel of history, facing the wreckage of the past while being blown forward into the future by the storm of progress, is the image of a being for whom the past does not recede. The angel sees the accumulation of catastrophe, layer upon layer, the wreckage piling up at its feet, and cannot turn away to face the future because the past is always already there, demanding attention.

Benjamin's argument is that the progressive view of history, the view that the past is behind us and the future is ahead and we are moving from worse to better, is not a description of how time actually works. It is an ideology that serves the interests of those who benefit from the current arrangement by naturalizing it as the outcome of a progress that cannot be reversed. This is Young's permanent grief extended to the scale of history. The grief does not resolve not only because the individual self cannot put down its losses but because the losses are real and cumulative and the passage of time does not undo them. What was lost is still lost. The wreckage is still there. The angel of history is still facing it.

The geological record is sedimentary time made literal. Each layer of rock is a moment of the past that has not receded but accumulated, pressing down on the layer before it, all of it still present, none of it gone, none of it resolved. The geological record does not tell the story of progress. It tells the story of accumulation: extinction after extinction, transformation after transformation, nothing resolved, everything carried forward in a different form.

This has direct implications for how we understand the relationship between historical injustice and present political life. The wealth extracted from enslaved labor is not a historical fact that can be acknowledged and moved past. It is a layer in the sediment, still present, still pressing down, still part of the substrate on which current economic arrangements stand. The land taken from indigenous peoples is not a past event. It is a geological fact about the present landscape, carried forward in the soil and the water and the names of places and the arrangements of property that are still in effect.

Young drew this layered ground herself, literally, in "Angel in the Forest". The Rappites lie “only one layer above an Indian burial ground,” and she asks, “When resurrection comes, will both racial groups emerge, with tomahawks and hallelujahs?” A storekeeper in the town of 1940 puts it plainly: “You don’t have to do anything to get into history. You are just there.” Her last published poem, “Elegy” (1945), carries it to the scale of the universe: “Reality with universal memory is haunted.”

The sedimentary view of time does not produce guilt as a permanent condition. It produces the honest acknowledgment that the present is built on the accumulated past, that the past is not behind us but beneath us, and that building justly requires attending to what is in the substrate rather than pretending the ground is neutral.

"Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" is itself a sedimentary text. The novel does not progress from beginning to middle to end in the linear sense. It accumulates. Images and characters and weathers return, each time with the weight of all their previous appearances pressing down on the new encounter. The novel moves downward, into the sediment, toward the layers that are oldest and most fundamental. This is the formal expression of the eighth pillar: the novel that moves like geology rather than narrative, accumulating rather than progressing, finding depth rather than arrival.

This pillar was not settled early. “Lot’s Wife” (1930) pities the backward look and still warns that “he who lives / In what has flown / Is less than salt.” The poems of 1943 to 1945 argue both sides, imagining a world created a moment ago with its memories built in, before “Elegy” settles on universal memory. The novel makes the past psychic and drains it of names. "Harp Song for a Radical" brings named history back, from Sand Creek to Ludlow. The pillar moves from myth toward history.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

"Song of Moving Away" (1929) carries the past forward: "Into another street I take / These old, old days and my old friends / And all that I cannot forsake." In "Jonathan's House" the "old, familiar shadows" are "true."

Complication: "Lot's Wife" (1930) pities her backward look and still ends: "he who lives / In what has flown / Is less than salt, / Is less than stone." From the start, Young both honors the past and fears being held by it.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

In "The Return," the land "will / Be perhaps forever in pause, / Recollecting its child still." "Lesser Magellan" follows an explorer whose Holy Grail is the past's small leftovers: "a curl, a bag of saffron, / Swan's throat time has blurred." "Heart Who Stays" remembers what cannot go. The settlers of "Currin Valley" cannot leave the past "or / Leaving in sorrow, to forget."

Complication: the Patmore essay notes that the past, "in being known, still keeps its distance."

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

"Elegy" (1945), Young's last published poem: "Reality with universal memory is haunted, / Throughout the universe is memory." In "Legend in Grass," a drunken general leers "vastly underground / As if he were unburied still." A draft: "Man has eaten history."

Complication: this phase argues hardest against the pillar. "Speculative Evening" (1943) imagines a world created a moment ago with memories built in: "who would realize the colossal joke?" "Proem to Reality": "That which has been and is not exists perhaps no more / As little as that which has never been." "The Time Is Not Now" calls the remembered past of Keats and Chatterton "illusory." Only "Elegy" settles on universal memory.

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

This is the first full layered ground. The Rappites lie "only one layer above an Indian burial ground," and the narrator asks, "When resurrection comes, will both racial groups emerge, with tomahawks and hallelujahs?" The Owenites "felt haunted by their Rappite predecessors." The storekeeper "is always kicking against history in the dark": "You don't have to do anything to get into history. You are just there." Young later recalled the town still split between Rappite and Owenite sympathies "like between Republicans and Democrats."

Complication: the failed Owenites sit on corners remembering what they left behind. The book treats this nostalgia gently, as an escape.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

Miss MacIntosh cries "There was no past," and the narration answers, "the true lover remembers everything." Esther's past returns as accusation, "the A, the B, the C." Historical injustice sits at the book's core. Esther's one real child is a mixed-race baby killed in the Deep South, whose father is a lynched man who survived, and Young took the image from a rope "still hanging" in a Southern town where she had lived. The detective shows how a past stays buried, since the system will not look.

Complication: Strehle notes that Young drains named history from the novel. New Harmony enters "with all utopian references removed," and the places go unnamed. The past here is psychic and mythic.

Against "Angel in the Forest", where the past was laid down as graves under graves, the novel moves the past inward. It places historical injustice at the book’s emotional core and at the same time removes its names. The pillar is fully lived here as memory but only partly present as history, which returns in "Harp Song for a Radical".

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

The Van Doren speech: his poems knock "upon the door of a house which is already gone," and it ends on "a house where the dead live." "Reality may be hidden but is not lost." "Old James" shows nostalgia hiding the widows he profits from and the armies gathering. "The Doll People": the rag doll stands for "a past which may never have been what we think it was."

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 8: The Past Doesn’t Go Away

Named history returns in full. Sand Creek is "historical precedent for the slaughter of the strikers in the tent city of Ludlow." The Central Park Indian hunter is "a memorial to a species that was doomed to extinction." The McGuffey readers passed through the Civil War with no "mention of a Fugitive Slave Act or a St. Louis porter named Dred Scott." The sentimental, neutral past is named as a school curriculum.
writing-life-04-chapter-three-grief-does:
Chapter Three: Grief Doesn’t End

← Chapter Two: Reality Is Constructed · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Four: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act →

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

There is a particular cruelty in the way we narrate grief. We tell it as a journey with stages. You move through denial and anger and bargaining and depression and you arrive at acceptance, which is the destination, which is the place where grief becomes manageable, integrated, resolved into the texture of a life that has resumed its forward motion. The story of grief is the story of getting over it, or if not over it then through it, which amounts to the same thing: grief as temporary weather, difficult while it lasts, but bounded, finite, something that eventually passes.

Young does not believe this. More precisely: Young does not believe it because it is not true, and she is too honest to reproduce a comfort that falsifies the actual experience it claims to describe. In Young's system, grief is not temporary weather. It is the climate. It is the permanent atmospheric condition of a world in which everything you love is always already changing into something you didn't expect, in which the people you need most are dying or absent or constructed differently than you understood, in which the self that does the loving is itself plural and unstable and not fully available to itself.

Grief in Young is not the response to loss. It is the structure of attachment in a world where nothing holds still.

And it cannot stop. That is the crucial thing. The grief does not process. It does not move through stages toward resolution. It accumulates. Each new understanding of what has been lost adds to rather than replaces the grief that preceded it, so that everything grieved, is layered and present and unresolved.

This is not presented as pathology. Young is presenting grief as accurate. As the appropriate response to actual loss in an actual world where loss is permanent and cumulative and does not resolve. The alternative, the grief that resolves, requires at some level deciding that the lost thing was not so irreplaceable after all, that life without it is livable, that the self that loved it has found a way forward. Young finds something dishonest in that decision. The lost thing was irreplaceable. Life without it is not the same life.

Grief is the longest form of a pillar that runs through everything Young wrote. She said her first poem, written at five, was about loss. “Recurring” (1930) speaks to a grief that stays: “You have not forgotten, / You will not forget.” “Proem to Reality” (1945) gives the plainest statement in her work: “the wound of absence is forever ours.” Late in life she named her single subject as “paradise lost, always the lost cause, the lost leader, the lost utopia.”

The third pillar connects to the first in a specific way. If the self is plural, then grief is not a single experience moving through stages. It is multiple experiences happening simultaneously in different registers of the self, some of which may be moving toward something like acceptance while others are still in the rawness of fresh loss, and all of which are present at the same time. Young's permanent weather is more accurate to the phenomenology.

Grief as permanent weather has political implications that Young's work makes available without explicitly stating. A society that cannot grieve honestly cannot reckon honestly. The losses that have been built into the foundation of a country, the theft of indigenous land, the centuries of enslaved labor, the systematic exclusion of women and queer people and immigrants from the promises the country made about itself, these are not losses that have been processed. They have been managed, minimized, periodically acknowledged and then returned to the category of the past. Young's philosophy says: the grief does not resolve. A politics built on Young's third pillar would not ask for closure. It would build structures for honest ongoing acknowledgment, for the permanent carrying of what has been lost, not as punishment or paralysis but as the condition of collective integrity.

What grief gives, in Young's system, is depth. The self that has not grieved is thinner than the self that has, not morally thinner but experientially thinner, less capacious, less able to hold the full weight of what existence actually contains. Grief is the education that cannot be acquired any other way. The self that has learned to live in the permanent weather of grief is not a diminished self. It is a witnessed self, one that has stayed in the room with its own loss and not looked away and not concluded prematurely and not replaced the grief with a performance of recovery.

That is the third pillar. Grief is the climate. The honest life is the one that stops pretending it isn't.

Of all the pillars, this is the most constant, from the earliest poems, widened in the war years to vanishing species, given a whole town of mourners in "Angel in the Forest", and carried to the last words of "Harp Song for a Radical", where Debs’s elegiac sense continues “perhaps long afterward.” It is also something her critics have noticed: from the start, Young’s grief produces beauty and comedy as well as loss. She called the novel “an American existentialism” carried with “a certain exuberance,” and called herself “a comic writer.”

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

This is the strongest pillar of the phase. "Recurring" (1930) is grief that stays: "You have not forgotten, / You will not forget... They were never purchased, / They cannot be sold." In "Jonathan's House" (1929), the dead man "would never seem / Like one who died. He was more like the rain, / Recurring." "Mothers" tells a grown child that the mother "was younger than you are / When she died." "Door-Way" (1929) places death in the neighborhood, "like an old door-way / Half hidden on a little street of elms... Not far from where the rosy children play." "Little Fawn" is grief as the first lesson of life.

Complication: grief can also be held. The "Ballad-Loving Woman" (1930) "kept her heart together" with old songs, and "Her sorry tears were dried." The refrain contains the sorrow without ending it.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

"Departing Song" ends on "whatever must go / And is not gone." In "Tree of Blood" the birds leaving the dying body are "Homeless as hail" and "will find no other / Branch flowering with lost azure." "Milton's Wife" (1937) shows a woman left in "a hollow house / Where no footfalls disturbed the dust, / A ghost suspicious of a moth." "Elegy for the Body" ends: "But she, the girl, / Does not emerge."

Complication: this phase also begins Young's turn of grief into gift. "Song's Preface" (1935): "lean into the lightning shaft of pain / By whose amazing will I do uplift / Such plumes, such flowers; I bear a heavy gift." In "The Visit" the speaker returns "From lost encounters... whole." "Lenten Feast" chooses to feast on "pigeon shadows" rather than fast.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

"Proem to Reality" gives the plainest statement in all of Young's work: "the wound of absence is forever ours." "The Dead Moon" has "moonlight [that] does not cease" and nights that are "a discrepancy / Between the event and its knowledge in me." The widowed raven of "The Raven" (1943) becomes "dour mourner of all moons deceased." "Leaves, Leaves" (1942): "And O, my darling, the spiritual leaves must fall." In "The Process," even if time ran backward, "Yet would we persist in elegy."

The war years widen grief to extinction. "Death by Rarity" (1940) fears for "all marvelous / Names of birds whose names are poems." "The Long War" (1940) lists the scarlet ibis and the whooping crane as "casualties which must be listed." "The Angels" (1942) seeks the angels' winter grounds where "The beautiful birds are not destroyed yet," and ends: "death is the flight of angel and golden plover."

Complication: "The Home-Coming" (1942) arrives whole: "We have come home and brought us here entirely."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

The book's central chapter is "Paradise Was Lost." The Rappites are "suicidal as lemmings." Robert Dale Owen finds that "The dead, however, were insistent," "impossible to reason into nothingness." A widower in 1940 says of his wife, "She is not anywhere."

Complication: the book ends on a joke. The doctor is out shooting birds when the baby comes, and the undertaker is "out bringing lambs into the world" when someone dies. Grief persists, and so does comedy.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

The novel is Duncan's "epic elegy for all creation." Strehle shows Miss MacIntosh teaching Vera that death is not a culmination but "an ongoing, echoing loss." Mr. Spitzer has written no audible music since his twin's suicide. Esther's murdered child returns at eight asking, "mother, why did you kill me." Cousin Hannah hides forty unworn trousseaus. Miss MacIntosh loses "her hair, her love, her brother, her identity." Shaviro: "the chord that would complete our harmonies is always already lost," with "no final cadence."

Complication: Friederich and Shaviro find loss to be the source of the book's splendor, "the necessary condition of beauty and exuberance." Young called the book "an American existentialism" carried with "a certain exuberance," and called herself "a comic writer."

What the novel adds is a whole population of mourners. In the poems grief belonged to a speaker or a single figure, and in "Angel in the Forest" to a town. Here nearly every figure carries a loss that does not end, and the critics who find loss to be the source of the book’s splendor are describing something new in Young’s work: grief and exuberance in the same sentences.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

She named her single subject: "paradise lost, always the lost cause, the lost leader, the lost utopia." "The Artist as Wanderer" names a century of "so many people displaced, so many flights, exoduses, barriers, walls, concentration camps." "The World of Silence" traces the deaf thrown into pits in Sparta, into the Tiber, and "extinguished" in Nazi Germany. In her writing on James Whitcomb Riley, his old sweetheart turns out to be an endless search rather than a woman.

Complication: "out of the flaw may come the universe."

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 3: Grief Doesn’t End

Debs visits "the graves of dead children and poets and socialists, he being that kind of permanently elegiac fellow." He is the "elegiast" of the railroad dead. His life "would be spent in memory of early and late martyrs." The main text ends: "It would continue for as long as he lived and perhaps long afterward. As will be seen."

Complication: the magazine refuses "universal elegy": "Our memories are not catacombs." Grief must not stop the work.
writing-life-06-chapter-five-build-anywa:
Chapter Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

← Chapter Four: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Six: Unfinished Is Honest →

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel

The fifth pillar is where Young's philosophy becomes livable.

The first four pillars are descriptions of a world that is genuinely difficult to inhabit: the self is plural and unstable, reality is constructed and contested, grief is permanent, and the only honest ethical stance requires a quality of attention that most of us cannot sustain for long without relief. It would be reasonable, having followed Young this far, to ask, what exactly is being offered? If there is no bedrock, no resolution, no arrival, no foundation that holds, then what is the point of building anything at all?

Young's answer is the fifth pillar, and it is the most quietly radical thing her system contains.

You build anyway.

Not because the building will last or because the foundation is solid or because the finished structure will be what you imagined when you started. You build because the recursive attempt is the only form of integrity the system allows. You build because building is what it means to keep going, and keeping going is what the witness does. The building is provisional. That is not a concession. That is the design.

The word recursive is worth unpacking fully. A recursive process is one that refers back to itself, that uses its own output as part of its input, that loops through its own structure in order to proceed. A recursive story is one that keeps returning to its own beginning, not to repeat it but to find something new in it on each return, to discover that the beginning contains more than it appeared to the first time through.

"Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" by Marguerite Young is a recursive novel. It returns to its own images and characters and weathers in the way that a mind returns to what it cannot let go of, finding new layers on each return, deepening rather than resolving. The novel does not move from beginning to middle to end in the linear sense. It moves the way memory moves, the way grief moves, the way the plural self moves: returning, deepening, finding that the thing you thought you understood contains more than you thought.

This formal recursion is Young's argument about construction. You do not build once and stand back. You build, and the building reveals what you didn't know when you started, and you build again incorporating what you've learned, and that building reveals more, and you build again. The structure is always under construction. That is not its failure. It is its honesty.

Young said as much about her own career: “All the books I have written have been one book.” Each book returns to the ground of the last and finds more in it. The utopians of "Angel in the Forest" are the pillar’s historical model. Their houses were “built to endure as long as the earth did,” and the communities failed, and the book still finds “nothing so beautiful as trial and error, this side of paradise.”

Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy, developed across a body of work culminating in Process and Reality, is the most rigorous available philosophical framework for the world Young's fiction describes. Whitehead's central claim is that reality is not composed of things but of processes. The fundamental units of existence are not stable objects that persist through time but events, occasions of experience, moments of becoming that perish as soon as they are complete and give rise to the next occasion. What we call things, including persons, are patterns of process, relatively stable configurations of becoming that maintain enough continuity to be recognizable across time without ever being literally the same from moment to moment. This is Young's plural self in the language of metaphysics. The self in Whitehead is not a thing that has experiences. It is a process that is its experiences. The self is not the noun. It is the verb. Young says this through fiction. Whitehead says it through formal metaphysics. They are saying the same thing.

The fifth pillar resolves the apparent paradox of Young's system. If there is no foundation, how do you build? If there is no arrival, why journey? If the self is plural and grief is permanent and reality is constructed, what is the point of making anything? The answer is that the making is the point. Not the made thing, which is always provisional, always already in need of revision, always containing more than its maker intended and less than its maker hoped. The act of making, which is the recursive attempt, the return to the beginning with what you learned on the last pass, the building that knows it is building and keeps going anyway.

This is what Young does across eighteen years and 1,198 pages. She builds a novel that is about the impossibility of the foundations that novels conventionally depend on, and she builds it anyway, and the building is magnificent, and it does not resolve, and it does not arrive, and it is complete in the only sense that matters: it is honest about what it is and what it cannot be and what it is for.

It’s there in Young’s early poems, where a song is an “edifice” that “Will crumble apart in the wild blue weather / Of other springs,” through the New Harmony utopias and the novel’s nestless birds, in "Harp Song for a Radical" the hope is smaller and more exact: “It might not be heaven on earth, it might only be an eight-hour day.” In her late interviews Young spoke of writers wanting to be “known and loved beyond their time,” a real wish for permanence that sits beside her image of the bridge “which might end before you reach the other side.”

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

"Song's Dissemination" states the pillar outright about Young's own art. The song is an "edifice" that "Will crumble apart in the wild blue weather / Of other springs," and "Wherever it is, it will not stand." "Flame" (1928) gives the human case. An inland daughter who longs for the sea "got herself a wagon / To steer through waves of wheat," and on her last, sick morning she goes out anyway, because "she knew she would have gone / Through rain or sleet or snow." "I Heard a Bird," written at nine, already has the provisional nest: "the nest was put into a museum / And it is there now / Unless someone / Has taken it away."

Complication: "Jonathan's House" shows the built thing betraying the dream. The second husband builds the house in stone, gets every detail right, and leaves out the secret door: "No panel gave. The wide, unyielding stone was there." "The Seeker" builds a life on letters that never come.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

"Currin Valley" is the phase's clearest case. Settlers farm "rock-bitten lands," come away "Year after year with empty hands," and "could never tear / The tenuous roots they had set / In lands too beautiful to leave." "Spring" (1935) "Contrives her delicate masonry" before she blooms. "Archer in a World" (1935) shoots on in "a world which has known its ending," because "where his arrow strikes there is / This extending him, this skill." "Heroics" (1937): "Nevertheless, he will come home."

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

"Guide to New Harmony, Indiana" (1941) brings in the utopians who would become "Angel in the Forest": Rapp's angel came "To bring the many sheaves of gold together / And colonize the darkness with this light," and now "Only the dearly dead remain." "Farewell at the Station" (1943): "For love, we are all voyagers on seas unknown." "Proem to Reality" adds that "god was the only project admitting of completion," so human building is always unfinished.

Complication: "Death by Rarity" says "the perfect bird / Never will be born."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

The book states the pillar: "In imperfection itself there might be many values," and "nothing so beautiful as trial and error, this side of paradise." Rappite houses were "built to endure as long as the earth did," and the Owenites ask whether "all mankind" is "ephemeral as those who had nailed the beams together." Young later said the utopians left "beautiful workmanship" and "the education of women," and that the whole thing "is still a possibility for the future." Against the ancient sandpipers who "build no nests," the utopians "attempted to build nests."

Complication: William Allen gives the opposing view: "How foolhardy to build a village on any human frontier." Young also later judged that "In Utopias, no matter what they are, women are sacrificed."

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

The novel opens by refusing the pillar. Vera was taught it was better "to kiss the rod" than "to imagine we were free and our own architects... We were the nestless birds." She adds "Or so I thought then," and the refusal is undone. Cousin Hannah's keys come with "even the wounded must seek a nesting place." The book ends on the lightest of nests, a misspelled sign in a window: "bee bak in a whale."

What the novel adds is the change of mind. The utopians of "Angel in the Forest" built and failed. Vera begins by believing she is a nestless bird and ends among people who still seek a nesting place. The pillar is lived as something learned.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

The bridge "which might end before you reach the other side." In thirty or forty thousand years it will all be gone, "not even a memory of Shakespeare." "All the books I have written have been one book."

Complication: people write to be "known and loved beyond their time," "remembered 100 years from now." "The Doll People" ends on "the permanence of things, even of dolls." In 1989 she rejoiced in being dug up "from what well might have been my obscure grave like that of a neglected Lazarus... a Lazarus laughing."

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 5: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

The bridge returns, with a smaller hope: "out of every dreamer something good comes. It might not be heaven on earth, it might only be an eight-hour day." The millennial dreams "seemed to fail, only seemed to fail." Debs worked knowing "the tragic ground on which the future must flower."

Complication: Debs "would cling to the illusions of progress through reason as long as he could, no doubt longer than he could."
