Chapter Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Chapter Six: Unfinished Is Honest · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Eight: The Past Doesn’t Go Away →

Pillar: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth · Across every book

Characters: Moses Hunnecker · The Stone Deaf Man

The seventh pillar is where the philosophical system encounters its own population.

"Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" is populated with characters who exist at the edges of the categories that social and political life uses to organize its population. These are not marginal figures in the sense of being incidental. They are the center of Young's philosophical attention, because the margins are where the categories show their seams, where the constructed nature of the social real becomes most visible, where the plural self cannot be forced into the singular mold without the forcing becoming undeniable. The marginal is not the exception in Young's system. It is the evidence.

Young had stated the principle as philosophy before she populated it with characters. In “The Contravalid” (1945) there are “No schemata exclusive of the cripple and accident,” and “The crippled dancer is the dance, at last, / The only truth.” Twenty years later the crippled dancer appears in the novel as a one-legged dancer among its company of the dispossessed.

Hannah Arendt's political philosophy, developed across The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism, offers the most rigorous available framework for understanding why the marginal is the evidence rather than the exception. Arendt argues that the political realm is not the realm of agreement but the realm of plurality. Political life, properly understood, is the life of beings who are fundamentally different from each other, who cannot be reduced to a common type or a common interest, and who nevertheless share a world. The space of appearance, Arendt's term for the political space, is the space in which plural beings appear to each other in their difference, not in their sameness.

Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism is directly relevant here. Totalitarian movements, she argues, destroy political life not primarily through violence, though they use violence, but through the destruction of plurality. They demand that every person become the same kind of person, that difference be eliminated, that the space of appearance be replaced by the uniform surface of ideological agreement. The destruction of plurality is the destruction of the political realm itself.

Young's novel enacts this analysis. The demand for the true self beneath the plurality, is a totalitarian demand in Arendt's sense. It destroys the space in which the plural self can appear honestly. It replaces the full complexity of the person with the simplified version that the demand can process. The community that holds difference without erasure is the community that refuses this demand.

The passengers on Moses Hunnecker's Grey Goose bus are not a community of shared identity. They are a collection of plural selves in transit, each carrying their own permanent grief and their own constructed reality, each appearing to the others in the partial visibility that the bus's shared space allows. What holds them together is not agreement. It is the shared condition of being in transit, of moving through a world that does not resolve, of carrying what they carry without the possibility of putting it down. The community of the bus is the community of witnesses to each other's plurality, not the community of people who have found their common ground.

Mikhail Bakhtin's theory of the dialogic offers a complementary framework. Bakhtin argues that meaning is not produced by a single voice speaking a single truth. It is produced in the encounter between voices, in the dialogue that occurs when different perspectives meet and respond to each other. "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" by Marguerite Young is dialogic in Bakhtin's sense, but it pushes the principle further than Bakhtin's framework anticipates. The voices in Young's novel are not only the voices of different characters. They are the voices of different selves within a single character, the plural self in dialogue with its own plurality.

This is the seventh pillar's image: the Grey Goose bus as the model of community. Not the community that has arrived at its destination and agreed on what it found there. The community that is still in motion, still carrying its grief, still holding the difference of its members without demanding that they simplify.

Young’s work follows the margins from the weeds and the “old, blind, broken ass” of the 1930s poems, to “The Contravalid,” to the Ozark families camped at the edge of New Harmony, to Debs’s union of all workers “irrespective of race, color, or creed.” It also records what this chapter does not: the racial and other blind spots of Young’s period, present in every phase of her work, including the novel’s first page, where Black passengers are “beings unseen, merely sensed.” Her awareness of these limits is sharpest in the novel and the Debs book, where she names the failure to see.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

The margins of this phase are Indiana's rural poor and old women: the women of Hawthorne Lane, the woman who chose china over bread, the farmer pulled from school who "tried to learn / The rules of English grammar by myself," the peddler woman, the hunter laughed at by his neighbors. These are the people the poems take seriously. No racial material appears yet.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

Prismatic Ground turns firmly toward the edges. "To the Strangest Lady" brings freckled rocks and dried snakeskins to someone who "likes wind-ragged weeds and me; / She thinks both are beautiful." "Plea for Sodom" asks heaven to spare a small city "for the sake of birds... And the old, blind, broken ass." "Advertisement" asks for payment in "a rabbit's paw" and "a crow's caw-caw" instead of silver, an economy of worthless things. "Paradise Is Still Lost" finds the fallen angels among stool pigeons, addicts, and a woman "walking the windy streets." "Milton's Wife" shows the wife of a great poet shut away and forgotten, an early form of a judgment Young later made about utopias.

Complication: the same poems carry period stereotypes. "Paradise Is Still Lost" has "slant / dark eyes" and a "Chinese gentleman, heroin," and "Rosary in Discord" has the phrase "Return slant-eyed." The blind spots found later in the essays are present from Young's first book.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

"The Contravalid" (1945) states the pillar: "No schemata exclusive of the cripple and accident," and "The crippled dancer is the dance, at last, / The only truth, the double-headed dwarf of paradox." "That Chance" (1943): "There is no absolute... But deviation from the law / In lonely items of the real." A draft scorns logicians "Omitting salty spinsters by that sea." "The Long War" gives worth to "Whatever is small, whatever deceives." In "The Clinic," the condemned man might be "The highest good to which mankind attains." "The Priesthood of Motion" sees in an old Black man in the cotton fields a stillness that is "a deception / And an exodus from cotton fields."

Complication: the unpublished portraits of an old Black woman by the sea, "She was my mother then," feeding "a white child," turn love into the old type of the Black nurse.

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

The Ozark families camp at the edge of town "like the lost children of Israel," and "God did never deliver these people out of any wilderness." Among a woman on a crutch and a grandfather with a "broken fiddle," the narrator finds "a feeling that man is in himself valuable, as man." Rapp's graveyard has no tombstones because he wanted no "individuality" carried into death, and Young saw the perfect society as one that shuts out "the fantastic, irrational, non-reasoning side of life."

Complication: Indigenous people appear mostly as the dead beneath the Rappite graves, described in the period's vocabulary of "papooses" and "squaws."

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

The novel's company is the culture's dispossessed: the stone-deaf man, the blind veteran, the blind painter, the one-legged dancer (the "crippled dancer" of "The Contravalid," twenty years later), the bald and one-breasted nursemaid, the schizophrenic mother of dream children. The final voice is the deaf lover's: "we be the silences because we are all loves." A hotel landlady gives enforced sameness its own voice: "There are no Negroes in this county." Moore notes the book's following in the gay literary community.

Complication: the Black bus passengers on the first page are "beings unseen, merely sensed." But the narrator frames this as a failure of sight, "no one has ever seen the other person." Here Young names her own limit, which the essays and poems do not.

What the novel adds is a narrator who admits her own limit. The poems and essays look at the margins without asking what the one looking cannot see. The novel’s first page asks it.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

"Indiana has given birth to many individuals but to no types." "The World of Silence": "The tragedy of those born deaf is not that they do not hear but that others hear." The deaf apologized to her for being "in the minority," and she saw an affinity among "the blind, the deaf, the crippled," and "the Negro." "The Artist as Wanderer" reads the Wandering Jew as "a crime committed by all men who would kill the dreamer and the dream." She hoped "the lower elements will never be got rid of."

Complication: "The Midwest of Everywhere" mentions worms sold "in Negro shanty towns" as local color. "The Doll People" passes over "old mammy dolls with nut-brown faces." "The World of Silence" favors lip-reading in line with its time and includes a generalization about Jewish deaf and criminality. Her method of the "archetype" pulls against her rejection of types.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 7: The Margins Reveal the Truth

Debs's union takes all workers "irrespective of race, color, or creed, excluding not even the least paint scraper or wheel wiper." On Chinese exclusion: "The souls of Chinese children are yellow butterflies." His fellow convicts' uncounted votes still have "value." The "working dead" are the book's center.

Complication: Kate Debs is satirized with her "nest egg" and "all her women's rights about her," and Mary Lincoln is "the squat black widow."
writing-life-13-conclusion:
Conclusion

← Chapter Eleven: The Crossing Point · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Bibliography →

How Each Pillar Developed Over Time

Pillar 1, Not One Self: first felt in her childhood as Harry and in the mirror of "Transition" (1930), argued in "That Cloud" (1944), made doctrine in the novel (1965), then qualified by her claim of a steady self (1965) and by great-man history in the Debs work. It peaks in the middle of her career and is partly pulled back late.

Pillar 2, Reality Is Constructed: moves from the epistemology of the graduate essays and "Bishop Berkeley" (1944), to the social danger of common sense in 1946, to the economic illusion of capitalism in the Debs work. Throughout, she holds that experience, including dream, is real, so the construction she attacks is the common-sense world rather than reality itself.

Pillar 3, Grief Doesn't End: the most constant pillar, present from her first poem at five through "Recurring" (1930), "the wound of absence" (1945), the novel's elegy, and the Debs book's closing elegiac sense "perhaps long afterward." In the 1940s it widens to extinct species. From the start, grief also produces beauty and comedy.

Pillar 4, Witnessing: begins in personal attention with Minna and the hunter who only watched (1934), becomes complicit in "The Clinic" (1941), becomes a tool of power in "Angel in the Forest" (1945), becomes refused along a color line in the novel, and splits into surveillance and testimony in the Debs work. It grows more institutional and more political over time.

Pillar 5, Build Anyway: stated about her own art in "Song's Dissemination" in the early poems, given its model in the New Harmony utopias (1945), first refused and then accepted in the novel's nestless birds, and measured by the small gain of an eight-hour day in the Debs work. Across her late interviews it sits beside a real wish for permanence.

Pillar 6, Unfinished Is Honest: formulated as the theory of the flaw in "A Crystal Principle" (1942), carried into the undertaker of "Angel in the Forest", built into the open form of the novel, and finally enacted by accident in the unfinished Debs book. It moves from a designed principle to the condition of her own life's work.

Pillar 7, The Margins: present from the weeds and the broken ass of the 1930s poems, stated as philosophy in "The Contravalid" (1945), given a population in the Ozark tents and the novel's dispossessed, and made into policy in Debs's union of all workers. Period blind spots run through every phase, though her racial awareness is sharpest in the novel and the Debs work.

Pillar 8, The Past Doesn't Go Away: ambivalent in "Lot's Wife" (1930), argued both ways in 1944 and 1945 before "Elegy" settles on universal memory, laid down as buried graves in "Angel in the Forest", made psychic in the novel, and documented in the Debs work. It moves from myth toward history.

Pillar 9, Language: begins with "even the nouns act like verbs" in the graduate essays, becomes a critique of language that invents false wholes in the 1940s drafts, turns political in "Angel in the Forest", shows inherited language and counter-language in the novel, and becomes the politics of naming in the Debs work. Its political half arrives late.

Pillar 10, The Sacred Is Here: travels from the theist nature-worship of "Worship" (1927), to God subtracted in the Patmore essay, to God as "creation's flaw" in "Noah's Ark" (1943), to "no God but what we dreamed" in the novel, to the sacred as labor in the Debs work. The vocabulary of angels, resurrection, and exile stays with her the whole way.

Pillar 11, The Crossing Point: the pillar that grows most over time. It is faint in "Biography" (1932), takes clear shape in "Slow Motion" and "The Funeral" (1941), gains the miller's thumbprint at the end of "Angel in the Forest" (1945), becomes the unlocatable conception in the novel, and reaches its strongest image in Dostoyevsky in the snow in her last book.

What the Record Shows

Taken in order, Young's writing shows a philosophy that was not stated once and then repeated. It was built in stages. It began as a feeling in the early poems: the lost mother's tracks in the snow, the mirror that multiplies, the God seen "only / In stars and flowers and shining eyes." In the Chicago years it gained a method from William James, a founding act of witness beside Minna Weissenbach’s bed, and its first prose statements in the graduate essays: sanity as "sharing the hallucinations of our neighbors," a world where "even the nouns act like verbs," and a God who "would hardly be missed." Between 1938 and 1945 it was argued in verse against Berkeley, Descartes, and Aquinas, and several pillars got their clearest statements anywhere in her work: the flaw that makes being "valid," the crippled dancer as "the only truth," "the wound of absence is forever ours," and God as "creation's flaw." In "Angel in the Forest" it moved into history and community. In "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" it was lived by characters across twelve hundred pages. In the interviews and essays Young explained it in her own voice. In "Harp Song for a Radical" she turned it toward labor, power, and the working dead.

The pillars did not all develop the same way. Grief is the most constant. The witnessing, the past, language, and the crossing point grew steadily and gained political weight late, and the crossing point grew most of all, from the minnow net to Dostoyevsky in the snow. The plural self peaked in the middle of her career and was partly pulled back late.

Some frictions never changed. The language of transcendence runs from "Worship" in 1927 to the "transcendental socialism" of her last decades. The soul as an exile from elsewhere, strongest in the poems of the early 1940s, is never resolved. Her wish to be "known and loved beyond their time" sits beside her bridge "which might end before you reach the other side." The period's racial and other blind spots appear in every phase, though the novel and the Debs history show her aware of them and writing toward them. These frictions do not show the philosophy is absent. They show how Young held it. She argued for the past pressing up and for a universe haunted by memory, for God as creation's flaw and for an angel she insisted was real, for the plural self and for a self that changes no more than "the color of our eyes." She did not see a contradiction, because in her world "the illogical is logic."

The record supports crediting Young with developing Radical Immanence, with one qualification. Every pillar appears in her work, most of them early, and she returned to each one over six decades and deepened it. That is how a writer develops a philosophy rather than touching on one. The qualification is that the name and the eleven-part structure are an articulation of what she built, not a design she laid out herself. She worked in images and scattered statements across poems, histories, a novel, and fifty years of occasional prose, and she left the ideas to be gathered. Her own last book supplies the terms for that gathering. Of the utopian dreamers she wrote that the dream "never really dies as some other dreamer must take over the dream." Naming the philosophy and giving it a structure is a way of taking over the dream, and the evidence shows the dream was hers.

The Sentence That Hasn’t Ended

This account of Young's philosophy began with a sentence about a sentence. Marguerite Young spent eighteen years writing a novel that refuses to end. The refusal is the argument. The continuation is the ethics. The sentence that hasn't ended is not a failure of resolution. It is the most honest description available of what it means to be alive in a world that does not resolve.

Young's philosophy, assembled from its pillars, followed across sixty years of writing, and placed in conversation with the thinkers it illuminates and is illuminated by, and extrapolated toward the political life it makes possible, is not a completed system in the way that philosophical systems usually claim to be complete. It is a recursive one. It knows that the building is provisional. It builds anyway. It knows that the grief does not resolve. It witnesses anyway. It knows that the self is plural and the real is constructed and the honest ethical stance requires a quality of attention that is exhausting to sustain. It sustains it anyway. Not because the sustaining is easy or because the arrival is coming. Because sustaining is what integrity looks like in a world built the way this world is built.

What Young gives us is not comfort in the cheap sense. It is companionship in the honest one. The companionship of a thinker who looked at the full weight of what existence contains and did not flinch and did not conclude and did not replace the difficulty with a consolation that would have required pretending the difficulty wasn't there. She stayed in the room. She stayed in the room with the hardest questions her philosophy asked.

The pillars together are the philosophical account of why the sentence has not ended, why it cannot end without lying, why the ongoing sentence is the only honest form that the engagement with this world can take.

It is saying that the world is here, and plural, and grief-saturated, and constructed, and sacred in the immanent sense, and incomplete in the honest sense, and populated at its margins by the people whose complexity the sorting systems cannot process, and layered with time that the present moment carries without always knowing it carries, and expressible only in a form that refuses to simplify, and worth building in, and worth witnessing in, and worth staying in the room with, without flinching and without concluding.

That is radical immanence.

That is the philosophy of Marguerite Young.

The question Young leaves us with is not how to end it. It is how to keep writing it with honesty and the attention and the willingness to return to the beginning and find what we missed the first time that the sentence, if it is to mean anything, requires.
writing-life-07-chapter-six-unfinished-i:
Chapter Six: Unfinished Is Honest

← Chapter Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Seven: The Margins Reveal the Truth →

Pillar: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest · Across every book

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The sixth pillar emerges from the first five as their ethical consequence.

Young's system does not only describe a world in which things do not resolve. It makes an ethical claim about incompletion: that the unfinished is not a failure but a form of honesty, and that the demand for completion is a form of violence against the actual texture of experience. This is not a limitation. It is a moral position.

The Western philosophical tradition has a profound discomfort with the unfinished. The claim must be statable, the argument must be followable, the conclusion must be reachable. The unfinished argument is not a philosophical contribution. It is a draft. This is the tradition's limitation, not Young's. The world does not resolve. The self does not arrive. The grief does not process. The construction of reality is never complete. A philosophy that requires completeness as the condition of validity is a philosophy that can only describe a world that does not exist.

Young's system accepts the unfinished as its natural state. Not because she could not finish it, but because finishing it would require lying about the world it describes. The sixth pillar names this acceptance as an ethical stance: the unfinished is not failure but integrity, the honest acknowledgment that the work is still ongoing because the world is still ongoing and the honest response to an ongoing world is an ongoing engagement.

Young had stated the principle in verse more than twenty years before the novel appeared. In “A Crystal Principle” (1942), the earth would be perfect crystal “Were it not for accident unknown / And least departure,” and the flaw is what makes it “valid in being.” Her later statement was shorter: “There must always be a flaw.” Of the novel she said it has no beginning, middle, or end “because life has no beginning, middle or end.”

Walter Benjamin's own work is famously unfinished. The Arcades Project, his massive study of nineteenth-century Paris as the origin point of modern consumer culture, was never completed. Benjamin died before he could assemble thousands of notes and fragments into the book he had planned. But the incompleteness of The Arcades Project is not incidental to its argument. The argument is about the accumulated fragments of the past, about the way that meaning emerges from the constellation of particulars rather than from the systematic whole. A completed, systematic Arcades Project would have betrayed its own argument by imposing the false unity of a finished system on material that resists systematic completion.

The unfinished is the honest form. Young understood this. Benjamin understood this. The sixth pillar names what they both knew: that the honest engagement with a world that does not resolve produces work that does not resolve, and that the work's incompleteness is not its failure but its most rigorous achievement.

The political consequences of the sixth pillar are the most challenging of all the pillars. Political life, as it is currently practiced, demands the finished product. The policy must be complete before it can be implemented. The platform must be coherent. The candidate must have a position, a clear and statable position, on every question. The unfinished is not a political option. It is a liability. Young's system says: this demand is the demand that produces the long con. The finished policy, the complete platform, the clear position: these are the products of a political culture that has decided that the appearance of resolution is more important than the honest acknowledgment of ongoing complexity. The policy that presents itself as finished is the policy that cannot be revised when it turns out to be wrong.

The Youngian political life builds the unfinished into its structure. It creates the mechanisms for ongoing revision, for the acknowledgment that the current arrangement is provisional, for the return to the beginning that the recursive construction requires. It treats the unfinished not as a liability but as the most honest form that political integrity can take.

The theory of the flaw takes shape in the poems of 1942, passes into the mouth of the undertaker in "Angel in the Forest", and becomes the open form of the novel. "Harp Song for a Radical", her last book, was left unfinished at her death, “a complete creation, without having been entirely finished,” in its editors’ words. That incompletion was not chosen. Young also wanted to decide or be in control, as when she tried to reclaim the Debs book uncut.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

The pillar appears mostly in reverse, in the stone house of "Jonathan's House" and the scattering song of "Song's Dissemination." The theory of the flaw has not yet appeared.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

"Experiment in Azure" holds the unhatched: "No one could tell what bird might be," and "the shell / Broken would be the broken sky." "Song's Preface" calls the song "fugitive," one that "comes no sooner than it goes again." The theory of the flaw is still a few years off.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

This is the phase in which Young formulated the theory of the flaw. "A Crystal Principle" (1942): earth would be perfect crystal "Were it not for accident unknown / And least departure: and valid in being therefore / And beautiful, the escape from each simple of total / Is the heartbeat thief, mistake, flaw." Its draft adds "there is a pattern in the anomaly." The giraffe (1942) is "a vain and vexed / But relevant mistake, and scheme of all our flaws." "The Pattern" (1941) names "these present flaws / Whereof the rain crow cries, rose petal falls." "Failing Perspective": "we shall never see the completed earth." "Of Deed, Love, Death": "our inclination is always the business unfinished." The five drafts of "The Submarine" show the method itself as a spiral that never closes.

Complication: the title poem "Moderate Fable" calls incompletion a curse. Seven bridegrooms come to the daughter of God and die before "the act of union entire," "cursed by severance."

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

Perfection is death. Owen's heaven is "a Parmenidean quietude, all crystal, stainless, and perfect, without wind, without motion." A baby's head is "a huge mistake of nature, like perhaps every other head." The undertaker warns that no one can remove the flaws from the universe without destroying it, the theory of "A Crystal Principle" put into a character's mouth.

Complication: when the Rappites leave Economy, the barns are "half painted" and the fields "half plowed." The unfinished can also mean abandonment.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

Young said the novel has no beginning, middle, or end "because life has no beginning, middle or end." Fuchs quotes its broken visions as "more complete in their incompletion than if they had been whole," and shows that when Young uses plot she uses it "to negate its legitimacy." Hannah's forty trunks come with forty keys, always one too many or too few. The ending stays in the conditional: Esther "would hang" her sign.

Complication: Vera first meets the unfinished with dread, calling the bald Miss MacIntosh "this unfinished thing... which had no business in creation." Vera's mother, for whom "everything was complete, even the incompletion," shows completeness as denial. Young herself was "hysterically anxious to finish," and called the book "very controlled." The openness is designed.

Incompletion as her novel’s moral position, what is new is scale. The flaw of “A Crystal Principle” was a principle stated in a poem. Here it is the design of a 1,198 page book, and the narrator first meets it with dread before the book teaches her to live with it.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

"There must always be a flaw." Her teaching threw out "beginning and middle and end" for "memory and observation, dream and reality, conflict and character." Clark read her gift of stolen hotel keys as a lesson that there is no closure adequate to any ending.

Complication: when Knopf wanted to cut the Debs book, she tried to reclaim it uncut. She wanted to decide when something was done, that she had “tried her best”.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 6: Unfinished Is Honest

The book is itself unfinished. It ends on a promise of the Pullman strike and the prison years that never arrive. The editors call it "a complete creation, without having been entirely finished." Weitling dies leaving "his unfinished treatise on moon and sun," the fruit "of fourteen years of mental toil." The Icarians' "statistics, statistics, statistics" and Weitling's "science without flaws" are the completeness the book distrusts.

Complication: this incompletion is accidental, the result of illness, mixed drafts, and death with "Harp Song for a Radical".

Chapter Four: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

← Chapter Three: Grief Doesn’t End · Radical Immanence Across Marguerite Young's Writing Life · Chapter Five: Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary →

Pillar: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Across every book

Characters: Esther Longtree · Vera Cartwheel · Walter

The fourth pillar is the one that does the ethical work of the system.

The first three pillars describe conditions: the self is plural, reality is constructed, grief is permanent. They tell you what the world is. The fourth pillar tells you what to do about it, which is not what you might expect from a philosophical system that has spent three chapters dismantling the foundations of certainty.

What you do is witness.

Not act, not fix, not resolve, not transcend. Witness. Stay in the room with what is actually there. See it without flinching and without concluding. Maintain the full attention that the thing in front of you deserves, the attention that does not look away when the looking becomes painful and does not rush toward resolution when the contradiction becomes uncomfortable. The witness is the one who can hold the multiple things at the same time, without requiring that one of them be more real than the other, without needing the scene to resolve into something more manageable than it actually is.

This sounds passive. It is not. It is the most demanding ethical stance Young's system makes available, and it is demanding because it refuses the satisfactions that make ethical action feel complete. The hero acts and the problem is solved and the story ends. The witness stays and the problem remains and the story keeps going and the witness keeps staying. There is no arrival. There is only the quality of attention brought to the continuing.

Young's novel is itself an act of witnessing. Her characters are not judged, diagnosed, concluded and the interior world is not positioned as inferior to the world outside it. It does not offer the reader the comfort of a clinical or moral frame that would explain who is right, who is wrong.

The length of "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" is not excess. It is the time required to witness properly. You cannot witness in summary. You cannot witness at a distance. Witnessing requires duration and proximity and the willingness to keep looking after the looking has become difficult, which it becomes almost immediately in a novel this committed to not looking away.

The practice has a source in Young’s life. The nightly reading to Minna Weissenbach, described in the previous chapter, was a witness of exactly this kind: full attention given to a world she did not share, kept up for about two years, without correction. Young’s creed, taken from Browning, was that “the poet is the great reporter.”

Young’s characters can also be imperfect witnesses. The characters who fail in Young's novel are not the ones who suffer. Suffering is not failure in Young. The characters who fail are the ones who stop witnessing, who replace genuine attention with a frame that makes the thing in front of them manageable at the cost of its actual complexity.

Young's fourth pillar is in deep, unacknowledged conversation with Simone Weil's ethics of attention. Weil argued that the foundation of ethics is not duty or utility or virtue but attention: the capacity to truly see the person in front of you, to give them the full weight of your regard without the distortions of projection or self-interest or the desire to make them into something more manageable than they actually are. For Weil, attention is an act of love, and love is not a feeling but a practice, the practice of keeping your eyes open when everything in you wants to look away or simplify or conclude.

Young arrives at the same place through fiction rather than philosophy, which means she arrives there with different tools and different evidence but the same essential claim.

The difference between them is instructive. Weil's ethics of attention operate between persons: you attend to the other, the one in front of you, the one whose suffering makes a claim on your regard. Young's witnessing operates at a different scale. It is not only interpersonal but intrapersonal: you witness yourself, your own plurality, your own grief, your own constructed reality, with the same attention you owe the other. Young's witnessing is Weil's attention made systemic. It is attention not as an individual ethical act but as a philosophical stance, a way of being in the world that shapes everything the self does and makes and builds.

A political culture organized around the witness would look radically different from what we have. What we have is organized around action: the decisive leader, the transformative policy, the revolution that changes everything, the election that finally gets it right. The political imagination is saturated with the fantasy of arrival. Young's system says: the story does not end. The problem is not the kind of thing that gets solved. The question is the quality of attention brought to the continuing. This does not mean political action is pointless. It means political action that is not grounded in genuine witnessing is dangerous. Every authoritarian movement in history has depended on the refusal of witnessing: the reduction of the complex plural self to a simple sortable category, the replacement of genuine attention with ideology, the decision that what cannot be processed by the frame does not need to be seen.

That is the fourth pillar. Stay in the room. Keep looking. Do not conclude.

The novel shows the witness at its fullest. In the early poems a hunter comes home with nothing because “he has stood all day and watched / The bright, unfrightened birds.” In “The Clinic” (1941), fifty faces watch a state execution through glass, and watching without stopping becomes complicity. In "Angel in the Forest", witnessing becomes a tool of power, and the missing witness becomes the way people vanish from history. In the novel itself a white detective will not look at the deaths of Black children. In "Harp Song for a Radical" the pillar splits between Pinkerton’s “The Eye That Never Sleeps” and Debs as spokesman for those “who had no words.” Across her work the witness grows more institutional and more political.

Phase One, Childhood and the Early Poems (1908 to 1934)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The clearest case closes the phase. In "Woodlands Far Removed" (1934) the hunter goes out to kill, the neighbors mock him, and he comes home with nothing because "he has stood all day and watched / The bright, unfrightened birds." Attention replaces harm. "Proud Lady" is vain not of rings but "Of orioles / And sky and cloud," a pride in what she notices. The farmer of "The Seeker" spends "hours and hours peering through a glass" at his postcards, the witness as dreamer.

Complication: the witnessing here is private and gentle. It has no institutions and no politics yet.

Phase Two, The Chicago Years, Prismatic Ground, and the Graduate Essays (1935 to 1937)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

This is the phase of the founding witness. For about two years, night after night, Young read aloud to Minna Weissenbach as the woman passed into opium dreams, refusing the drug each night, and stayed through balloon fish, golden cockerels, and near-comas. Dowling says she realized she was providing "the verbal passport" to another world. Her creed, taken from Browning, was that "the poet is the great reporter."

The poems complicate witnessing at once. In "Wild Deer" (1936) a woman means to burn a fire to frighten off the deer, and instead "She listened for their coming." In "Death in Lilliput" (1937) the giant stumbles into a tiny world, the lady dies, and only then does he see "The chrysalis... spotted wings": "Her eyes were shut / Where his were wide." He sees too late. In "The Dark Wood," being watched is the terror: "They all watched her." The "Two Angels," asked to testify about a dead girl, admit they "Cannot collect the melody / We have heard of but have not heard." "Daniel" (1937) gives his account "As a matter of record" and doubts his own faith.

Complication: the witness can arrive after the harm, the watcher can be the threat, and testimony can fail.

Phase Three, The Philosophical Poems (1938 to 1945)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"The Clinic" (1941) is the decisive poem. "Fifty faces peering against glassed screens" watch an execution in "the room the state has walled / Transparent to its glassy eyes." The warden weeps and writes "The man you kill tonight is six years old," and the poem asks, "Who will ever shut a final door / And watch the fume upon a face?" Witnessing without stopping is complicity. "The White Rat" (1943) makes the scientific gaze a cruelty: the rat runs "Caged in a theatre of emptiness," and the poem asks, "Does God with diamond eyes look down on these / For the purposes of what intrinsic studies?" In "The Parachutist" (1944), "So multiple is every witnessed lady / Who dissolves like vapor on a glass," and "Seeing, is it believing."

Attention as love appears too. "Flea Circus on Times Square" describes a showman who "would never mistake one flea for another," because to themselves "each is very different from the other." In "Night Watches" (1942), "we are the jewel-eyed watchers in space."

Complication: this phase turns witnessing toward institutions: the state execution chamber, the laboratory, a God who studies rats.

Phase Four, "Angel in the Forest" and “Complex Life and Complex Letters” (1945 to 1946)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Witnessing becomes a tool of power. Rapp is "the sole eye witness to the authentic Posey County angel." Elders at funerals have "no official function but to be eye witness." Of one killing: "the only eye witnesses to this murder were the murderers." Frederick Rapp listens to the Count "with the utmost intensity" and "came almost to fraternize with that very Devil." The record leaves people out: much is said of Owen's materialism "but not a word as to the lady and her spoons."

Complication: this is the phase's main turn. "The Clinic" showed useless witnesses. "Angel in the Forest" shows witnessing as authority, and the missing witness as the way people vanish from history.

Phase Five, "Miss MacIntosh, My Darling" (written from the mid 1940s, published 1965)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The form is witness: monologue after monologue, each figure given full attention without being answered. Vera's role is listening: "So I listened to Esther Longtree's tale of woe, listened all morning." Near the end she holds back her own grief, listening "as one might listen for one lonely heartbeat in the midst of the great silence."

The sharpest material is the white detective in Esther's mind, who solves white children's deaths while "the deaths of the little black children were not his business, there being so many and so unimportant." Esther's dead child Walter is "my black mystery whom the white detective will not find." Witnessing is refused along a color line, and the refusal is the injustice.

Complication: the witness keeps silent at a cost, and Vera wonders what might have happened had she spoken.

“The Clinic” showed witnesses who were complicit, and "Angel in the Forest" showed witnessing as a tool of power. The novel shows who goes unwitnessed, and names that refusal as the injustice.

Phase Six, The Occasional Prose, Interviews, and Self-Interpretation (1940s to 1995)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"The poet is the great reporter." "I'm a mirror." The essays prize witnesses: Miss Greenwood, who notices what Old James cannot see; Dorothy Caruso, who "takes down in shorthand the speech of her husband, living or dead"; the nurse Mrs. Houghton at Poe's cottage. "The 'type' is always a laziness of vision." She faulted Doris Lessing's Martha for an idealism that "begets violence," and Henry Miller for a "romantic individualism, which also blows trumpets and waves flags."

Complication: "I'm never much interested in individuals, even my closest friends." In "Old James," Miss Greenwood ends as "herself a collaborator." Young took sides: she wrote to Kennedy about atomic tests, recorded "Poets for Peace," and championed Debs. Moore's account of her treating an intermediary "like a lackey" shows that her attention was uneven.

Phase Seven, "Harp Song for a Radical" (written in her last decades, published 1999)

Pillar 4: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The book gives the pillar's fullest politics. On one side is Pinkerton's "The Eye That Never Sleeps," the spy McParlan among the Molly Maguires, Booth watching John Brown hang, and Lincoln's son removing "flaws of fact" from a manuscript. On the other is Debs, "the most radiant spokesman for the dead souls of America who could not speak and who had no words," and Thoreau's railroad sleepers: "Each one is a man." Family Bibles show records "with statistics altered or wholly missing," so that a person "might have been blotted out completely."

the-eleven-pillars:
The Eleven Pillars

Radical Immanence · The Marguerite Young Society

How the Pillars Came to Be

The Eleven Pillars on this site are the final form of a philosophy I developed over several years of reading Marguerite Young. They did not arrive all at once.

I found the first five pillars first:

  1. Not One Self
  2. Reality Is Constructed
  3. Grief Doesn’t End
  4. Witnessing Is the Core Ethical Act
  5. Build Anyway, Knowing It’s Temporary

Later I found five more that extended them:

  1. Unfinished Is Honest
  2. The Margins Reveal the Truth
  3. The Past Doesn’t Go Away
  4. Language Shapes What’s Possible
  5. The Sacred Is Here

The last pillar, the Crossing Point, came after that. It works differently from the others. It is the form that holds the first ten together, so it is not always counted alongside them.

Because the books on this site were written along the way, some of them reflect earlier stages. You will find books built on five pillars, books built on ten, and pillars called by older names such as the plural self, illusion as primary, recursive construction, or sedimentary time. The workbook Here Is Enough also gathers twelve teaching essays under the name pillars. I have left these books as they were written, because they show the philosophy taking shape.

Wherever the numbering or names differ, the Eleven Pillars are the final version.

art-12-art-inspired-by-miss-macintosh-my:
Art Inspired by Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

← Appendix: Daily Studio Affirmations for the Radical Immanent · Art When Here Is Enough

Coral Russell began making art after she retired, when her daughter sat down beside her and taught her how. The lessons were practical, pastel and pencil and acrylic, but the subject kept finding its way back to the same book. These pieces come from inside Marguerite Young’s novel, where a bald woman hides under a wig, an opium dreamer lies in her room, and every object seems ready to turn into something else.

Where a title carries a line from the novel, the page and line number come first and the words from the book sit inside quotation marks. Select any picture to open it full size.

1. 2-32 “all was imagination in this life”

Pastel. A red and orange flame sits inside a brown husk, held in rings of green that open onto a purple dark.

2. 14-45 Catherine and the Black Coachman

Acrylic. A blue cone and a black cone ride a smeared gray carriage of strokes while a white point drifts ahead of them across a field of fire.

3. 18-3 “the knowledge that the external world”
